WARRINGTON AND _DISTRICT SUNDAY

That much-coveted honour —the championship of Warrington and district --was comoeted for on the Cemetery Hotel greeu on Saturday afternoon, in the preseuce of a large crowd of enthusiasts. The result was a fine victory for G. Ball, jau., who in the final defeated J. W. Jolley by 21-10. Happily the weather conditions favoured the event and some smart bowling was witnessed. The Mayor (Councillor Dr. Joseph) was an interested spectator of the closing stages of the corup3titioa, and he afterwards handed the cup to the champion.

I IFTII ROI NI). The four g •mes in tLis round were, for the most part, productive of comfortable wins. T. Ellison ( Wnitecross ) led throughout against A. Forster (Cemetery), although the latier put forth strenuous efforts, and at oue time seemed like drawing level. The nearest he got, hoAever, was 9-10. Ellison made an auspicious statt, securing a couple of points horn his first end. Following another single for the White- cross man, Forster opeted his account but made very slow headway, Ellison having a lead of 7-3. Forster gradually improved his position, and at the 16th end the score stood at 10-9 in Ellison's favour. Then Elli,on ran to 14, Forster registering another single while his or ponent took his total to 16. Forster had another turn, but on reaching 13 he came to a stop and Ellis n had no difficulty in seeming his 21.

RYLANDS RECS V CEMETERY HOTEL. The first of the home and home matches between Cemetery Hotel and Rylandi Rees was played on the Gorsey-lane green on Saturday, and the match was a very interesting one. There were only two of the wireworkers woo Ir,st their games, and these were F Mider and W Daniels IA ho met E Gleave and A Forster respectively.

The brothers Langley were as usual in good form. W Langley met J Bibby, and a keen struggle ensued. They kept even nearly all the way and peeled with 4, 7, 12, but from the 19th ead, Biboy had a good run, alai afterfi ends led 17-14. Langley added Ave in the next four ends and led 19-1 S to score a good double on tne 30th end and in by three points.

It was only on the last few ends that El Williams (RI ands) showed any superiority over W Butterworth for at the 23rd end the players peeled with 15 eech. Williams bad a run of three to lead 18-16 at the 26th end. This proved to ba Biitterworth's last score and the wireman ran home by five points.

Leading 20-10 at the 20th end, H Eyes seemed to be well io for a sweeping win but before be could record his winning wood, Wood had made good use of the jack and run his score to 17 at the 30tb ei.d thus losing by only four points.
W Roughley (Rylands) played a good game against the individual merit competition %inner, liali, jun., and won 21-11 in 30 ends.
The Cemetery team will have a Lard struggle this afternoon for they have a heavy score to wipe off and the wireworkers ere strong 1 avourites-

CONSOLATION COMPETITION. LIBERAL CLUB V. PENKETH PARR. The villagers made the journey to Warrington on Saturday to meet the Liberal Club in the first home and home match in the anal for the consolation com- petition and alter many interesting games had been played they lost by 83 points, not one of their team having returned a winning card. Undoubtedly the best game of the afternoon was that between J Firth (Liberals) and Jeff Bowyer, for the Penkethite only lost by a couple of chalks inn ends. The Liberal Rot well away on the first ends and soon had a lead of 13-7. However, up to the 23rd end horn the 14th be only scored one chalk and Bowyer had run well with the block and led 18-14. One single on the 25th end was the villager's last score and with a good run of well- judged woods the Liberal just managed to win by the a couple ofsnoints.

Several of the Liberal players gained flne victories but the interest in the games was kept up by such as the one between B Webb (Liberal) and w shave. Playing an even game from the first the players repeatedly peelea and at the 29th end the !score was 17 each. On the nest length Shave gained a lead of two points but Webb bowled well to win 21-19.

J W Jolley (Bull's Head) gained an easy entrance tn the semi-final by defeating E Taylor (Senior Con- servatives) by 21-0. The players peeled at four but from that stage Taylor never made a formidable show, Jolley always having at least four points in hand.

There was a fairly interesting contest between J Holland (Senior Conservatives) and Nelson Fielding (Cemetery) and it took the Conservative a long time to get the measure of his opponent. The players were on even terms at 2 but Holland had a run of successes and led 74. Each man was playing well and at 8 the players again peeled. Holland, however, was in great form and had the upper band to the extent of 17-11. Fielding made another determined effort and at the twenty-sixth end was only one point behind 17-16. Holland got a couple of singles and Fielding's secy.° rose another point. Holland now ran to game and triumphed by 21-17.

It was, of course, Pxpacted that G. Ball, jun., would figuie in the penultimate stage, and he made no mistake about it. He was drawn against H. Williams (Rylands) WllO made a very poor show and was never dangProus foe. Ball always had the game well in hand and won by 21-11.
The Examiner, Saturday, August 17, 1912.
Furniture.

div.head: TUE SEMI-FINAL.
div.p: TUE SEMI-FINAL.

Excitement ran high when the semi-final was entered upon, for all the players are noted exponents of the game. T Ellison showed somewhat disappointing form against J Jolley, who had six points to hi credit when the Whitecross man had registered only one. Elliscn then forged ahead and for some time there was not much to chose between the players, although Jolley always maintained a slight lead. At the thirteenth end the pcisition was 10 9 in his favour. Befure Ellison got another wood in, Jolley had run to 16. Then be secured a single hut Ellison had the good fortune to notch a couple end the score stood at 17-12. Two more points were all that Ellisln placed to his credit and Jolley ran out winner by 21-14.

There was a battle royal between G. Ball, jun., and J. Holland and until well on in the game it was impossible to tell who would be the finalist. The con- testants peeled at 2 and 6, after which Ball had a run or successes and took his score to 0. The Conserva- tive.reprerentative, however, played gamely and at the fourteenth end led by 10-9. then Ball got a nice one in but Holland capped it with a couple. Ball again drew level and the players peeled at 12 and 13. Then Ball had all the luck for a spell and by really clever bowling got ahead to the tune of 19-13. Beforei he could make further progress Holland's score had risen to 16, but Ball then got the necessary couple and achieved a well-merited victory.

div.head: TIIE FINAL.
div.p: TIIE FINAL.

The final did not pro—vide ''''''' a tussle as had beau anticipated indeed for a time there was only one player in it, G Ball. He led by 11-1, but by degrees Jolley found his form and at the seventeeth end the players were equal with 13 apiece. They again peeled at 14, after which Ball put in some brilliant bowling and carried the score to 20-14 in his favour. One end was so close that it was impossible to tell at a glance whose wood was "in " and on a measure- ment being taken, the decision %vent in favour of Ball. Jolley took his total to 1 when Ball secured the winning point and was warmly acclaimed champion for 1912.

div.head: PRESENTATION OF THE CUP.
div.p: PRESENTATION OF THE CUP.

- - - - On the completion of the final the handsome cup, which is the gift of Suits Limited, was presented to the champion by the Mayor. Mr. G. F. FREEMAN' briefly requested his Worship to perform this pleasing duty. The MAYOR thanked the association for having exhibition of bowls. He could not claim expert given him the opportunity of witnessing knowledge, but he ,believed the final must such a fine have proved most Interesting to the best connoisenrs of the game. He was a great admirer of out-doorlsports, and he considered bowls was one of the best games. they could possibly have. (Hear, heir.) It was within the reach of all ; it was quite as interesting as golf or cricket ; and it served the purpose of msintaining the health of the body and the mind, as well as training the eye and the hand. He believed there was a proverb—and if there was not there ought to be—to this effect : " Slow at play, slow at work." Those who were good sportsmen and acquired proficiency at such a game of bowls must also be good workers, and he maintained that they must he thoroughly steady in their lives if they were to come up to the standard of play they had witnessed that afternoon. (Applause.) He congratulated the winner and the runner-up upon having afforded such an Interest- ing and pleasurable game. (Applause).

Mr. G. BALL, jun., in accepting the cup, said he was proud to be the winner, but at the same time he sympathised with his opponent. It had been a pleasant gatoe and if Mr Jolley bad been victorious, he (Mr. Ball) would have been the first to congratulate him. (Applause) Mr. T. P. BRADSHAW, in proposing a vote of thanks to the Mayor, said they greatly appreciated his kindness in attending, when he had so many official duties to attentl to. His Worship must, however, have been well repaid by a game of howls which it had been worth anybody's while to witness. The association was doing all in its power to further the healthy recreation of the workingmen of Warrington and district. (Applause.) Mr J WILLETT seconded and said the contest had been one of the best he had ever witnessed ; the play had been so consistent. He hoped that would not be the last time they would heave the pleasure of the Mayor's company on the bowling green. When they could get toe leading public men of the town to patronise the bowling world,it was a sign that they were going in the right direction. (Applause.) Mr JoLLEY, the runner up, supported and thanked the officials for the excellent way in which the competition bad been conducted.

The vote was heartily pissed. The MAYOR, in iesponding, said it wis a real enjoy- ment to him to witness such games—an enjoyment he was sorry he did not take to earlier in life. He bad, however, been greatly occupied with work, but he would new have to consider the advisability or revers- ing the procedure and coming amongst the bowlers more frequently. He should be very glad to be an adept at the game—in fact he would give something to be able to play as wallas Messrs. Ball and Jolley. (Applause.)

div.head: Warrington Works Association. SEMI-FINALS
div.p: Warrington Works Association. SEMI-FINALS

Th. final stages of almost all the bowling competi- tions in town have now been reached and on Satur- day the semi-final games in the competition promoted by the Warrington Works Association were played befere a large attendance on the Horse and Jockey Green. As we predicted last week both the Asylum team and Crosfields No. 5 were thrown out and the finalists to meet on the 24th are Fletchers Moulders and Howley Tannery.
FLETCHERS MOULDERS V COUNTY ASYLUM. Handicapped at 45 the Asylum men started 25 points behind their opponents, but they made a determined stand and eventually only lost by 23 points.
Darbyshire led the way for the Moulders when he disposed of A Peckett by 15-5 in 33 ends. The moulder was in good form and played his woods well.

J Jones (Wiowick) played a winning game against J Vernon to win finally by two points in 19 ends. Vernon had the best of the first 10 ends and led 9-5 and this he increased to a lead of 13-9 at the 10th end. Jones got the block and ran up to game with three beautiful doubles.
A Randles, the captain of the Moulders team had hard luck in his game with %V Rudge for after having led 10-6 at the 12th end he lost ny 11-13 after 20 lengths.

Playing steadily all throngh his game with J Ilankinson (Winwick), J Isherwood gained a praise- worthy victory, for, after having been in arreais from the first to the 16th end when the game was 9-10 against him he pulled up exceedingly well to win by three points. From the 16th to the filst end he got two doubles and two singles to his opponents one double.

With a lead of 10-7 at the 14th end J Broadhurst was easily the favourite against E Harper (Winwick) but victory was not to be easily gained and the Winwick man showed that he was a very tough customer. With only 10 points to his credit and his opponent only wanting one for game, Harper got the blocs and played his woods so well that at the 23rd end he had peeled with 14. Broadhurst, however, managed to get one in on the next length to win by the barest possible margin.
The Winwick men thoroughly expected S Welsby pulling it oft when he met P Lyall and their expecta- tions were justified for after 22 well contested ends he won by 15-12.
F Isherwood (Moulders) did not get going at all in his genie with 0 Jones who won at the 13th end by 15-4

Pealing at 8, 12 and 14, J Cooper (Winwiok) and W Barton were indeed a well-matched couple and the game was keenly watched, for all were eager to see which of the two would win. With the score equal at the 19th end and only one wante3 for game the excite- ment was intense. Barton just managed to get the winner by a few inches.

CROSFIELD'S NO. 5 V. HOWLEY TANNERY. It is a rattier singular thing that the Ilowleyites finally won by five points, whim) was the exact number of points they had to concede their opponents. There were some run-away wins on either Ride.

One of the few exciting games was that between J. Hands •(Crosfields) and Jack Ditchfleld for the latter only won by two points in 20 ends. Hands pulled up remarkably well from the 10th end when be was 5-10 in arrears. At the 17th end Ditchtield only wanted one to his opponents five, hut however at the 19th end he bad only a lead of 14-13 and the last woods were keenly anticipated. Ditetteld got in with one ,which was the winner.

The captain of the Howley team did rather better than the opposing skipper, for he won i 5-14 over J Woodward. Everyone thought the Sospery man had the game in the hollow of his hand, for at the 12th end he led 10-5. Those in the know of Clare's st lying powers and surprise woods contented themselves to wait and see. Things did look black against the Howleyite at the 20th end, ;Own he had ten points on the card sod his opponent only wanted one for game. With the jack in band be set some good lengths end rained a single and two doubles to win by the odd chalk.

The tospery captain was up against James Ditchfleld who was in fine form. Matters were fairly even at the beginning but from the Bth to the 13th ends the How. leyite made headway to gain a led of 11-6. Overend then had a turn and at the 18th end the game was only Id.ll against him. Two singles on the nest lengths put Ditchfleld home amidst the lutid cheers of his sup- porters.

There Wa3 some doubt as to which team had really won for the scoring bad bePn so alternate, hut ths Elowleyite's did not fail to let themselves go when it wss known that their side had entered the flual by five points.
A good attendance is expectsd on the 21th when the final will take plact and the match should be a very good one.
Several games in the iniividual merit competition were played and the results will be found iu another column.

div.head: FOOTBALL NOTES.
div.p: FOOTBALL NOTES.
Getting Ready at Wilderspool.

Warrington Football Club are making every Treparation for the opening of the season at Hudders- Ileld on Monday, September 2nd. The players have 'ettl"7ll commendable keenness, and there was one of e best gstherinas for practice on Monday evening lhat the officials have any record of. About 25 men (I°.ntled the jersey and proceeded to work the Btlfluess out of their limbs with running and punting.

-- Among the familiar faces were those of Dickenson (;110 is looking forward to a well-earned benefit), brooks, who has got rid of his injury and hopes to B,a.v„e a good season; Bradshaw, with a knee which requires teeing; Renwick, Waywell, Daintith Young Jolley, all as fit as the pro- al fiddle. z There was another turn out for training on Wed- and to-day there will be a practice match. . div.head: WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL.
div.p: WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL.
OFFICIALS' SALARIES RAISED.
WARRINGTON'S LOW DEATH RATE.

There were discussions on a variety of topics at the meeting of the Warrington Town Council held at the Town Hall on Tuesday evening. 'The Mayor (Councillor Dr. Joseph) presided and there were also present : The Deputy-Mayor (Alderman Forshaw), Aldermen A Bennett, John Evans James Evans, W Pierpoint end J Smethurst, Councillors G Archer, T H Ashcroft, W H Hellion, T Birtles, .3 Broadhurst, T Chantler, E Cunnington, .3 Dickenson, J Halliwell, C Jackson Holmes, W II J Jenkins, F T Lashford, Dr McKee, J Pemberton, H Roberts, J Sankey, J Skeiland, T S Steel, 0 Toole, Messrs J L Whittle (town clerk), A T Hallaway (deputy town clerk), W S Haddock (gas engineer), .1 M Murray (director of education), Dr G W N Joseph (assistant medical officer), and J Gray (water engineer). PROPOSED EXTENSION OF SANKEY SANA fORIUM. . .
The Health Cominitree-b-a-d.c—on-sldered the question of providing consumptive sanatoria under the Insurance Act.

At a meeting on July 10th it was decided not to join in the scheme for a joint sanatorium for the boroughs of South-West Lancashire. The Borough Surveyor was instructed to prepare an estimate of the cost of pro- viding new pavilions at Sankey in accordance with the report of the Medical Officer. A Sub-committee was appointed to deal with emergency cases of tuberculosis. The question of the provision of sanatoria under the Insurance Act was further debated at a meeting on July 17th and a report and estimates of the probable cost of alterations and extensions at Sankey sanatorium necessary to meet the requirements laid down by tbe Departmental Committee on Tuber- culosis were considered. The further consideration of the matter was deferred pending a meeting with the Local Insurance Committee. The Medical Officer was authorized to act as temporary medical adviser to the Insurarce Committee on sanatoria benefits. The follow- ing day the Committee met the Sanatorium Sub- committee with reference to the provisi n and adminis- tration of sanatoria benefits under the Insurance Act d it was resolved that a charge of El 14s per catient per week be made for the temporary treatment at Sankey of tuberculosis cases. The consideration of the ,(Permanent arrangements under the Act was adjourned and the Sanatorium Sub-committee was invited to inspect the Sankey pavilions on July 24th. The Health Committee requested the Borough Surveyor, after consultation with the Medical Officer, to prepare specifications, plans and estimates for the purposes of the extension of :Sankey sanatorium in order to comply with the requirements of the Insurance Act. Alderman JAMES EVANS, in moving the confirmation of the minutes oh the committee, said the whole ques- tion of the sanatoria was in a transition condition, and it would, therefore, be as well if he did not make any remarks about it that evening.
WARRINGTON'S LOW DEATH RATE. ONE ADVANTAGE OF UNSEASONABLE WEATHER.

Alderman JAMES EVANS, continuing, said the de.th- rate of the borough for the past four weeks had been only 7.7. It was a record that had never before been reached in the Borough. Their little " misdoings " of the past had been made much of, when they did not. figure so favourably es now, and were sent to the ends of the earth, but now that there was something that might be made some capital of, the same parsons might let the people know that Warrington was not the city of darkness some had portrayed it. Councillor JENKINS seconded the passing of the minutes. _ _

The MAYOR said there was no doubt it was a matter of great congratulation that the death-rate was so low. One important factor in the death-rate was the weather. This cold, stormy, disagreeable weather often acted well in the matter of health, whereas in very hot weather the death-rate would probably have gone up. At the same time what the Alderman had said showed that the general sanitary conditions of the town were good. When they suotracted from the death-rate diarrhma and other complaints set up by the hot weather and decomposition of food, it showed that the general sanitary conditions of the town were very satisfactory. (Hear, bear). The minutes were then approved. COUNCILLOR BROADHURST CHANGES HIS OPINION. HIS FIRST DEPUTATION.

On the minutes of the Sanitary Works Committee appeared a report on "The Conference of Cleansing Superintendents." Councillor BROADHURST said be had been of opinion that money spent on deputations had not been well spent, but in reference to the Conference named in the minutes, some of his impressions had been wiped away. This was the first time he had ever represented a com- mittee on a deputation. .

Councillor PEMBERTON : Shame. (Laughter.) Councillor fluoADHuresT said it was a surprise to him to find that Warrington had nothing to learn from the grent city of Manchester in connection with sani- tary matters. (Hear, hear.) Manchester prid more for horses than Warrington did, but he did not think it got the same return for its money. Warrington aiso occupied a good position with regard to the destructors. At the same time we might learn a lesson in the cleans- ing of the grids. In Manchester what was got out was emptied into a box. while in Warrington it was put on the ground until collected, and that was not beneEdal, as children were in tie hatiit of playing about it and might contract diseases in tb.st way. (Hear, bear.) The minutes were approved. TAR-SPRAYING EXPERIMENTS.

The Paving and Sewerage Committee had resolved that the Borough Surveyor be authorised to hire a machine and to tar-spray Manchester-rosd, Winwick- road and Bold-greet. Councillor SKELLAND asked ithst similar treatment should be accorded to Bewsey-street. He contended that there was not a dustier street in Warrington, and it was impossible for householders to keep their rooms clean. _ .

Alderman SMETHURST supported the suggestion. Councillor BHUTAN asked whether the time had not come when, instead of hiring a machine, they ought to buy one. The tar-spraying of various roads in the neighbourhood of Warrington had been attended with complete success. He moved that the minute be referred back with a view to considering the advis- ability of purchasing a machine. ColloCillOr SKELLAND seconded. Alderman BENNETT said part of Manchester-roadthad been tar-sprayed with exoellent results. There had not been the slightest trouble since. Councillor PEMBERTON said a great deal depended upon the way in which the tar-praying was done. The roads mentioned in the minutes had not been selected because they particularly needed treatm-nt—the use of the machine was only an experiment. When the com- mittee did ddcide upon something definite, it wanted to securelthe best results. Many authorities had made an " awful hash " of tar spraying experiments, with the result that some people had declared that the system was no use. If properly done, however, it was an excellent thing. Coundillor BELLIAN said there had been sufficient experiments in various parts or the country to convince anyone of authority of the wisdom of buying a machine.
The amendment was withdrawn, Councillor Milan intimating that if nothing definite was done, he should bring torward a special resolution.

ST. ELPHIN'S PARK. GARDEN OR PLAYGROUND? At a meeting of the Town Hall,Parks and Baths Com- mittee, a deputation consisting of residents in Salis- bury-street and neighbourhood attended and complained of the noise end annoyance caused by children playing in St. Elpbin's Recreation Ground, and requested that it be forthwith closed preparatory to the laying out of the same as pleasure gardens. After a full considera- tion the deputation were informed that as soon as the footbridge over the river at Howley had beam com- pleted the recreation ground would be temporarily closed. Councillor ARCHER moved an amendment that the minute be referred hack. He said that at the last meeting of the Council they herd with what pleasure the opening of the park as a recreation ground had been %%slowed by the inhabitants of the School Brow and Dalton Bank districts. The children bad taken full advantage of the privilege and he thought the com- mittee might have weighed the matter in the balance a little longer and have allowed the children to have the benefit of the ground. There were not too many recreation grounds and open spaces in Fairfield Ward and the pleasure of many children ought not to he sacrificed tor the sake of a few residents in Salisbury- street.

Alderman BENNETT agreed that there were not enough Jecreation grounds in the neighbourhood—indeed that WBB true all over.the town. They were, however, apt to lose sight of the tact that, after all, it was not merely playgrounds for children that were required. They were more essential than anything else but the Council ought not to overlook the claims of the 'welts. It would be nice to have a garden in St. Elphin's Park where the older people could sit and read or walk about quietly sun peacefully. The true ideal was to cater for all sections and classes. Councillor PEMBERTON seconded Councillor Archer's amendment. He said it was understood that the open spaces were required for the children to play upon. St. Elphin's Park was the most expensive piece of land the Crewel I ever bougett ; they gave three times as much as it was worth. For the smile money they could have obtained tour times toe amount of ground space in the vinicity. lhe older people woo wisued to sit and read could use the forms that were provided round the bowling green. It would bean abominable thing if the children were deprived of the playground. Alderman JAMEs EVANS said there should be open spaces for chiloren, but the grown-up people were also eotitled to consideration. St. Erphin's Park seemed a suitable place to provide a little resort where the older people could sit rind read. Councillor ASHCROFT hoped the park would be thrown open to the cuildien, as there were hundreds who liven so far away from the Howley Briage that they would not, be able to Wake Use of Victoria Park. They might also erect a monument to Aldermen Bennett in commemoration or his efforts to keep the children out of the park. (L 'tighter.) . . .

, Councilior BIRTLES said that if the land were laid Out in the same way as the land adjoining the bowling green in Victoria hal( it would he satisfactory. Councillor liftoepinntsT said it would be a great shame to debar the cuildren from playing in the park.

If the committee wished to r,eautcry ;hi spot so that the worSing,nan could sit and enjoy his pipe there, they might comiueuce with the recreetioa grouud at Saukey which was a wending disgrace LO them. Alderman BEN:eerr pointed out that in connection with the new sehool to be erected hear Paogate-lane, they had bought a pie:e of land which would serve the purpose of a children's playground. TR° MAYOR said he should vote against the amend- ment, not because of any waet of interest in the children—he gave way to nobody in that respect—but he certainly thought there ought to he a limit and that adults should also be considered. The sp,ce available in St Elphih's Park was too small for a cnildren's play- ground and its use for that purpose would intertere with the beauty of the spot. It was at present a romantic bit of landscape. He must give the committee one crumb of consolation. They were often slated, but he thought the way in which they bed laid out the bowling green and grounds was very good and that, it further developed, it would add to the beauty of the scene. Councillor SEEL-LAND said the claims of Bewsey Ward, in regard to open spaces, ought to be consteerea. Councillor STEM. supported the use of the park as a children's playground. A great many children in the neighbourhood of School Brow and Battersby-lane, who at present had no recreation ground, would have an opportunity of enjoying themselves. Councillor JACKSON HOLMES said that at the last meeting he stated tuat his sympathies were always a ith the children, and that he was glad they had a place like Sc. Elphin's Park to play in. There were parts of Fairfield Ward—such as Brick-street, Battersuy-lane and Crossley-street—where there was no possible chance of providing a recreation ground. ,He heartily supported the idea that there should be a playground in that ward. It was a little difficult to say wnether St. Elphin's Park was an ideal spot for the purpose There were two classes ,of people to be considered—the old and the young—and whether they could have it com- bined park and recreation groudd he did not quite see. There would be no harm in relerring toe ndati.er bane fur further consideration. Councillor BIRYLKS said they should not overlook the danger to the children lions the rn...tor and tram car traffic which passed the para. The voting was as follows :—For the amendment : Councillors Steel, Ashcroft, Broadhurst, Toole, Jackson Holmes, Pemberton, Archer, Cunniugton, Skellauct and Cuantler-10. Against : Tue Mayor, Aldermen James Evans and Bennett, Couucillors Hallieell and Sankey —5.

_ Alderman JAMES EVANS said that if the amendment was persisted in, the result might be that no tar spray- ing would be done. No doubt Bewsey-road eouid be added to the list of the thoroughfares to be experi- mented upon. COM:16110r ROBERTS said the question of tar spraying had long passed the experimental stage. It was per- fectly absurd to put forward the idea that the committee might make a mistake with regard to the machine they might purchase. If they did make a mistake, they would do it with their eyes wide open. There was any amount of information and practical evidence within a few miles of Warrington to prove that tar spraying was being done Bucceasfully and very advantageously. If it were only with the object of keeping the dust down, it would be well worth while tar spraying the streets. CoUncillOr PEMBERTON said ,Councillor Roberta wee quite wrong ; the faots were dead against him. He tthe speaker) could prove all he had said. Grappenhall- road, Stockton Heath, was tar sprayed by the County Council but the experiment was a ghastly failure. He would not be a party to buying a machine to achieve similar results in Warrington ; it would be throwing money down the gutter, Councillor TOOLE said ha understood that one of the best machines on the market was being hired for the experiment. The Council ought not 10 refer the minute back but should first see how the machine did its work. Councillor BlcurAAN said the roads he had praise were sprayed by the identicil machine that was employed on the road referred to by Councillor Pemberton. The only difference was that the other roads were treated in a better manner bsfore they wars sprayed, end Councillor Pemberton knew it, too. Councillor PEMBERTON : No, I don't. The MAYOR said there was a difference between rural and town districts with regard to tar-spraying. Tbe disadvantage ,in the rural districts was that it tended t, destroy vegetation and fishes. They had no fishes in Warrington, he believed. (A VOICE : "Yes we have and ANOTHER VOICE: "In the market.") On every other ground tar-spraying must ha an advantage. Councillor Bellian ssid that if he had an avanranoe that the committee would proceed with tle matter enrneatly, be was prepared to withdraw the amendment. Up to the present they bad made no effort. Conncillor Pemberton: I think that reflection of Councillor Bellian's, is unfair and improper. There has been no demand for a tar-spraying machine and I think it h 3 an unwarranted attack on the committee.
The Examiner, Saturday, August 17, 1912.
engines, and with respect to other organizltion's details His report is to be printed and considered by the committee. The minutes were approved without discussion. INCREASES OF SALARY. .

Five increases of salary to Corporation officials to date from the let inst. were recommended by the General Purposes Committee. The proposed increases were:—Mr A M Ker, deputy borough surveyor, from £250 to £3OO per annum :Mr T H Spinks' assistant town clerk, from £2OO to £250 per annum ; Mr Alfred Starkey, registration clerk, from £l4O to £156 per annum; Mr Walter Sumner. local taxation clerk, from £l2O to £l3O per ROMEn ; and Mr HS Essenhigh, clerk, from £lOl to £ll4 per annum. The Mayor, in moving the adoption of the minutes, said the increases were all well-merited on the grounds with which all the members were familiar. Alderman FORSHAW seconded nnd said each of the officials named was a worthy servant of the borouah. Councillor PEMBERTON did Lot approve of the salaries being raised to the extent it was proposed to raise them. He agreed with what the Mayor and Deputy-Mayor had said about the officials. There was no doubt they were excellent, but advances of VA a year were altogether too great. There wero many tradesmen in leading shops who were not earning any- thing like the amount that these officials were, and they had all C-e worries arid anxieties of the bipiness. Advances of £25 to Messrs Ker and Spinke would have been ample and be moved an amendment that the minute be referred back. No private firm would think of raising salaries in that way. With regard to Mr. Starkey, he (the speaker) understood he did private work, outside his occupation. The MAYER : I believe he has given that up. Councillor PEMBERTON: If thot is so, I won't say any more about it. A committee was appointed to inquira into the matter. It met once, and we heard nothing more about it. Like many other Corporation committees, it has died a natural death. The Council ought to consider that rates of 8s in the £ were detri- mental to the interests of the town, ea they made manufacturers hesitate about setting up works here. Councillor CUNNINGTON seconded the amendment. Councillor TooLE hoped the Council would not send the minute back, but grant the increases. (Hear, hear.) He was sorry that many members of the Council had taken their departure. If they had been men enough they would have remained and voted on the question that evening. He believed the ratepayers were desirous that the servants of the Corporation, in every depart- ment,should receive adequate recognition of their work. Councillor BIRTLES said the Corporation had valuable servants in those named in the minutes, and it was to the interests of the Corporation that they should be paid well. He hoped Councillor Pemberton would not press his amendment. (Hear. hear.) Councillor CHatemeß : Is there any maximum in regard to these salaries ? Tee MAYOR : There is no maximum. _

. Councillor ASH CROFT said an advance of Li a week to an official who was alreedy reoei7illg .£4 a week was too much. No firm in Warrington would grant it. The speaker also endorsed Councillor Toole's expression or disapproval of the action of those members who had " slunk oqt " before the vote was taken. The MAyolt said that evidently those who were absent either agreed with the advances or their opposi- tion was so slight that they did not think it would be worth while to be present. The voting was as follows For the amendment : Councillors Skelland, Ashcroft, Chantler, Pemberton and Cunningt on-5. Against : The Mayor, Aldermen Forshaw' Smethurst, Bennett, John EVlaB and James Evans, Councillors Steel, Toole, Billies, Sankey, Jackson Holmes and Jenkins-12.
The increases were therefore approved. Councitlor ASHCROFT : 1 hope the mune will be recorded. _ _
The MAYOR: We are not ashamed of our names. _ .
_ Councillor TooLE : I think the names of those who left the room should also be recorded, if possible. The klAyou : It is not in the standing orders. Otherwise it might have been done.

div.head: ;Die minute was therefore referred back. THE GAS PROFITS.
div.p: ;Die minute was therefore referred back. THE GAS PROFITS.

Alderman JOHN EVANS, in moving the adoption of the minutes'of the Gas Committee, said toe cntef item was the acceptance of tenaers tor about thirty thou- sand tons of coal, which was a portion of what they required for the year, at an increased price of 2s. per ton on the once last year. The committee migtit therefore have a difficulty in niaintaing tea profits at such an abnormal level as last year. There were several reasons tor the increase in the profits on the Gels Department. During the coal striae it was necessary to break into the stock of coal which had been Wog at the Gas Works for many years, and which was bought at 7s. 61 per ton. That coal had been written down every year and the depreciated rate in a great measure accounted for the profit, added ti the increased demand for gas during the year: Since the stock of coal was broken into curing the coal strike several fires had broken out through sp-intaneous combustion, which necessitated the emptying of that store and replenisaing it again by at least six thousand tons in addition to the yearly supply. The minutes were confirmed. COUNCILLOR BROADHURST'S PLE 1 FOR THE SMITHS.
Councillor BROADHURST said that in view of the fact

that tue committee had reduced the price of gas to con- sumers, would it not also be possible t) reduce the price of washed breese, or small coke, used by the smiths ? The Corporation had charged him (the speaker) 235: for 23 cwts., thus maintaining the increased price . . . . .

levied during the coal strike. He asked the committee to to grant a reduction, so that the blacksmiths could work more economically. Councillor PEMBERTON Is Councillor Broadhurst thinking about himself or the ratepayers if it is the ratepayers, we get as much as we loin for the coke. Ttlo MAYOR : He is a ratepayer himself. Counoillor PEMBERION : Yes, and he is a smith too: (Laughter). Of cJurse, ne is justified in buying in the cheapest market.

div.head: HOWLEY BIDE.
div.p: HOWLEY BIDE.

Alderman SMETHURST, in moving the adoption of the minutes of the Bridges Committee, siid he was pleased to hear how highly the new Howley Bridge was appre- ciated by the public. Last Thursday no fewer than between 2,000 and 3,900 people passed over it—which was something to be proud of. (Hear, heir). He suv- gested that a small piece of land in the park should be railed off and covered with sand, in order that tie children might dig in it. Toe MANOR: Warrington. by the sea. (Laughter)..

- , Councillor ARcHitit said he was sorry that at 'the opening ceremony no representative of Howley Ward had the opportunity of tendeling the thanks of the residents in that locality for the blon conferred upon them. From all quarters he had heard how much the bridge was appreciated and regret was expressed that it was not provided many years ago. The MAYOR said that, after the proceedings were over, he regretted that one of the members for Howley Ward had not been asked to speak. Councillor JACKSON Horzugs said he thought Fair- field Ward ought to have been recognised at the ceremony, as it was also greatly interested its the new

bridge. Alderman JOHN EVANS said the means of access to the bridge were somewhat of a puzzle and he had on many OCORSiODS been asked the way to it. Alderman BENNEIT said that if any memb era of the Council had any lingering doubt as t, the absolute necessity for town planning, he advised them to go to Howley and study the question in the light of what Alderman Evans had said. Alderman SM ETHURST said he was pleased the public bad awakened to the necessity for a De./ rsad to the bridge. He had been fighting for it in the Cmnoil for four or five years. The minutes were appro,-ed. WHO SHOT THE SWAN?

Speaking on the minutes of the Town Hall, Parks and BAthe Committee, Alderman BENNETT expressed his abhorrence of the cowardly and stupid action of the man who shot one of the beautiful swans on the river. He had been waiting with some eagerness to hear that the culprit had been apprehended, but unfortunately he had not been discovered. He hop3d the man would fial that he had earned the execration of every rigat- minded person in the borough. TEM FIRE BRIGADE EQUIPMENT.

div.head: WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS. Rev. A. M. Mitchell and Alcoholic Stimulants.
div.p: WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS. Rev. A. M. Mitchell and Alcoholic Stimulants.
ALLEGED EXTRAVAGANCE.

The fortnightly meeting of the Warrington Board of Guardians was held at the Workhouse on lVedneeday, Mr E L Bent presiding. There were also present : Mrs Simpson, Miss Broadbent, Revs T R Matthews and A M Mitchell, Messrs A J Jolley (d.puts-chairman), 3 Billinge, A Brooks, G M4tber, W Houpton, J A Rnshworth, W C Brooks, J A Hughes, A Bottomley (clerk), R I Partridge (assistant clerk), and W J Brown (master).

STIMULANTS IN THE IIoSPITAL. In reply to the Rev. A M Mitchell, the Clerk stat,.d that the requisitions to be sanctioned by the Board included stout, whisky, wine and half a bottle a champagne. The Rev A M 1111Tc}trmi said that in the teturns submitted some time ago the amount to be expended on stimulants was put down at .4120 a year. At the rate they were going on they would be very much in advance of that sum at the end of the present year. Quite recently, prominent members of the British Medical Association, notably Sir James Barr, had declared that to administer alcohol in hoSpitale was wore or less useless. . . .

Mr RUSH WORTH : There are different opinions. The Rev A ?I MITCHELL : Toe British Medical Assoc ation was pretty unanimous a'iout it. Having quoted statements of Sir James Barr and others, the rev gentleman submitted that the Board was spending money very extravagantly. They ought to curtail and no,lto keep increasing the amount of expenditure on alnholic drinks. The CHAIRAIAN said stimulants were only given as medicine, waen ordered by the medical officer. The Rev A M MiTchELL : I quite understand that. lam speaking about its use as a medicine. We never see the doctor's book. No doubt a record is kept, but I think that record ought to be submitted to the Board. If lam not mistaken, I mentioned the matter some time ago, and there was some sort of understanding that the boos should he submitted.

The CLERK : You think wrongly, Aft Mitchell. The CHAIRMAN : It has not tqaert customary to piece the book on the table, but you can obtain this informa- tion privately if you wish it, instead of bringing it before the Board.
The Rev. A. M. MITCHELL : All these things ought to be done in a proper, businesslike way—not one member running to the doctor or somebody else to get information.

The CLERK said Mr Mitchell might desire the pro- duction of the book, but the majority of the Ward might be against Ulf toe Board gave an instruction for the book to be placed on the table it would, of course, be complied with. The Bev. A. M. MITCHELL said he did not think any member of the Board had the right or legal power to object to any book kept by an official being placed on the table.
Mr HOUGHTON : What do we appoint a medical man for ?—to attend to the patients in the hospital. The Rev. A. M. MITCHELL : Not to provide them with alcohol.

Mr. IioUGHTON: We must respect his recommenda- tions. I don't Walt there is anything excessive done here. The Workhouse Master will bear me out that no stimulants are administered, except when ordered by a medical man. The MASTER : That is quite right. Mr. HOUGHTON said his own private medical attendant, vvno was a teetotaller, ordered him to take champagne during his recent illness. "If it had not been for that" he added "I should not have been here now.,, Mr. INIATKER: These discussions only arise from a fad of Mr Mitchell's. • The Rev. A. M.NIITCHELL : No, no. Mr.MATHER : We know very well that alcohol has its uses, although it can be abused. Mr Mitchell makes a point of always attacking alcohol. I guarantee he is not more temperate in his habits than I am. Why should he always be " picting "at alcohol ? We can only put it down as a fad. He never tackles tea, which is doing more berm to-day than alcohol. He Eays nothing about starving the body with fruit and that sort ot thing, to the injury of the brain. (Laughter.) The sooner this sort of thing is dropped the better. The CHAIRMAN : I agree with Mr Houghton and Mr Mather that this is taking up the time of the Board nnnecessarily. I wish you (Mr Mitchell) would refrain from bringing such questions forward. The Rev A A NIITCHEI.I. gave notice that at the next meeting he would move that the medical officer's boog be produced at each Board meeting.,

HOSPITAL DIET V. PRISON FARE. The Rev. A. M. MITCHELL inquired whether the hospital diet included bread about an inch thick and butter or margarine. He bad been told by one who had been in the hospital that, he would much prefer to be on prison diet than on hospital diet in the Warr inuton Union. That was a strong statement and it was right that the Board shoufd Inquire into it. Mr. MATHER : Before we take any notice of that statement, we ought to have the name of the person who made it.

Mr. A. BitooKs : And when he was in prison and what for. (Linghter). RusirWORTII : Can we interfere with the diet ? The CHAIRMAN : The diet is laid down by the Local Government Board and we cannot alter it. Mr. MATH ER pointed out that the diet table was in the Batirdroorn acid could be inspected by any memoer. The CH AIRAIA N: Mr. Mitchell perfectly understands that, but he is always bringing these matters forward to make himself highly popular. It is most antioying. The Rev A M Mrrcirni, You have no right to make a statement like that. The CHAIRMAN : Your own common seose ought to ' tell you that it is ridiculous to talk like that. rhe Rev A M MITCHELL rose to speak again, where upon M oUo.cirrox exclaimed "I protest, sir." The Rev A M MITCHELL: You may protest, but I protest Isti to You are goofitnhgattokdinodt.his, Mr Chair- man—to make The matter then dropped.
PARGITE OFFICIALS' SUPERANNUATION.
The Cot tsge Homes Committee considered the,ques-

tiou of the superannuation allowance to be grante;d to Mr end Mrs Fairhurst, and unanimously recommended the Finance Committee to add ten years to the service which Mr and Mrs Fairhurst have actually seried, for the purpose of fixing the allowance. The minutes were approved. GRATUITY TO THE ASUSTANT :MASTER.

REV A M MITCHELL AND THE LATE MAsTER'S ILLNESS. At a meeting of the Finance Committee it was resolved that, subject to the sanction of the Local Government Bcard, a gratuity of £5 be paid to Mr Moss, assistant roaster of the Workhouse,in recognrtion of the extra duties performed by him during the illness of the late master, and also for the period during which he was appointed by the Board as acting master. The Rev A M MITCHELL asked whether any of the extra expense ihedrred during the long Blues.; of the late master was met by Mr Awhery, or were the expenses of the illness entirely charged to the Union ? The CLERK : If it is the Board's desire, I think I can answer the question.. . . . .

The CHAIRMAN : Is it the Board's wish that the Clerk answer the question ? (Cries of " aye.") Mr JOLLEV : What is meant by the question? The CLERK : It is putting me in this position—that I heve to tell Mr Mitchell and tee other reemoers present, something which Mr Awbery has told myself and others privately. The question of his private lite has nothing to do with the Board. Mr MATHER. : I don't think that is Mr Mitchell's question. His question is: Has Mr Awbery paid any- thing towards the expenses—what you may call public expenditure, on nursing and extra remuneration for the staff.

Mr JOLLEY : I should like to ask another question. Will Mr Mitchell explain whether there was any addi- tional expenditure incurred at all ? The Rev AAi MITCHELL : Was there not a nurse specially assigned to Mr Awbery during tivit time and must there not have been some incidental expenses ? The Guardians paid lor some assistance—something like 30s a week and rations for a special man. I quite agree that Mr Moss ought to have some recognition, from whatever source it comes, but my point is that it is Mr Awbery who ought to mace the recognition. Mr W C BROOKS : Was it not set out in Mr Awbery's conditions of appointment that he should have medical attendance in case of illness ? . _

Mr JOLLEY : I respectfully suggest, as a pint of order, that the matter immediately before us is the gratuity to Mr Moss. If Mr Mitchell objects, let him move an amendment that it be not paid, instead of rambling all round. The Rev A M MITCHELL : I would not say anything against the grant, but I don't think it is a fair and reasonable thing to propose that this expense should be put upon the ratepayers. Mr A BROOKS said Mr Awbery's position was exactly on all-fours with that of any ctn.r officer of the Union. At the present time they bad an officer who had been lying ill for a long time and who had had special attention—proba'Ay not the att,ention Mr Awbery had, because the nature of the illness did not need it. brit whether it was Mr Awbery or any one of the officials of the house, under the same conditions he believed they would have had the same treatment. It was probably through lack of knowledge of the conditions that Mr Mitchell had raised the ques- tion, and he would be well-advised to let it drop. Mr Awbery only received the same treatment that any other official would have received under like circumstances.
MISS BROADBENT : I understand Mr Moss is going

to spend his holidays with Mr and Mrs Awbery. I dares say they are going to express their gratitude ny enter- taining him during his holidays. Mr. JOLLEY contended thnt the discussion was quite irregular. If Mr. Mitchell wanted to raise a discussion he should have moved an amendment to the minutes and not have dragged in a lot of side issues or irrelevant matter iu the form of conversation which made other people appear to disregard the standing orders. The minutes were then approved. A (tUESTIoN OF REPRESENTATION.

Mr ilottutrroN raised the question of the representa- tion of the various puts of the Union and contended that some parishes should, on the basis of population, be entitled to return two members to the Board,

Mr. W. C. BROOKS said Warrington had two-thirds of, the population and assessable value of the Union but. it had only ten representatives as compared with 18 from the outside parishes. If there %%eta going to be a revision, it should apply all ronno. Mr 'MATHER : l'ru aftaid you are on with a big subject. .

_ Ntr A BRooKs said that if there were a redistribution, Warrington would probably get an overwuelming majority, or the country districts would only return one representative for two or three parishes. No definite proposition was brougut before the meeting.
SEVENTY THREE. I've gazed upon my native bills,
For three score years and ten Near to the scehes where I was born

And loved s I much since then. I cannot climb the mountains now; Upon their rugged breast How often in the years gone by I've sat me down to rest. My ffet are wandering to the grave So Lear the shids of death, And there is little I can do
But give away my breath. And yet it may be well to say While stitl on earth we live When evil dies it should to us
Be easy to forgive. Then I would bid a kind farewell
To all I've known before; Who have not yet forgotten me Whom I shall see no more. Oh never think this life is all.
Beyoud methinks must be A better world where we sball meet In glad eternity.
Now she has gone who was to me The blessing of my life ; Who never gave me grief or pain My fundly cherished wife. •
And when my fleeting dye are o'er My deepest hope is this To meet her in the universe, Again in peace and bliss.
S. KENYON.
Blackpool, July 26th, 19:2.

The Examiner Saturday August 17, 1912.
What, asks Mr. THE HOUSE OF WINSTON CHURCHILL LORDS AND ITS in his reply to Mr REFORM. BoNAn LAW, are the

miserable quibbles by which the Conservative Leader seeks to justify rebellion? They are "that Home Rule was not mentioned in the election addresses of certain Ministers, and that the preamble of the Parliament Act has not yet been carried into effect." The first quibble has no significance. Some Ministers men- tioned Home Rule in their election addresses and some did not. If Mr. BONAR LAW intends to suggest that some members of the Govern- ment were afraid to mention Homeßule when they were asking for public support, or were • themselves not in favour of the passing of a Home Rule Bill, there is not a particle of justification for such an opinion. Home Rule has been the policy of the Liberal Party for twenty-five years. There is now not more than one member on the Liberal benches who does not vote in ibs favour, and it is more than doubtful if he would retain his seat were he to take the opinion of his constituents as

to whether he is representing their views on the Home Rule question. The policy of a party at a General Election, and in advance of it, is declared by its leader, and if Mr. BONAR LAW wishes the people to believe that Mr. ASQUITH did not mention Home Rule he must have vastly overrated his power of conveying false impressions. It is preposter- ous,of course,to represent that the Parliament Act was passed as an end in itself. It was passed as a means to an end—the carrying into practical legislation of measures as to the nature of which the country was already fully acquainted. When the Conservative Leader resolved on making use of his second quibble, he must, in a phrase long familiar, have been "sorely gravelled for lack of matter." What in the world should make him anxiousifor the'carry- ing out of the preamble of the Parliament Act? No possible reconstruction of the House of Lords could be satisfactory to the party which has been accustomed to rely on that body for the destruction of Liberal measures. If the House of Lords were to be reconstructed it would most certainly not 139 on a basis which would give more than three fourths of the seats therein to the hereditary enemies of Liberalism. There would be some such balance as made fairness of judgment probable and fairness of action possible. The hereditary principle would disappear in so far as it confers a Parliamentary qualification on "the tenth transmitter of a foolish face," though, of course, a Peerage would not be in itself a disqualification for the position of legislator. The House of Lords would, in fact, be severely weeded out, greatly reduced in numbers, and changed into a practicable working body with a good, sound basis of brains. How would such a change as that help Mr. BONAR LAW? What should lead him to suppose that a Second Chamber, reasonably constituted, would be a more powerful engine on his own side than a House in which the vast bulk of the Members have used their powers and their privileges on behalf of his party, right or wrong, through thick and thin? The Lords, we may be sure are not eager to be reformed, despite certain resolutions adopted in a panic. Nor, we may be sure, is the Conservative Leader in the House of Commons any more anxious for Peerage reform than, let us say, Lord WILLOUGHBY DE BROKE.

In fact, insistence on the preamble of the Parliament Act on the part of a Tory Leader comes as near to imposture as makes no matter. The insinuation, we suppose,is that the Government has broken some pledge. It has broken no pledge whatever. The pre- amble iof the Parliament Act indicates that there will be a reconstruction of the House of Lords when a suitable opportunity presents itself. There is nothing pressing about such a matter. There is no wrong in delay. No advantage could arise out of hurry. The Parliament Act would be as operative in a reformed House of Lords as it is under exist- ing conditions. If there were any difference tr trend in a reformed House of Lords it would be in the direction of Liberalism. It could not be otherwise. The present House will probably hang up the Home Rule Bill as long as it can. A House reasonably reformed, and composed of men, as might be expected, of more than average mental calibre, would just as probably pass the bill in the first session in which it was sent up. But the I Government cannot manceuvre for possible advantages of this description. It has in hand a series of great measures which will absorb all the energies of Parliament. The Parliament Act being passed, the reconstruc- tion of the House of Lords can wait. It is not a question of urgency. Whenever it takes place it will not satisfy Mr. BONAR LAW, nor will it.be to the taste of a very large majority of the present Peers.

Festina lente must THE TOWN HALL. be the motto of the Council in regard to the suggested enlargement of the Town Hall. The scheme is at present in a purely nebulous state, and much discussion and con- sultation of experts must take place before it can assume a concrete shape. The one absolute essential is an enlargement of the present Council Chamber or the con- struction of a new one. As a munici- pality we have tolerated the cramped accommodation of the present chamber for 40 years, and we cannot agree with Alderman Bennett or the old song that" it don't seem a day too much." Warrington is at least a quarter of a century behind the times in respect of the meeting place of its administrators. But the problem of provid- ing an adequate Council Chamber, in or attached to the Town Hall, is decidedly complex, for no one would wish to see the character altered, or the harmonious lines destroyed, of the old residence of the Patten family. Another and bolder scheme involves the addition of wings, east and west, for the accommodation of the municipal offices as well as the Council. It seems to us that the Committee might do worse than call in an eminent con- sulting architect, and also invite suggestions from the local members of the profession, before deciding the extent and limits of the I scheme.
Last month a party "SAME AS JOE." of sixty-two British

manufacturers toured Canada. At Winnipeg they were inter- viewed by an influential organ of the Western agriculturists "The :11" rain'Growers' Guide." With careful fairness the inter- viewer prints the opinions of two Free Trade and two Protectionist manufacturers. One of the former pointed out that "a Protective tariff always falls on the Consumer"; and the other, from Leicester, was shocked at the low quality of hosiery and underwear the Canadians wear. " I should think," he said, "it would not do you any harm to get better clothes at lower prices." But we turned with keener interest to read what the two Protectionists had to say. First there was Mr. Thomas Brown, described by the inter- viewer as "a wholesale grocer from Birmingham, the home of the great Joseph Chamberlain."

"When asked for his views on the trade question, this gentleman said: 'Tariff Reform, same as Joe.'" And then this excellent sample of the ready- made thinker went on to talk about farming, and the chances in Canada for his farmer son. The other Protectionist was Mr. George W. Goodchild, of London, who, as the inter-

viewer quaintly observes, "certainly gave excellent reasons for desiring a tariff." He is the selling agent for a number of manufac- turers of machine tools, and "though he looks fairly prosperous, and is apparently able to pay his way on a two months' trip to Canada, he assured the Guide representa- tive that there was no money in his business, either for him or for the manufacturers whom he represents." Mr. Goodchild's grievance was that "England is flooded with foreign-made machine tools, chiefly of American manufacture." Well,we have looked up the quantities. Last year we imported £214,000 worth of machine tools, of which £193,000 worth came tram America. But, on the other hand, we exported £760,000 worth, or more than three times as much. And further, the Census of Production shows that in 1907 (and the amount has much increased since) we manufactured in this country, for our own use and for export, no less than £2,715,000 worth. Mr. Goodchild's "flood " seems to flow the other way. Two other things he said:
" In England a trust to raise prices is impos- sible becaube of the Free Trade policy." and, with respect to the workman, he told the interviewer.
"Oh, of course, he benefits by Free Trade, but you see I am not looking at it from his point of view."
We ought to be grateful to the Winnipeg journalist for catching Mr. Brown of Birmingham and Mr. Goodchild of London in so candid a humour.
'There cannot fail to be TORY HEART- some heart-searching SEARCHING amongst_ the more

thoug-htful members of the Tory Party when they are confronted with a systematic propaganda of lawlessness conducted by their own leaders. The first symptom of it appears in the revolt of the Tory candidate for Rochdale against Mr. Bonar Law's "Blenheim Orange" style of oratory. The Tory Party, which largely represents rich vested interests, which has long been able, thanks to the veto of a House of Lords that is little more than an annexe of the Carlton Club, virtually to dominate the course of legislation whether in or out of office, and which through the plural vote has been able to secure majorities in the House of Commons which did not at all reflect the opinion of the British democracy, is singularly ill-advised in advocating violence as a method by which a political party should make its protest against legislation which it dislikes.

In another column Mr. S. Kenyon sings his "Swan song" at the age of 73. Many old Warrington friends of Mr. Kenyon will perceive with regret a note of pathos in the verses.

* * No one needs convincing that there has been a heavy rain-fall of late, but a few facts thereon will not be found uninteresting. During the 16 days of August, up to and including yesterday, only four have been without rain locally, and on the other 12 days a quantity of water estimated at 1,333,000 tons has fallen on the borough. The total rain-fall for this year, up to yesterday morning, equals the total up to the last day of October last year. No wonder holidays are a bit unpopular at present.

* • "Workman Jim " was a frequent speaker at Tuesday's Council meeting—he seems to have become emboldened by his triumphs on the Tariff Reform platform and positivelyto effervesce with eloquence. One or his topics was deputations. He had been of the opinion the money spent on deputations was not well spent—until the Sanitary Works Committee sent him on the deputation to "The Confer- ference or Cleansing Superintendents." Councillor Broadhurst has returned with a high opinion of deputations—he might almost be said to love them—and a conviction that Warrington can teach Manchester some- thing about sanitation. His mind is per- ceptibly broadening..

* There was another topic on which "Work- man Jim" vastly amused the Council. He valiantly took up the cudgels on behalf of the blacksmiths who, he thought, were charged too much by the Gas Committee for fuel. They had actually charged him 235. for 23cwts. of "washed breeze," and he pressed for a reduction in price so that black- smiths could work more economically. What admirable altruism! Some people might have thought that being a smith himself "Workman Jim" was looking after No. 1. Perish the thought! All Smiths are not alike in this respect. « * *

Mr. Harold has been treating Eddisbury Unionists to samples of his political wisdom within the grounds of Combermere Abbey. After saying that the people were not going to be allowed to dis- cuss Home Rule, quite regardless of the fact that it has been discussed for the past 25 years, the Member for Warrington said " he believed Mr. Asquith dare not face a civil war in Ulster, which his policy had directly incited." If there is any civil war in Ulster (which we do not for a moment believe) we suppose Mr. Smith and the other bold con- spirators will hold themselves innocent of all blame. Theirs is a peculiar mental attitude, and we are glad to learn that it is exciting the close attention of the Attorney-General's office. * * Mr. Philip M. Oliver, the prospective Liberal candidate for the Knutsford Division, has been assisting the Liberal cause in the various constituencies where bye-elections have recently been contested. Although Mr. Oliver has not been speaking very much inside the Knutsford Division, he has been busy outside. At Holmfirth, where Mr. Sidney Arnold, M.P., the newly elected member was a personal friend, Mr. Oliver appeared several times. In the Crewe election, Mr. Oliver also addressed several meetings at Crewe, Alsager and Sandbach, while in the North-west Manchester contest he spoke at seven different meetings. Mr. Sidney Arnold, the victor of Holmfirth, was in the Knutsford Division a few months ago where he addressed a village meeting at Lower Peover. * * *

One of the most striking—as, in certain aspects, it will be one of the most amusing— of official documents promises to be that which the National Health Insurance Commissioners will have to issue shortly containing the names of the approved societies under the National Insurance Act. The psychological problem was long ago suggested of why huruan beings of our own race, and, therefore, presumably intelligent, should band themselves together for social and benevolent purposes in bodies possessed of strange titles; and it assuredly will be raised again when this particular list is published. Necessarily it will include the Independent Order of Oddfellows and the Ancient Order of Foresters, to say nothing of those other old familiar friends the Order of Rechabites, the United Ancient Order of Druids, and the Royal Antediluvian Ordez

of Buffaloes. The Society of Blue Female° promises to strike a fresh note in the friendl?' societies colour scheme; and we shall wait withinterest to see whether the rhilanthropi Order of True Ivorites, the Ancient Order of Romans and the Independent Order of the .Golden Fleece accompany them in the author- ised list.
