div.head: SMOKE. ALDERMAN_BENNETT AND LOCAL
div.p: SMOKE. ALDERMAN_BENNETT AND LOCAL

POSSIBILITIES. [To THE EDITOR OF THE EXAMINER.] Sir,—l have read the recent articles and letters in "The Examiner" on this question with very much interest and pleasure. They seem to indicate that the public are at last awaking to the enormity of the nuisance of which I have so long complained, and they fill me with hope for the future. The magnitude of the evil is self-evident, in spite of all attempts to belittle it. For the smoke which pours in such unnecessary volume from so many of our local chimneys not only destroys vegetation, ruins our build- ings, is fatal to cleanliness and destructive to beauty, but, in my opinion, is distinctly detrimental to health. I venture to add that it is also wasteful and uneconomic to the last degree. All round the town the trees are gradually disappearing, and it is only certain carefully selected kinds which are able to make any sort of successful struggle against it. I admit, of course, that the evil is aggravated by certain poisonous vapours, which are even more injurious than the smoke, and which ought to be subject to the strictest possible control. It is driving us to substitute terracotta for brick and stone and is ruining the fine old structures which are the pleasing heritage of a :nore artistic age. It makes our dream of a "Beautiful Warrington," in any real sense, a practical impossibility. It is a source of untold labour and expense to every housewife in the town, involving enormous labour at the wash-tub, and it adds materially to our laundry bills. It shuts out the sun- light, which is the fruitful source of health and the best and simplest germicide, and it is a fertile source of lung trouble, whilst as a local doctor lately pointed out, it seams to be the cause of the exceptional death rate in the town, from measles and from kindred diseases. Moreover, owing to the lamentable supiness of the adjacent authori- ties, it is more and more invading the suburbs, and ruining some charming residential districts. To every one who cares for cleanliness and likes to breathe pure air, who wants to dwell in agreeable surroundings, and who wishes to enjoy the full measure of health and cheer- fulness which ought to be the common lot, it is an unmitigated nuisance. Why, then, are we 'content fo tolerate it, and to sit down idly under its black shadow? It is because certain ,well-meaning people who have not studied the question declare that it would interfere with trade, and that we had better have the smoke than lose the industries. With the last contention most of us would probably agree, although I sometimes think we pay a frightful price for our industrial success; but I challenge any of your readers to produce a single instance of any industry which has been driven fro:n a town because the authorities have carried out the law in reference to smoke abatement in a reasonable spirit, which is all we ask; and I venture to affirm unhesitatingly that we need not lose the industries and can effectu- ally prevent the smoke. And all that is wanted to secure these ends is the steady pressure of an enlightened public opinion. To cure the nuisance would involve a little extra care; it might involve a certain amount of preliminary expenditure; in certain cases, old and insufficient plant might possibly have to be "scrapped," and, so long as the public are disposed to take it "lying down," the average manufacturer does not want to be bothered, and is quite content to leave things as they are. But, if the law imperfect and unsatisfactory as it is, were only carried out; and if the officials wer€ steadily backed up by the Council, and by the general sense of the community, the manufacturer, in self defence, would begin to enquire into the matter. He would take care to employ properly qualified stokers. He would over-haul his plant, and look into the numerous appliances which are now upon the market. He would find, right at his very doors, the example of Messrs. Joseph Crosfield and Sons to encourage him, with their record of enormous savings. He might learn from Messrs Bibby and Sons, of Liverpool, a similar and equally impressive lesson. He might readily obtain particulars of scores of other firms who have been able to secure not less encouraging results. And, if he would only condescend to visit our own Municipal Electricity Works, he would be shown a chimney which was once one of the worst in Warrington, and would learn that the apparatus which enables this department to consume its own smoke has also enabled it to consume slack instead of coal, and saved the ratepayers several hundred pounds a year. He would speedily discover twenty different appliances for dealing with the nuisance, some of them well-tried and thoroughly effective. He would consider alternative methods of obtain- ing the power he needed, such assuction gas, the municipal gas supply, electric motors and the rest. He would quickly realize that,by a little judicious expenditure and reorganiza- tion, he might not only save the public from this constant scourge, but add substantially to his own dividends. And he would find that, even in the case of the great forges, which are, of course, the chief offenders, and claim, upon quite inadequate grounds, to be outside the' law, the nuisance may be greatly limited, if not indeed completely cured. Our really public-spirited and enterprizing manufacturers will probably be glad enough to go into the matter on their own account, but it seems necessary to apply to the remainder the stimulus of a gentle spur. Spasmodic observations followed by mild reproofs will evidently not suffice. The observations should be systematic and con- tinuous. The reproofs (and we might make them as polite as possible at the outset) should be followed by increasingly severe remon- strances. If these should fail they should be backed up by cumulative and increasing fines. I venture to predict that we should then see very great and satisfactory changes. And all that is wanted to secure this end as I have said, is an enlightened public opinion such as "The Examiner" is doing its best to promote. Councils are the creatures of the men who make them. They are always a little disposed to ." kow-tow " to the wealthy, nearly all of whom, by the way,take care to live beyond the nuisance which they cause. They have an ill-founded notion that the workingmen believes the nonsense that is talked upon the subject, and that it pleases him to be told that "more smoke means more work," and that "the more of it there is the better." The workingman is not the fool they take him for. He cannot get away from the grime and dust into the country. .His home is right amid the reek of the great chimneys. His children have to live in the contaminated air. His wife is doomed to one long and futile struggle to keep things clean. And he is just as fond of blue skies and fresh air as anybody else. Moreover, if he thinks

at all, he knows that much, at any rate, o the dense volume of smoke which pollutes our local air is quite avoidable, and that, if we really took serious steps to prevent it, instead injuring the manufacturers by persuading them to use the best appliances, we should materially contribute, in the end, to their success, which all of us alike desire. But the British workingman is a singularly patient fellow. He has borne his drear life, in his mean streets and amid his grim surroundings, so long that he has come to look upon them as inevitable and to bear his dismal and unnecessary lot as best he may. I venture to affirm unhesitatingly that it is unnecessary; that, if he only will exercise his vote and influence wisely, he can not only stop the smoke, but put an end to the mean streets, and even hope to ultimately get sufficient open spaces, and that, instead of hindering local trade, he would help to put it on a sounder and more economic footing, and to make it brisker and more prosperous than before. He can make a good start in , November. He can flatly decline to give his vote for any municipal candidate of any party who will not pledge himself to carry out the provisions of the Public Health Act, and to vote, if requisite, for its amendment. And then we should assuredly soon see a new and very different spirit in the Council, and it would not have to be said again that it had been left to one unfortunate and misjudged individual for nearly twenty years to fight the battle practically single-handed.—Faith- fully yours,
ARTHUR BENNETT. Paddington House, near Warrington, 15th August, 1912.

div.head: VICTIMISED TRADESMEN.
div.p: VICTIMISED TRADESMEN.
REMARKABLE CASE AT WARRINGTON.

JEWELLERY FOR NOTHING. One of the most remarkable cases ever heard in Warrington came before his Honour Judge Stanger K.C., at the County Court on Thursday. It was the sequel to the amazing victimisa- tion of local tradesmen by a woman who, posing as the possessor of abundant means, was alleged to have obtained valuable goods on approval and then to have sold them and decamned. The present action was brought by Messrs Miller and Company, jewellers, Sankey-street, a -tainst Mr and Mrs Henry Maddock, Padgate-lane, Warrington, for the return of a solid silver tea tray, an electro-plated kettle, and a gold keyless watch, or their value (£32 10s.) together with damages for their detention. Mr T 13 Leigh, barrister, Manchester (instructed by' Messrs Arthur Browne and Company) appeared for Hie plaintiffs and Mr Burghs, banister, Manchester (instructed by Mr T S Steel, of Warrington) for the defendants. The case for the plaintiffs, as outlined by Mr. Leigh, was that a woman calling herself Mrs. Julia Leverson appeared in Warrington, nobody knew whence, about the month of April and called upon the plaintiff's firm. In the first instance she had repairs done to articles of jewellery and ultimately, she made a number of pur- chases, paying for the goods, and in that way gaining the confidence of the manager. After these transactions she suggested that she should be allowed to take the silver tray and the kettle on approval for a friend of hers who, she said, would be sure to buy them. The manager said he could not allow that except on the condition of "cash or return." Mrs.Leverson said the cash would be forthcoming that day or the following day and the articles were delivered at her lodgings. The gold watch was obtained under similar circumstances. Mrs. Leverson did Dot return the goods, nor did she pay anything for them. On the 26th June it was discovered that she had absconded. In the meantime the manager had made repeated applications for the goods or the cash, and had been "put off" with a variety of tales. It was found that the female defendant had obtained possession of the articles. She told a detective that she had known Mrs Leverson for quite a short time, and bad purchased the articles from her. The prices given were somewhat material. For the tray, which was worth £l9, she paid £4 ; for the kettle, which was worth £3 10s, she paid 17s 6d ; and for the watch, which was worth £lO, she paid £4 18s 4d. It appeared that Mrs Maddock had purchased from Mrs Leverson,who was almost a stranger to her,a great variety of articles including household linen, curtains, carpets, drapery eic., which woul.l be the subject of a second action. Mrs Maddock was not in business but lived at home as a private resident, with her husband. She purchased toe goods at prices which he would be able so show his Honour were, on the average, one-third of their real value. Within a short space of time she pur- chased goods which were really of the value of £O7 lfis. 2d. for £3O 4. 4d. When the officer visited the house a pair of curtains and some carpets which Mrs. Maddock had acquired from Mrs. Leverson were actually in use. Mrs. Maddock said. "I felt uneasy and I wished to establish my claim. That was why I put up the curtains and put down the carpets.' In the course of an interview, at which a detective 'was present, the husband said he would return the goods, that he did not want any that did not belong to him, and that he would take a cab and bring them to the Police Station in order that the question of ownership might be gone into. In point of fact, he did not return them. Mr Maddock took the advice of his solicitor and apparently he thought he could establish a goad claim to goods that had been acquired in that way. Discussing the legal position, Mr Leigh said that if the goods were stolen and Mrs Maddoca knew they were stolen she was a receiver, but there were many intermediate positions. The goods might have been acquired by fraud just short of larceny, in which case she was not a receiver of stolen goods, but might have acquired them without thinking it wise to make any inquiries. A warrant bad been applied for and granted against Mrs. Leverson in respect of some of the things she bad taken, but not in respect of the three articles which were the subject of the present action. The warrant had not been executed because Mrs. Leverson had disappeared. She was " wanted " at Rugby and elsewhere for similar practices. If it had been a transaction merely on approval or of "sale or return," with no additional terms, it was quite clear that the property would Mae " passed " the moment Mrs. Leverson adopted the transaction by selling the goods to somebody else. In the present case, however, it was a transaction of " cash or return." which made a vital difference. It was not the intention of the parties that the property should " pass" and be was told that in the retail jewellery trade there was a custom that the property did not "pass" when goods were delivered in that way on those terms. If the property did not " pass," the defendant was in this position : tbat.Mrs Leverson had no title at all to the goods. His Honour : Certainly if the property had not " passed" she received no title. A person cannot sell what does not belong to her. Mr Leigh further submitted that the way in which Mrs Leverson obtained possesson of the articles con- stituted larceny by trick and that would not" pass' the property. His Honour: Obtaining by false pretences would. Mr Leigh said that dealing with the first and second alternatives, it did not become necessary to inquire Into the conduct of the defendants. If he took the line that it was fraud, however, there was a voidable title and it became necessary to inquire into the con- duct of the defendants. Then and then only their bona- fides or their avoiding of inquiries because they felt uneasy would become material to his Honour's consideration, as to whether the property had "passed" or not. His Honour: If it were not larceny by trick, how could it be fraud? You are not alleging false pretences. George Eccles, manager for the plaintiffs, was then called. lie stated that Mrs Leverson actually paid for articles to the valve of over £lOO. She told him a great deal about the people she knew. She said Miss Julia Neilson was her neice„ that the late Sir George Lewis was a relative and had left her some money, and that she had a nephew who was a solicitor in London and had 23 clerks. She said he made her an allowance each week. She frequently told witness about a lady friend in London who was very wealthy and who would eventually want a diamond bracelet, worth anything from £2OO to £250. She wanted to take a bracelet to show it to her friend, but be declined to allow her. She went to London and in a letter to witness she stated that her friend had given her money to buy the bracelet and that when she re- turned she would arrange everything satisfactorily. The matter, however, never advanced any further. Asked why he had confidence in Mrs. Leverson, wit- ness said that seeing she had spent over £lOO and bad told him about the people she knew, he concluded she was respectable and quite in a position to have the goods on approval. Mr. Leigh : Between the transactions about the tray and the watch did she call to see you at all ?—Yes. More than once ?—Yes • almost every day. Witness further stated' that Mrs. Leverson had said the watch was for the lady who had had the tray. In regard to the purchase of the watch, she came and asked him to show her one just like the first one she had had, as that bad given so much satisfaction. He showed her one or two and she selected one which she thought would suit the gentleman. Mr. Leigh: What gentleman ?—The husband of the lady who had the tray. His Honour: Before she purchased one something was said about the husband. How did the husband crop up? Witness: I asked her about the payment for the

tray and kettle, and she said she could not get the money because the woman wanted to see her husband about it and be was out of town. She further stated that if the lady and gentleman liked the watch the three articles would be paid for all together. He then let her have the watch on approval. Mr Leigh : What about the price ?—£lo. Was that mentioned to her ?-oh. yes. She had stipulated the price to be the same as the other one. Mr Leigh : How long was this after the tray ?—Ten days. When was the watch delivered to her ?—On the 15th June. After that date had you any more meetings with her ?—Yes. Mr Leigh : Was nothing said about the return or pat ruent in respect of these goods?—She kept excusing herself, saying she had not seen the parties together and that the gentleman had been out of town. She had one continuous list of excuses. She also hinted at the possibility of the diamond bracelet transaction. His Honour : That was auothe: bait she was dangling before you ?—Yes, I suppose so. (Laughter.) Witness continuing said that Mrs Leverson hasi said that the wealthy lady trend in London would come for the bracelet and pay for it. His Honour : Did it not strike you as being singular that a lady in search of a diamond bracelet should come all the way from London to Warrington ? Witness:She had said the lady's husband had a business in Manchester and that, whilst in the neighbourhood she would call to see the bracelet. Of course she did not come. (Laughter). Witness ridded that he had got a bracelet from litrmingbam on approval. Mrs.Leverson had handled it, hut he did not like to trust her with so much as that. Shortly afterwards he heard of the woman's dissappearance. He had visited the defend- ants house on the Bth July in cotepany with Mr Hodgkinson and Detective Sergeant Reddington. Mr Madeock did not come in until they had been in the house aborit half an hour. He (witness) told Mrs Maddoce that he had come to identify the goods. She asked him to wait until Mr ;Maddock came and, whilst ' waiting for the husband, they spoke ab est Mrs Leverson. When Mr Madoock came in he said he had bought the things from Mrs Leverson. The female defendant had said during conversation that she felt uncomfortable about the carpet and curtains and had made use of them. He (witness) did not take the goods away because Mr Maddock said he would think it over and something was said about seeing a solicitor. Mr. Burgis: The transactions with Mrs. Leverson from beginning to cad, were perfectly reasonable ? Not from beginning to end. At the time did you think you were acting reason- ably ?—Wheu I was getting paid for them, yes. I Did you tbink so when she was getting things on approval ?—Net then. Witness added that he was told about Sir George Lewis and Miss Julia Neilson and those two facts made him think Mrs Leverson was a woman of some substance, and he was also told about a nephew in Manitoba. Those things made him have more confidence in the woman. Mr. Burgle: Would you go further and say you were put off your guard ?—At the time I was. Mr. Burgis : Would you be surprised that a woman with no business experience would be put off her guard by the same statements made to her ?—No. Has the defendant told you that exactly the same story has teen told to her as was told to you ?—Yes. Dolvou still think there was anything dishonest in the det endant's conduct ?—Yes. Altbough you bad the same story told to you and you believed it ?—I won't say dishonest, I don't think she acted as she might have done. Incautious ?—Yes. Do you 'know this Mrs Leverson sold a good many things to the defendant and got money when those things were delivered ?—I don't know. His, Leverson was a woman with a very plausible tongue ?—Most plausible. It quite got round you ?—She would get round any one. (Laughter). Do you know she has got round a large number of people in Warrington ?—P ossibly so. Always with the same story ?—With slight variations Continuing, witness in reply to further questions by Mr fsurgis, agreed that he and all the other people had been substantially " let in," in the same way. When he went to the defendant's house Mrs Maddock came to the front door and as soon as they got inside and she was asked about the goods, the produced the tray and watch. Carpets might possibly have been mentioned. She read out from a book a list of the things she had had from Mrs Leverson. Mr Burgis : Did she say "This shows I could have no suspicion about it after she had read the things out? —I dou't know that. She also said she had paid for goods she had not bad from Mrs Leverson. You have sold a lot of goods to eirs.Leverson ?—All I have sold her she has paid for. Some of the goods he continued, she had had on approval, and he knew some of them had been sold to other people. He knew that Mrs. Leverson lodged in Museum-street and he had been down to the horse. He believed criminal proceedings had been taken against Mrs. Leverson but he did not know exactly what the warrant was for. She had promised to pay for the goods she had heti. How did Mr. Hodgkinson come to go with you and Detective Reddington to the defendant's house ?—We both got to know the had gone. Had the police told you anything about Mrs.l Leeerson's escapades and do you know she had a £6O tratisaction with a Mrs. Bruce at Ediaborgh ?—I know she"- had some articles from us. Mrs. Bruce and Miss Bruce went to London with her and nothing more had been seen of Mrs. Leverson since. By Mr Leigh : It was incautious of Mrs. Maddock to buy the tray for £4 as it was an absolutely ridicu- lous price. It was solid silver and ball-marked. Detective-Sergeant Reddington said that when he went to the house of the defendants at 196, Padgate- lane on July 4th Mrs. Maddock was quite candid over the matter and when asked about the goods produced a book containing a full list. He had taken a statement from defendant in which she said that she met Mrs. Leverson at the beginning of May at 7, Ring-street and got into conversation with her. Mrs. Leveraon asked her if she would like a piece of white silk to make two blouses. Mrs. Leverson also said she could have a habit at Is. per yard on condition that she made a blouse up for Mrs Maddock. She agreed to haste the silk and paid her es for it The next time she saw Mrs Leverson she was asked if she would like six yards of grey material at Gs, from which a dress could be made. She saw Mrs Leverson about twice a week up to her going away and she gave the officer a list of all goods she had purchased from her, which included dress materials pieces of lace, carpets, curtains, silks, table cloths, pillows and bed clothing, a silver tray and spirit kettle £4 175 Gclehe tray £4 and the kettle 17s Gd. She had kept all the goods in her possession, except one pais of blankets and teethes pillows which she had sold. She had also paid Mrs Leverson for a long list of goods which she bad not received. This list included silk, cloths, oil-paintings to the value of £3 a set of stoles, and martin furs £6 10s, one marquise ring, £3 4s 4d, one gents' solitaire ring, Le 14s. 108., carpetting and other expensive artieles ranging from £4 downwards. She had paid Mrs. Leverson for them and had not received them. Witness paid another visit to the house on July Bth, accompanied by Messrs. Hodgkinson and Eccles, and when Mr.Maddock put in an appearance he said he could not understand that the goods were let out on approval. Mr. Hodgkinson and Mr. Eccles explained how the goods had been obtained by Mrs. Leverson, and Mr. Maddock said, " I don't want anything that is not my own, but I would like time to consider this matter" Before they left the house Mr. Maddock said he did not want anything in his house that was not got honestly. The Chief Constable was wishful that the things should be kept by him or restored to their rightful owner. Cross-examined by Mr Burgis the detective said Mrs Leverson was one of the cleverest thieves known to the police. She appeared to have deceived people all over the country with her plausible stories. Whereor they were told they deceived the people. The police had interviewed a Mrs Bruce who said Mrs Leverson had had £6O from her and that Mrs Maddock had been giving her (Leverson) money. I Mr Hargis : I submit that was not true and that 'there was no suggestion of the amount alleged to have been received from Mr and Mrs Maddock. Arthur Hodgkinson, director of the firm of Messrs W Hodgkinson, Ltd., Bridge-street, Warrington, gave evidence supporting the officer's and the first witnesses statement of what took place at the house. He said Mrs Leverson had paid him considerable sums of money but he did not trust her entirely. Prior to Juno he had only allowed her to have goods in small quantities on approval to show her customers. She said she had a wedding order which wound come to about £2OO and he was considerably impressed by her story and let her have coods in larger quantities. At this point Mr Burgis submitted that there bad been no case made out, although he was not averse to calling his client. His Honour : Do you mean on the ground that the property had 'passed " ? Mr. Burgis: Yes; or on the other hand that it was a voidable contract. Clearly, on these admissions, we were acting bona-fide. Mr. Burgis argued that Mrs Leverson had obtained the goods by. representing that she had a prospective purchaser, and he had evidence to show that she had his client in view.s His Honour: What she led the manager to believe was that the sale would not be to Mrs Maddock but to some other lady, that she was a mere go-between, and that the lady wonld pay cash Mr Borgia : It was a contract entered into on misrepresentation. Mrs Maddock, 196, Pad gate-lane, Warrington, was , then called and after stating the circumstances under I which she met Mrs Leverson, who posed as a dressmaker went on to deal with her transactions with the woman. Mrs Leverson told her a tale to the effect that a big wedding in London had been postponed on account of I the engagement being broken off, and she had therefore' a lot of goods on her hands. She offered some of them to witness and she bought some goods from her, as she I gave names of other purchasers. On the 20th May they had agreed about the £4 17s. Gd. for the tray and kettle. His Honour: Before you saw them ?—Yes. How came you to be satisfied that £4 was a fair price when you had not seen theta, because trays vary so much?—She described the tray and said it was in pledge and bad not been pawned for its value but for £4 and that it was worth more than that for old silver. Had she explained why she wanted to sell it for £4 when she had all those rich relatives ? She said it was a lady friend of hers who bad the jewels in pawn. She said it was practically

div.head: Photo _rrell. THE INDIAN CAMP IN PARK-AVENUE, OFF KNUTSFORD-ROAD. Inset, a Chief in full head-dress.
div.p: Photo _rrell. THE INDIAN CAMP IN PARK-AVENUE, OFF KNUTSFORD-ROAD. Inset, a Chief in full head-dress.

new and also that there was not a scratch on it. When she (witness) received it, the tray was practically new and when she remarked upon this, Mrs Leverson said it had been reburnistied before it had been put into pledge. Witness expressed a doubt as to its being real silver when she saw it, because she had heard of stamps being faked, but Mrs Leverson told her that she could take it to any jeweller in town and get it valued. Mrs. Leverson told her a similar story with regard to the watch. She would not have bought the goods if she had thought they were not straight. By Mr. Leigh: She had had £l4 worth of goods I before the 18th May. The price of the goods for which she had paid Mrs Leverson since that date was about I £7O. Sue made the last payment about the midale of June. She sold some of the goods she had received from Mrs. Leverson. Mr. Leigh : In regard to the £6O furs, could you understand why she was going to let such a bargain as that go away for £6 10s ?—Witness made no reply. Continuing, witness said she did [not ask to see the pawn ticket becanse Mrs Leverson had lots of them. Mr Leigh : Did you not think it such an extraordin- ary thing that this woman who had known you such a I time, should let you have this plum, this sealskin coat, for £6 10s.? I though that it would be a good bargain but not worth £6O, but about £lB, as they generally get a third of the value of an article in pawn. 1 thought it was considerably stretching a point to say it was worth £6O. Can you understand why this lady should give you this great bargain when she might have got more for it ?—She bad not the money to get it out of pawn. Did you not think it very extraordinary ?—No. Quite the thing you would pick up any day, a bargain of that sort ?—No. Witness added that she did not get any receipt for goods she bought from iMr s Leverson—only for the dressmaking accounts. Mr Leigh : Why not ?—Because I put my trust in her and she had my confidence. At one time Mrs Leverson said she had a large hotel in London. Did you ask the name of it ?—No. Why not ?—Because I was not inquisitive. Further questioned witness said she sold some of the old goods which she did not want. You thought it was a cheap way of replenishing your goods, new ones for old ?—Yes. Did you never inquire about this mysterious wealthy relation in Scotland ?—No. Witness further stated that when she expressed doubt as to the genuineness of the tray, Mrs. Leverson said "I won't deceive you in any way. lam connected with a wealthy family. When I was married I bad £23,000." (Laughter). And you were re-assured by that ?-17,-s. Mr. Burgle, addressing His Honour, said that the case was a most serious one for his clients because the suggestion against them was dishonesty. It was a case of two people who had been deceived and of the tradesman, who should have known better, who bad been victimised. Where there was a sale of goods on approval the vendor had no right to the return of the goods, the purchaser onlv having that right. The proper course for the plaintiffs to have adopted was to have sued Mrs Leverson for the price. He contended that under the contract or sale on approval the purchaser alone had the option to return and that as soon as the purchaser had dealt with the goods by selling them to defendants, she thereby adopted the contract, and the title in the property became vested in her and afterwards in the defendants. The plaintiffs were thereby deprived of all right of the goods. The hearing was adjourned for the continuation of the legal arguments, until OctoberlOth.

THE TERRITORIALS. MIMIC WARFARE AT KIRKHAM CAMP. Our local Territorials have this week been under- going the more severe part of their annual training at Kirkham camp, and manreuvres on a large scale have been very satisfactorily carried out, in spite of the trying weather. Satur- day was a memorable day for the men, as they took part in the great review of the Territorials of the West Lancashire Division on Blackpool Race- course. Imposing as was this ceremonial parade, the most does not seem to have been made of it from the standpoint of recruiting for the forces. To quote a writer in the " Manchester Courier " : " One of the finest parades of Territorials in this country, certainly in Lancashire, was held at Black- pool on Saturday, and a great opportunity of recruit- ing and popularising the voluntary arm of our defensive forces was badly missed. It has been my good fortune to attend all the big parades of Regulars and Territorials and most of the mameuvres for many years past. I have never seen a more compact parade of Territorials than that of Saturday, or, taken on the whole a finer body of men. Here we bad assembled the whole of the West Lancashire Division of the Territorial Force, numbering about 10,000 troops— all the branches, Artillery, Engineers, Infantry, Army Service Corps, and the Medical Corps, complete with their equipment. The parade was held on the Clifton Park racecourse, and a better spot could not have been selected. The weather was perfect. What happened? The troops were marched in at the " back-end "of the town, and after the parade they went back the same way—Blackpool with its tens of thousands of visitors knew nothing—except for a few placards —that a great military parade had been held in its midst. Two or three thousand of the general public were at the parade. Half a million people were is Blackpool on Saturday. Blackpool possesses, I suppose, the longest sea parade of any town in the kingdom. Instead of "smuggling" the troops into the town, why not have marched them to the racecourse via the Parade? All Black- pool would have known, and all Blackpool would have gone to the racecourse. It is such a pity that a really splendid spectacle was missed by the public. The men had been in camp a week, were bronzed and fit; from their camp to the racecourse and back was a distance of 18 miles. These men, who sacrifice their time—and money—ought to have been greeted by an enormous crowd. Oeneral Bethune was obviously very pleased with the men as they marched past. The French military attache must have been very interested in all he saw—this wonderful display of unpaid patriotism. Batteries and Infantry went by in splendid unison; indeed, it was difficult to believe that these men were Territorials and not Regulars." During the week an elaborate scheme of mimic warfare has been engaged in. The " Examiner " correspondent in camp sends the following notes : SATURDAY. Blackpool was "invaded "to-day by the many thou- sands of Territorials encamped at Kirkham and Welton. The public were allowed to witness the great review of the troops which was held on Clifton Park Racecourse. Major-General F L Lindsay, C. 8., D.S.O. was in com- mand of the division and he was accompanied by the officers of the divisional headquarters staff.

The following units took part in the review : „ Royal Artillery :-2nd West Lancashire Brigade ".F.A., 3rd West Lancashire Brigade R.F.A., Lancashire Brigade R.G.A. (Heavev•Batteries). Royal Engineers :—West Lancashire Division R.E., and Western Telegraph Companies R.E. North Lancashire Infantry Brigade :-4th and sth Battalions Royal Lancaster Regiment; 4th and sth Battalions Loyal North Lancashire Regiment. South Lancashire Infantry Brigade : 9th Battalion Kings Liverpool Regement ; 4th and sth Battalions (P.W.V.) South Lancashire Regiment. A.S.C:—West Lancashire Divisional T. and S. Column.
R.A.M.C.—lst and 3rd West Lancashire Field Ambulances.

The troops commenced arriving at noon and it was an inspiring sight to witness the muster of the men with their boots white with dust. A large crowd of people was assembled round the gates, and many War- rington faces were to be seen among the spectators. On entering the spacious enclosure the troops were supplied with rations and soon afterwards a move was made towards the review ground. When the various units were in position in review order, they almost filled the centre of the course. The artillery, engineers and infantry were in line of quarter column and the A.S.C. ani R.A.M.C. were formed up in line in the rear. General Bethune and his staff arrived at 2.30 and were received with a general salute, the Union Jack being at once run up to the top of the saluting base. The General then rode round each unit and the band of each played while he inspected the troops. Then came the" march past" which in the case of a review like this, can only be seen to be appreciated. The splendid horses of the mounted units and the soldierly tearing of all were very favourably com- mented upon. Our local lads received a splendid reception and well it was deserved. The writer has never seen such steady marching, not even at the Royal Review before the late King Edward at Knowsley Park three years ago. Officers, non-commissioned officers and men fully merited the high praise they received from their Colonel at the close. A percentage of men in each battalion were allowed to stay in Blackpool, their rifles being conveyed back to the camp in the transport. Shortly after "lights out " a general tire-alarm was sounded and very quicky men came tumbling out of their tents in various stages of " undress uniform." It was a false alarm however, and the men were dismissed by bugle-call before they reached the alarm post." The weather throughout the day was splendid and high lalpes are entertained that toe second week under CaritliS will not be spoiled by rain. Captain H G Roberts arrived in camp tt-Jay and took over the command of his company.

SUNDAY. The weather in the early morning was rather threaten- ing and the men were ordered to wear great coats for church parade. The fears were groundless, for the rain kept off and the day was warm. At 9.30, all the South Lancashire Brigade assembled in a square under the' command of the Brigadier, Colonel Mac!le. Among those present was Colonel J. D. Edelsten, formerly Colonel of the Warrington battalion and now bon- secretary to the West Lancashire Territorial Associa- tion. The service was conducted by the Rev. W. Bracecamp and a splendid address on " Temptation " was delivered by the chaplain to the Liverpool battalion. The singing was accompanied by the War- rington Band under Bandmaster Wainwright and a. special feature was the singing of a small choir of boys of the drum and fife band. The men were free after dinner to go out of !camp and many men took advantage of the splendid weather and visited Blackpool, Lytham, St. Armes and other places of interest in the vicinity. The camp is thronged with visitors this afternoon and presents a very pleasing spectacle. Men are proudly escorting their wives and sweethearts round the lines and explaining various details to them. The road from camp to Kirkham is quite a picture, the gay dresses of the ladies contrast- ing with the various uniforms of the soldiers. Lieutenant Egerton Fairclough arrived and took over his command.

MONDAY. The 6.30 a.m. parade was held on the parade ground when the battalion formed up in quartet column. The men were instructed, by the ollicers and section commanders in "judging distance" drill- There was no further parade until after dinner when the battalion fell in at 1.30 for a march to Preesall, neer Fleetwood. The route taken was via Great Singleton and Hambleton, a distance of about 13 miles. The men stuck to their tiring march in a very creditable manner, singing and whistling cheerily all along the route. On arrival at Preesall, the men, after a short delay, were provided with rations and blankets and oil-sheets. Some of the men were accommodated in the schools rind chapels of the village while the others spent the night in the open. Communication was open all night through a chain of signalling stations.
TUESDAY.

The battalion was roused at dawn and after being served with coffee, marched down to the foreshore and took part in Ileld-firing with ball atnnmaition. Canvas screens had been erected in the sand and into these a hail of lead was poured. Probably most of the shots fell in the sand. A large crowd of people assembled to witness this rather minsual sight and elaborate pre- cautions bad beea taki,n to ensure the safety of the spectators. The march back to camp commenced at 10 o'clock and home was reached in a little over four hours. The umal feet inspection followed and the men whose feet were affected by the march were attend to by Dr Stott and his merry men. The sight in camp this afternoon is a very interesting one ; men are to be seen lying in all positions fist asleep. Col J D Fairclough, the late commanding officer, has visited the camp and received a warm welcome.
WEDNESDAY.

The battalion had a rather easy day. 'Battalion drill was the order of the day. The signallers were out on a Collective test under Lieutenant Campbell. Sports were held in the afternoon and great amusement was caused by the obstacle race, the competitors having to crawl under a pole, then under a ground sheet, over a transport waggon, and vaulting horse, through a tent, and finally they had to wade through a pit. A sad event occurred to-day when one of the cooks belonsine to the R.A.M.C. was buried in Weeton Churchyard with [military honours.
TIII:RSDAY.

The weather to-day is very threatening and the men paraded in overcoats. Tne battalion was instructed to escort and protect a convoy proceeding from Preston to Kirkham. The convoy got into camp without, encountering any of the enemy. Before the battalion marched out of camp, Colonel Fairclough called one of the men out of the ranks and concratulated him on behalf of the battalion on his heroism in rescuing one of his comrades who had fallen into the pit. FRIDAY. . .

To-day the South Lancashire brigade form-e-d—t;-iand- ing force, advancing under Colonel Macfie. The North Lancashire brigades under Colonel Adams, concentrated all efforts to capture St. Michael's Bridge and offered a strong resistance. Most of the firing was by the Artillery, but a very sharp fight occurred between A Company of the 4th South Laucashires and A Com- pany of the York and Lancaster regimenhe who met in a field and were within three yards of one another when hostilities ceased. THE RETURN HOME.
The battalion will return home on Sunday, the first train being due to reach Warrington about 3.30 p.m.

div.head: SINGULAR PACVNBROKING CASE.
div.p: SINGULAR PACVNBROKING CASE.

A case which, through contradictory statements of a girl witness was dismissed, was heard at the Warrington Police Court on Tuesday by Councillor Henry Roberta (in the chair), and (Aber magistrates. Under the Pawnbrokers Act a girl Lamed Elizabeth Am n Bibby, 30, Bowes-street, was summoned for having given false iufermation as to the name and address of the owner of a jeeket which she offered in pawn at Messrs. Jneksone, Orford-lane. Helen Parker, married woman, GG. Forster- street, was charged with having erocared the girl to commit the alleged offence. Mr A Browne, prosecuted and Mr T S Steel defended. Mr Browr e pointed out that the offence wit 6 which the girl was charged was commonly known as "duffing," which was, trying to palm off on to pawnbrokers for a greater anemia, goods which were of less value. Mr Birchen, the ranger of the establishment had had considerable experience in the pawn brokers business and on the 20th July when the girl offered a jacket in pawn be at once saw it had not been worn for some time and his suppici, es being aroused he asked the girl who had sent It. She replied that her father had sent her but Mr Birchall di,believ- ing this statement said she, had better go and bring her father and he would keep the jacket until she returned. An hour afterwards the girl returned with her sister find both of them stated tbat their father had sent them. They said what they would do if toe tanneger would not give them the jacket. He eeein teld them he did not believe their father red bent them and gave information to the police. The process of "duffing " had been going on for a consider- able time and a stop would have ta to put. to the prac- tice. Inquiries were made by Deteeti•e Sergennt Holland who found that the jacket belonged to Mrs. Parker. Mr. Birchen was out cycling on the 30th e oly when he met Mrs Parker who said the police had la,en to see her. She begged of him not to prosecute her and said she would rather make a hole in the river than have to go to the police court again. She ie-Haitted having been warned by the police about two :se, irs ago. The girl bad asked 4s. 6d. on the jacket which had been purchased from Mrs, Welsby, a second hand c,ot has dealer, of School Brow, along with a blouse for 3.4. 93. He wished to withdraw the charge against the gal who he thought had been the tool of Mrs. Parker weare they thought was the ring leader. Mr. Birchen having given evidence, the girl was called into the box and she denied that Mrs. Parker bad sent her to pawn the jacket. Her version was that she went to borrow is. from Mrs. Parker, who lent her the jacket which was handed to her by Lae defendant's daughter. Mr. Browne having obtained permission to treat the girl as a hostile witness cross-examined her and the girl admitted that she had told quite a different tale to the police. She again said that Mrs. Parker's daughter had handed her the jacket. The Chairman said the care must be dismissed. At the same time they felt the girl was responsible for the action as she had made statements which were abso- lutely contradictory. This had caused them to look tpon the business with a great deal of suspicion, but proof was not forthcoming. Mr. Steel mid that the case having been dismissed be bad nothing more to say. The Chairman said he thought it was better not to say anything. The case was dismissed.

div.head: MOTOR PROSECUTIONS. SEQUEL TO A SMASH AT WHITLEY.
div.p: MOTOR PROSECUTIONS. SEQUEL TO A SMASH AT WHITLEY.

The magistrates at the Daresbury Petty Sessions held at Stockton Heath on Tuesday were occupied a oon- siderable time hearing a case in which William Chadwick, Cringlewood, Whitegate-drive, Blackpool, was summoned for having driven a motor-car in a manner dangerous to the public at Whitley, on Jnly 22nd. He was further charged with driving without a licence. Mr. Steel appeared for the defendant. The case was a sequel to an accident near Grime- ditch-lane end. It was alleged that defendant, instead of keeping to the left when rounding the curve, travelled on the right, with the result that his car collided with a cnr belonging to Mr T A Dine, of Hartford, which was being driven from Warrington to Northwich. Toe oczupants of both cars were thrown out,and the defend- ant's car was so seriously damaged an to be beyond repair. On inquiries being mane of tho Blackpool police it was found that defendant's licsnce had expired about three weeks prior to the accident. The witnesses for the prosecution included Walter Gregg, who was driving Mr. Earle's car and who stated that at the time of the accident his car was almost at a standstill. The defendant's car was travelling at about 15 miles an hour. The defence was that Mr. Earle's car was being driven in the middle of the road at a speed of twenty live miles an hour, and it was in an endeavour to avoid- it that defendant turned to the right. With regard to the charge of driving without a licence, Mr Steel stated that before starting on his tour the defendant went to the Blackpool Police Station to renew his licence, and was told that he could not have one until the old one bad expired. The defendant said he would forfeit the remaining days during which the old licence ran, in order to get a new licence. He explained to the Blackpool police that he was going on a tour and that he might be away 14 days. He was told that it was not necessary, and that be could call at any police station on his way and obtain a licence. Time defendant, however, forgot that he bad not taken out a licence, but if be had tried at any other police station he would not have been able to get a licence because application must be made in the district in which one resided. The Chairman (to Mr H Roberts) : The Blackpool police must have known that the information they gave was false. It is surprising that an important centre like Blackpool does not keep a proper staff capable of giving licences on application. Mr. Steel : I believe that is so. Whether it is a slander on Blackpool or not— The Chairman : I don't say it is a slander, but if it is true it is a disgraceful condition of things. How- ever. we will leave it there. Mr Steel : I have even made an application to the Chief Constable of Blackpool that the constable should be here but he said it was not necessary, as be had written a letter. _ .
This letter was banded ta the Bench, but was not read in Court. •

The Chairman : It is a most improper positipn for the Blackpool authorities to take up, In my opinion. After bearing considerable evidence on both aides the magistrates retired, and on their return the Chair- man raid the charge of driving without a licence would be dismissed and a fine of 40s. and costs would be iLflicted in the other case. Walter Gregg, the driver of the Hartford car, wag summoned for failing to produce his licence when demanded by P.C. %Veiling. The defendant said be had a licence, but when it was demanded it was in another suit of clothes, he having forgotten to remove it. He was ordered to pay the cost. William Newsome, chauffeur. 34, Walton-villages Liverpool, was summoned for having, on the 20th July, in Victoria-square, Stockton Heath, while driving a taxi-cab, failed to produce his licence. Mr. Browne appeared for the defendant.—Sergeant White said that when asked to produce his licence, defendant said I am very sorry, but I have left it in my other clothes at home" It was, however, ascertained that the licence had expired.—Mr Browne said the defendant took out a licence on the 3rd July, 7911, and he was under the impression that it did not expire until the hackney carriage licence expired, namely, on the 15th August. This was the first charge which bad been preferred against him. The defendant was fined 10s. and costs.

div.head: Borough Pollee Court.
div.p: Borough Pollee Court.

MONDAY.—Before the Mayor (in the chair), Aldermen Bolton and Pierpoint, Messrs A Jolley, G Pilling, W Furness and W Roberts. SERIOUS ASSAULT ALLEGED.—Martha Jane Cunning- ham, 18, Cockhedge-lane, was charged with unlawfully wounding Annie Grady, of 30 James-street, on the 10th inst.—Chief Inspector Williamson, in asking for a remand for seven days outlined the facts of the case and said that on Saturday night the prisoner had a dispute with ber husband and had to clear out .Pf the house. She went into the-house of Mrs. Cuckran, 30, James-street, where the complainant who was a vcidow stayed, and considerable drinking of beer took place. Cunningham waut away, but returned at 11.15, alleging that the complainant had not paid for her share of the beer. A quarrel took place and Cunningham threw a cup at Mrs Grady, inflicting a nasty wound on the bead. They went into the street, whera they commenced fighting. Cunningham seised the complainant by the Shoulders and bit her bottom lip in a savage manner. Grady had to enter the Infirmary suffering from two ugly wounds. The case was adjourned for a week. LICEKSING TRANSFEM.—The following transfers were granted :—Glassmakers Arms, (Beerhouso) from Richard Robinson to Joseph Caldwell. Golden Grove, from Joseph Caldwell to Alfred Peters. Off-licence, • 12, Leicester-street, from F Binks (deceased) to Sarah Jane Bioko. Off-licence. Bolton's-yard, from William Pierpoint to Sydney Bolton. Off-licence, Thelwall- lane, from John Lythgoe (deceased) to Mary 1,3 thgoe. TUESDAY.—Before Councillor Henry Roberts (in the chair), Colonel Edelsten, Councillor C Jackson Holmes, and Mr J R Young. A WORKMAN'S TflEFT.—Rtchard Lawless, 16, Norman-street, was charged with stealing from Cock- hedge Mills ten pieces of leather, value Sc. 6d , the property of Masers. Armitage and Rigby. Chief Inspector Williamson stated that for a short time the prisoner bad been employed by a firm of contractors who were carrying out repairs in the mill, lie had to work at a time when the machinery was stopped and had access to a large portion of the mill. It was not until he was arrested for drunkennes at Widnes that the theft was detected, and he was found in possession of four pieces of 2 inch belting, which had been taken from the weaving department of the mills. Continuing

the Inspector said that all the works in the town suffered more or less through thefts of that kind. The prisoner was at that time 'wearing a portion of the leather on his clogs.—Prisoner, who pleaded guilty, was fined Os or in default 14 days. WEDNISDAY.—Before Mr. J W Hayward (in the chair), Councillor C Jackson Holmes and Mr NV T Williams. TnErT or BooTs.—Margaret Livingstone, 38, Garabaldi-street, was charged with stealing on the 13th inst., a pair of boots value 45., the property of Thomas Domville, pawn broker, 31a, Priestly-street. —Chief Inspector Williamson stated that about 4.30 on the day in question, Mr Flanaghan, the manager of the shop had, in consequence of having had things stolen from the front of toe shop, kept a careful watch. He saw the prisoner come to the front of the shop and handle a pair of boots which were hung up. !-.113e got them off and put them under her shawl aud went to her home which was just opposite the shop. As she was about to " enter the house the manager caught up to her and she said these boots are are my own. Information was given to the police and Detective-Sergeant Metcalf visited the woman at her home and she said "I have got jot this trouble through being very foolish." When charged at the police station she replied " not guilty." Prisoner who said she had only taken the boots to try on was sent to prison for one month with hard labour.

ALLEGED EMBEZzLEMENT.—George Jameson, a cab driver of no fixed address was charged with embezzling Ils, the monies of Hugh F. Greenhough,cab proprietor, Warrington, on the sth July.—Chief Inspector William- son in asking for a remand described the prisoner as a tramp: cab driver who had worked a great deal in Warrington. On the day in question be was sent to drive a lady from Beamont Schools to Central Station. She gave him an envelope containing us as payment of a small account to Mr Greenhough. Not having had a receipt or received any notification from Mr Greenhough she wrote and asked about the matter. The prisoner bad left Warrington in the meantime and a warrant was issued with the result that be was arrested at Widnes the previous day and admitted the offence to Sergeant Reddington.— Prisoner was remanded for a week. THEFT FROM LODGING-HOUSE.—Harriet Massey, 5, Stanley-street, was charged on remand with stealing between 24th June and the 10th July articles of bed- clothing from a lodging-house.—Chief Inspector Williamson said the prisoner had been engaged by a Mr McCabe as deputy in his lodging-house in Stanley- street. She came to the town six months ago in com- pany with a man. She went to lodge with McOibe and he engaged her as deputy. On Mrs McCabe making the beds she missed the things which it was afterwards ascertained had been pledged with different pawnbrokers in town.—Massey was sent to prison for 21 days.
TliTlP.SDAY..—Betcre Mr J Rymer Young and other

magistrites. A DEAR. SMOKE.—Harry Furness, of Furness-street. was summoned for smoking in a tram car on August 3rd and also with assaulting John Henry Cook, a tram con- ductor. From the evidence it appeared that the defendant boarded a Cemetery car in Church-street, proceeding to the Central Station. He was under the influence of drink, and was smoking a cigar. The con- ductor warned the defendant against smoking in the car, but he persisted in doing so. When the conductor asked the defendant: for his address, he pulled him about, and also threatened him. The conduct of the defendant was a source of annoyance to the occupants, and he made use of bad language. Defendant,who said he was sorry, was fined 40s. in each case.

div.head: Examiner, Saturday, August 17, 1912.
div.p: The Examiner, Saturday, August 17, 1912.
ROYAL COURT THEATRE.
"The Girl from the Jam Factory."

This play, which has been performed twice nightly during the week to enthusiastic and appreciative audiences, fully establishes the claims made for it by the producer, Mr. George F Story. It certainly is new and original and highly dramatic in action, the piece presenting, in the hands of the exceptionally capable company of players brought together, and headed by Mr. Story, a picture of life which is of intensely human inteiest. Some of its episodes appear daring in their startling truthfulness to nature as We see it manifest itself in the liver of men and women, but the art of the actress succeeds in main- taining the (sympathy of her audience for the heroine in al the vicissitudes through which she passes to her ultimate salvation. There are features in this drama which compel the consideration of all who profess themselves silicitous for the amelioration of the lot of the work-girls in our large manufacturing centres. The author, Mr. Frank Dix, provides the material form and Mr Story and his company give it life, and the rapidly moving panorama of incident allows no interval for dulness to intervene. The principal character is of course the Factory Girl—Maggie Dench—sustained by Miss Maude Stewart-Drewry, aud her impersonation exhibits to us a fine character study of the habits and manners of the ordinary working girl of London's East End.. Her dramatic power, which is remarkable for so young an actress, and her emotional instincts, are exercised most judiciously with the greatest effect ia the many critical situations which the drama unfolds. Mr. George F. Story plays the pirt of Rainy Mullius, a young sprig of no particular occupation, who ultimately btossoms into tha professional book-maker. Mr Story in his acting is v,latile and versatile, his speech and his actions provoking continuous mirth. He is indeed, the life of the play. The part of Old Abel (Maggie's uncle) a bibulous old schemer who sponges on his niece for his board and lodging and stoutly maintains his tight to apply his Old Age Pension solely to the gratificatiou of his craving for liquor, is played by Mr. Dan Mining and in the hands ot this capable actor is one of the strong elements in the success of the piece. A dominating figure in the play, up to a certain point, is that of Theodore Cornell, a wealthy and not over scrupulous financier, and this character was impersonated by Mr. E. Story-Gofton, a consummate actor of great experi- ence, whose delineation gives the most perfect realisa- tion of the relentless usurer who will allow no hindrance to stand between him and the accomplish- ment of his schemes, but who at last falls a victim to the vengeance of his poor clerk, Scrivsie Hicks, who has been tyrannised over to the p int of revolt and under a fieuzied inspiration shoots his employer. Mr. Story-Gofton is a most capable and finished actor and his presence on the scene commands the rapt attention of the audience. The clerk, Scrivvie Hicks, was acted by Mr. Royce Milton, who gave a most con- sistent portraiture of the poor dependent scribe. In the scene where he turns the tables on his master and terrorises the man to whom he has hitherto cringed, Mr. Milton rose in his strength as if transfigured by the justice of his cause. This scene was rendered nmst effectively. Leonard Merton—the ptoprietor of the factory—was played by Mr. Eric J. Laugham— who gave a spirited rendering of a somewhat weak and thankless part. The Rev. Peter Rock, a devoted cleric, working in a poor parish in Bermondsey was very faithfully depicted by Mr. Fred Goodwins as also Doctor Abbis by Mr. Johnston Clive. The small but important parts of Perkins (valet to Merton) and Inspector Dewhurst of Scotland Yard were efficiently performed by Messrs. J. Williams and G. Francis. The other female characters were Esther Morrison, an heiress represented by Miss Florence Rutter with a naturalness which wasmost charming,and Flo Hastings of the Six Little Dicky Birds Troupe, very cleverly played by Miss inlet Kendal. The success of the company during the week should ensure crowded audiences at both houses to-night.
