div.head: OPEN-AIR POLITICS.
div.p: OPEN-AIR POLITICS.
TORY REVOLUTIONARIES.

The Warrington Progressive Labour League resumed its open-air campaign on Monday evening when a largely-attended meeting was held at Bridge- Foot. Mr. J. Elwell presided and the principal speaker was Mr. Robert Lewis, of Manchester, _

The CHAIRMAN briefly reviewed the work of the Liberal party since it took office in 1906. He made special reference to the abolition of Chinese Labour in :south Africa, the extension of the Workmen's Compensation Act, the passing of the Trades Disputes Act and the attempts—temporarily checked by the House of Lords—to deal with the education and licensing questions. Latterly the Old Age Pensions Act had brought untold benefit to millions of people. Now they had the Insurance Act, which the Tories were crying about E 0 much. That measure dealt with some of the most pressing social problems that could con- front, any country. With regard to th 4 sanatoria benefit, experts told them that consumption could 11, wiped out in two generations, and if the Act did nothing but help them to grapple with that scourge it deserved their goodwill and appreciation. The Act helped the worker at the time when he most needed help. Many men provided against sickness but a large proportion, through indifference and carele4sness, bad neglected to make any provision. The result was that when sickness had overtaken them, they had had to go to the Guardians and beg almost on their knees, for assistance. What p licy had the Conservatives to bring before the country? They had hal tne sorry exhibition recently of sirne leaders of that party

wanted to see him going over. (Laughter.) Sir Edward Careen was going over, but a story was told oft. general who in the Crimean War was in the midst of the bullets all the time—but it was where the ammunition waggons were. (Laughter.) He (the speaker) had an impression that that was precisely where these rebels would be found when the time of struggle came. (Hear, hear.) The only part of Ireland where they got intoler- ance was the part where Protestantism said it was strongest and best Was it fair that the population of one province Ehould dictate the policy of the rest of Ireland ? ("No.") The Roman Catholics asked for no special privilege, for they recognised that the Irish question was one of politics and not of religion. They were not prepared to barter their political freedom for any privilege a Government might be prepared to grant them ecclesiastically. ftlr Boner Law and Sir Edward Carson could talk as they liked, but before two years were over, a Parliament would he set up in Dublin. (Applause.) The Government was also

REDRESSING THE GRIEVANCE OF THE WELSH PEOPLE. Many people felted about Disendowmeut and said it was robbery. The Wein case, however, had been before the electorate at repeated general elections with the same result. Even in the worst year of Liberal reversal-Iboo-27 men were sent to the House of Commons by the Welsh constituencies to demand DiFeqahlishment in that country. At present 30 of the 03 Welsh members w,re returned to support that policy. As for the other three, they had majorities of 9, 13 and 57 respectively (Laughter.) The endowments Abich were dealt with in the Bill were gifts to the whole nation. True they were a gift for religions purposes, but one section of the community had collared the swag and now, because they were called upon to surrender Borne of it, they turned round and said "Robbery." The Bill would take away the special privilege of a particular sect. If they took the most favourable figures that Lord Hugh Cecil could

div.head: FIRST WATERPLANE FLIGHT UP THE THAMES.
div.p: FIRST WATERPLANE FLIGHT UP THE THAMES.

A remarkable waterplane flight was made on Saturday by Mr. F. K. McClean, who flew from Eastchurch to Westminster. Mr. McClean flew between the upper and lower bridge of the Tower Bridge, and under all the others, until he reached Westminster. Unfortunately, on making the return journey, the airman found a, steamer in h:s way, and

in attempting to change his position be tilted too sharply, resulting in a "sideslip," caasing some of the stays to break. The machine then had to be towed into the Lon- don Docks. The picture shows the machine passing under Blackfriars Bridge, and, in the inset, Mr. McClean.

div.head: PREACHING REVOLUTION.
div.p: PREACHING REVOLUTION.

If during a strike a leader of the workingmen had attempted to give utterance to half the revolutionary things that bad been said by Mr. Boner Law, Captain Craig and others, he would soon have found himself in prison. (Hear, hear.) IVhat, was wanted was progress by evolution. They did not want to resort to those cruel methods which often put back the clock of pro- gress and rivetted the chains more firmly upon those who tried to force progress by revolution. The other part of the Conservative policy was tariff reform. Would Protection, if adopted now,briug abcut any different results from those which were experienced in the old days when it was in operation in this country ? It destroyed our trade in the past and he contended it would do so in the future. The missionary of tariff reform, when he first propounded his polioy,told us that cotton, wool and iron were' going," and that, we were a decadent nation. The country was never in such a prosperous condition as at the present time. (Applause.) Our natural resources were nothing in comparison with those of Germany and America. Half the iron produced in this country was made from foreign ore. On the other hand, Germany produced nearly all the ore she consumed, while America produced practically the whole of the ore I from which her iron was made. We got our spelter from Germany and our tin from other countries. Nearly all the minerals which went to make the industries of this country so prosperous, came from abroad. Our great natural resource was coal; our next resource was the industrious people of this country, and we did not want to keep those people down as slaves. We wanted to see them rise to their manhood and live better, cleaner end more hopeful lives. He believed the policy of the present Government tended to uplift and broaden the outlook of every worker. (Applause.) If tariff reform was a curse in France and Germany—and the workers of these countries would tell them they believed Free Trade would be better for them—if it encouraged trusts and made it impossible for trade unions to exist there, what would It be in this country which was so small that the whole of the industries could soon be under the control of combines ? Tariff reform, he contended, would cripple moat of the trades of this country and tend still further to enslave the workers. (Applause.) Mr. R. 'Awls began his speech with a reference to the North-West Manchester election. He was bound to say, from his knowledge of Manchester elections, that they never had a candidate who more splendidly advocated Liberal principles than Mr Gordon !lowan. (Applause.) The other candidate was not in it, and if it had been a question of brains, the Liberal would have been at the top of the poll. ;Applause). There were, however, a great many people in that neighbourhood a ho could not see why they should be called upon to pay for the insurance of their workers, although they quite admitted that they made their living out of them. It was only fair and right that the people who earned a living for somebody else should he insured, exactly the same as the building and the machinery. (Applause). The human machine was the motive power of industry. One employer who objected to paying under the Act said " I am going to get nothing out of it," but he was going to save a great deal on workmen's compensation. He was going to avoid a number of minor .accidents, for the man who went to work in a good condition of body and mind was not so liable to meet with accidents as the man who was in poor health. With regard to employed persons, a complaint some- times heard was that the benefits were not payable before six months had elapsed. There was not a friendly society in any part of the country which was prepared to take in aaybody who cards) along, withont a waiting period. There were, however, some which, for the payment of about ss. down, were prepared to take the responsibility of paying out henelits straight- away. The most magnificent feature of the Act was the provision for sanatoria and the treatment of consumption. Illustrating the need for that provision, Mr. Lewis pointed out that the South Manchester Board of Guardians had opened a sanatorium at Abergele and the Clerk to that authority had stated that it had made his heart ache to see the number of men and women who had come to him when they were beyond cure, and for whom there was no hope. The Board proposed to double the accommoda- tion because there were so many people in their area who must have sanatorium treatment if their lives were to be saved. The sanatoria clauses of the Act were to come into operation at once. They could not,however, have everything done immediately in a cut and dried way,and yet the Tories said the Act ought to have been delayed until everything was ship-shape for the treatment of consumption. Seventy-five thousand people died every year of consumption, and the immense majority of them were poor. The Tory pro- posal meant that at least one half of those 73,000 would go down into death without any hope, if there was any postponemont of the sanhtoria clauses of the Act. Were they prepared to endure that ? No. What they wanted was to secure some measure of treatment whereby consumption could be prevented. Nobody was ever born with it. Consumption was a develop- ment, arising largely from conditions of living. The Act would look after the health of the workers and safe- guard them from the evil influences which bad so long dragged them down. And yet the Tories said " VVe want to put it off." They would PUT OFF ANYTHING except tariff reform—and they would put that off when there was a danger of losing an election. (Laughter 1 and applanse.) Everybody knew that tariff reform was the rottenest plank, the most hypocritical suggestion that ever been made in this land. (Applause.) The whole programme of the Liberal party was comprised in freedom for the individual and a larger share for the the Individual of the wealth he produced. In produc- tion of the nation's wealth he must also he safeguarded from untoward accident and illness. The Liberal pro- posals with regard to
IRELAND were simply a matter of justice. "06," said Mr. Boner Law," we will tight." (Laughter.) He (the speaker)

rake together, only 163,060 were members of the Church in Wales, whereas there were 0G9,000 members of the Nonconformist aenoroinations. Who ought to rule— the majority or the minority ? The Government also intended to pass another much-need reform—" One man one vote." (Applause). He did not mind confessing that he hoped it would not only be manhood suffrage but that intelligent women would also have the vote. (Applause). The Government was going to settle the education and licensing questions. (Applause). Brewers ' and parsons might do what they liked, but before this Government went out of office, they were going to have such an era of Liberal legislation as some or the old men had hardly dreamed of. (Applause). Mr. CorrEun.r.,, in proposing vote of thanks to the speaker, referred to Unionist professions with regard to housing reform. He pointed out that the Liberal party intenoed to go to toe root of the difficulty by dealing with the land question, and housing reform would naturally follow. (Applause).

div.head: COUNCILLOR KENDALL AND THE MANCHESTER ELECTION.
div.p: COUNCILLOR KENDALL AND THE MANCHESTER ELECTION.

The incessant rains of Wednesday evening renderr•d it impossible to bola an open-air Liberal Meeting in bt Austral; Ward as arranged and the meeting was there- fore held in the Liberal Club. There was it fir attvnd- ance and the chair was occupied by Mr A Tilling who, in calling upon the speaker, Councillor James Kendall (Manchester) expressed their deep regret at not being able to hold the meeting in the open-air as originally intended. NORTH-WEST MANCHESTER ELECTION.

---• Councillor KENDALL, who has charge of one third of the North-West Manchester constituency, spoke at some length on the recent election there. One of the first things he saw when he came to Warrington was the big blue bill with the result of the election on it and also the words "The Government or the stamps have Rot to be licked." He had just come through the great fight and knew some- thing about the constituency. It was not a case of licking the Government in North-West Manchester. It was an absolute defeat he would admit, and it was one the people in the constituency were disturbed about. It simply showed that in by-elections in that division there was something which did not exist in many other constituencies in the couutry. He was chairman of the residential portion of that division and after having gone carefullyithrough the figures be had found—and his findings were confirmed by Unionist officials—that in that part of the constituency there had only been a turn-over of 50 votes. That did not say there was much licking of the Government. The Insurance Act was not popular with pertain sections of.ithe people and the Conservatives were going about telling lies about the Act. If anyone lied hard enough there was always someone who would believe what was said. He felt sure the residential portion of the town was sound and solid for the Government and that they appreciated the workings of the Liberal party. Tartu in a city like Manchester there was that old monstrosity the plural voter, the man who came into Manchester for perhaps onfy an hour per week for his business and got a vote on the same terms as the man vino payed his rates and taxes there and worked in the constituency. The politics of the man who only came in the town for an hour were cot very serions and if he happened to get a bet for a new hat he voted for the sake of getting new headgear. If a man had got 6 to 1 on Sir John Bandies the chances were that his vote would go for that gentleman. (Hear, hear and laughter.) The great imperial questions were treated use shuttle-cock by those men. (Hear, hear.) He believed the election was lost through the plural voter. (Hear, hear.) That was probably the last, time they would use their plural votes and it was not likely they were going to vote for a Government which was going to wipe away one of the greatest monstrosities of the 20th century. Everyone ought to be. thankful the Liberal Government were carrying through the franchise reform. (Hear, hear.) North-west Manchester would not go the same way at a general election he felt sure. Both tho bye-eletions had been lost, but look at the number of successive times they bad won on the occasion of a general appeal to the people. Tnere were people who did not take a byo-election seriously and thought it did not matter how they voted. Continuing the Councillor said that ever since the Liberal Government came into power in BAG they had been stopping what was known as the swing of the pendulum." (Gear, hear.) They had tackled three great interests in the couutry—clericalism, land and liquor, and they were sitting on the top of them and not letting those three great interests sit on the top of the British public. Dealing with the Insurance Act and the objections raised against Lloyd George, the speaker said that Lloyd George did things in a piactical and tangible way as he had done by placing the great Insurance Act on the Statute Book. (Gear' bear.) The class of people who denounced hint were those who had self interests at stake and thought more about them- selves avesthan the good of the community at large. There glorious programme of social reform for the Liberal party and they had started well with the Budget, tne Old Age Pensions, and now the Insurance Act, and there were other things to come for the good of the people of this country. (Hear, hear.) They would not fear a general election when once the benefits of the Act had been received by the people (Applause.) Sir John Handles had said that the issue ' at Manchester was not Tariff Reform, and now the seat had been won,it was claimed as a Tariff Reform vktory. (Shame.) The Tory party was the party of anarchy. It was the Lib q.als proud claim that they had had to protect the King against the Lords and aristocracy of the country. (Hear, hear.) In regard to the preroga- tive they had protected the King. When the Tory party were giving sanction to rebellion, bloodshed, spoil and war and doing all they could

to cause it, they lost men like Mr. Cockshutt, who felt he was not going to be a party to such tactics. There would be a great cleavage in the near future, for there was a party of men who would not to bow down to the tariff reform doctrine. (Hear, hear.) He would like to see Sir Edward Carson's name removed from the privy list because it was a great anomaly that such men should be members of that Council and should be allowed to go about and speak as he did. (Hear, hear.) Liberals had a stern fight before them and if only they would all pull together they would win, and it would be a win for the people. (Applau3e.) A vote of thanks to the speaker on the proposition of the Chairman was unanimously given.

div.head: GOVERNMENT AND .TORY LEADERS.
div.p: GOVERNMENT AND .TORY LEADERS.
SPEECHES AND ACTIONS BEING NOTED. Sensational Development. UTMOST RIGOUR IN CASE OF LAWBREAKING.
The "Dundee Advertiser," an influential journal circulating in Mr. Churchill's con- stituency, in its issue of Thursday, contains the following announcement :

We have good reason for stating that the Government are at present watching very closely the sayings and doings of Mr. Bonar Law, Sir Edward Carson, Mr. F. E. Smith, and other leaders in the Unionist party. It is regarded as doubtful whether any- thing these gentlemen have said or done so far brings them within the law, but there is ground for believing that acts of a lawless character are in preparation, of which persons in high position are cog- nisant, and which will bring inflammatory speeches already made into a legal relation- ship with the facts. Mr. Smith has told the country that something very startling is in preparation and will probably take place before the resumption of Parliament. Sir E. Carson has proclaimed his inten- tion of going over to Ulster and breaking every law that is possible in order that Englishmen may be " kicked " out of apathy. In the event of disturbance the Govern- ment will act with the utmost rigour and with stern judicial indifference to the position of offenders. In somewhat similar circumstances, it is worth recalling, Mr. Parnell and several of his associates were arrested and lodged in Kilmainha m. TREASON FELONY INDICTMENTS _ BEING PREPARED. _

In relation to --t-hi-s—s—u-bje-c.t---a. significant passage appears in a letter by Sir W. P. Byles to the Liberal Press on Wednesday Sir William writes : There are signs that Mr. Bonar Law is preparing a retreat for himself. He says, "I don't anticipate civil war "—that is to say, lam only trying to frighten you. To that end there is to be another demonstra- tion in Belfast next month, followed, no doubt, by another pogrom of poor Catholic workpeople. Then the Bill will pass, and I confidently predict that Mr. Bonar Law will draw in his horns, for he probably knows that indictments for treason felony are preparing in the Attorney-General's office.

div.head: PRESENTATION TO A SECRETARY.
div.p: PRESENTATION TO A SECRETARY.

A very interesting ceremony took place at the works of William Robertson Ltd.,Latchford on Saturday last, the occasion being a presentation to Mr T Collins. the late secretary of the company, who is going out to Australia in the interests of tlis wife's health.

Mr. Wareing (manager) expressed 'lJB—sorrow at losing the valuable services of Mr Collins. Mr Collins had been with the firm since the incorporation of the company 13 years ago, and he believed that the firm owed its prosperity in a great measure to his efforts, his able judgment and diplomacy. lie was very sorry indeed for the cause of their departure for Australia,and he sincerely hoped that the change would do Mrs Collins good, and restore her once again to good health. He had the greatest pleasure in asking Jr Robertson to make the formal presentation. Mr Robertson (chairman and managing director) also expressed his sorrow at Mr Collins severing his con- nection with the firm. He had known him for about 20 years, and be felt he was losing a great friend. Mr. Collins w s a very able commercial man, well versed in all the branches of the engineering trades, and he had always found him to he courteous and attentive to his duties. He also mentioned the fact that Mr Collins was a Fellow of the Chartered Institute of Secretaries, a very notsqs di, ino ion, rnl se felt sure that any firm who might employ him in his new c .untry would get a very able Man, or if be went into business on his own account, he had every confidence in Mr Collins making a success of it. Mr Robertson said he was sure Mr Collins would look back on his connection with William Robertson, Ltd., as a very happy reminiscence. He had the greatest pleasure in asking Mr Collins to accept an illuminated adclress and a purse of gold, and for Mrs Collins a cabin trunk, from the directors, staff, work- men and a few friends. Mr Robertson then presented Mr Collins with a swan, gold-mounted fountain pen, being a present from Mrs Robertson sod himself. Mr. Collins in reply said he did not know bow to thank them all. It was a very trying time of One'li life to leave old associations and friends, and it was very hard for bim to break his connection with the firm, as, being secretary since the commencement of the com- pany, he felt as though the work had becomes part of himself. He also thanked Mr. and Mrs. Robertson for the pen, which be knew would be of the greatest ser- vice to him in his new life. Mr. Collins hoped that the relations of the workpeople and the firm would always be of the same cordial nature as in the past, and that the firm would have the same prosperity—better if possible—in the future. He had the greatest pleasure in accepting the very beautiful illuminated address and the purse of gold Dri his own account and the cabin truns on behalf of his wife, and he thanked all alie had in any way associated themseivea with this presenta- tion.

_ Mr Short mentioned how sorry they all were to lose Mr Collins, and he knew they would miss him very much in the future. He hoped hewever, that Mrs and Mr Collins would have every prisperity, and that Mrs Collins would soon regain good health. Mr Wareing then introduced the new secretary to the company, Mr R Monk, and be hoped that they wbuld give him all the help they could. Mr Monk in reply hoped they would give him all possible help, and if in a few years hence he could command half the respect they bad for Mr Collins, be would be well satisfied. fhe ceremony closed with a vote being passed wish- ing Mr and Mrs Collins every prosperity and happiness in their new sphere.

Wycliffe Congregational Church. The Rev William Evans, of Llandulas, conducted the services at Wycliffe on Sunday last, when his fine presence, voice and powerful sermons proved very acceptable and inspiring. In his address to the children in the morning he spoke of his recent visit to Verona and drew helpful leesons horn a Latin motto inscribed on h building there" Pro summi fidei, summus amor." "In return for much confidence, much love." Love grew not by faint mistrust but by confidence and trust. Faith increased love. Mr. Evans sermon to the older members of the congregation was based on John iii., 8, " The wind Wowed) where it liateth. . . . so is everyone that is born of the Spirit." Mr. Evans' exposition of the theme was much appreciated. At the evening service a numerous congregation assembled and listened with great pleasure and profit to a forceful sermon on Rev. xxi. 27, "There shall in no wise enter into the Holy City anything that defiled). . . . . . but they which are written in the Lamb's book of life." The preacher said that the long list of names, and of genealogies, in the Book of Chronicles seemed to us unnecessary and wearisome but they were dear to the Jew and of vital importance to him because they represented those who were enrolled in their Book of Life. The children of Israel claimed relationship with God, the Fount of Life. Unbroken descent in the line of Israel was a title in itself. Neither wealth nor capacity could of themselves obtain entrance. Birth seas the test. Hence enrollment in the Book of Life depends first on our conscious relationship with God the Father, through His son. Connection and character make the claim valid. Genius is not to be mentioned in the same breath with gentleness ; power is not so good as purity. All the preachers preached this, and for us it raised personal questions. Are you an enrolled citizen ? Are you an enfranchised soul ? Is your name on the burgess roll of the Heavenly City ? We are born tha children of God. We can be born again through the love and power of Jeans. To be twice born is best Tne preacher for to-morrow (Sunday) is the Rev. A. Lee, of Seaforth.

CHAPTERS. ELIZABETH DUTTON " WIFE, WIDOW AND MAID."
'ORY OF THE DUTTONS, OF DUTTON.

The roadside tragedy at Tarvin brought to an end the long line of the Duttons of Dutton. From Odard, who took Dutton from William the Conqueror, to John Dutton, father of the unfortunate bridegroom twenty generations had succeeded each other. The direct line now came to an end. Three years later upon the death of John IDutton the Dutton estates passed to his daughter who by her marriage became Lady Gerard. The young bride so tragically and pitifully bereaved was a member of the Egerton family, her grandfather being Lord Chancellor of England whose homestead was at Dodleston five miles west of Chester. Her friends and family felt the pathos of her sad experience and erected over her rest- ing place a fine memorial_

Here is interred Elizateth Dutton eldest daughter of Thomas Egerton, knight, eldest son of Thomas Egerton, knight, who bears the office of lord Chancellor of the great seal t f England and baron of Ellesmere. She was the wife of John Dutton, of the most ancient family of the Duttons. But a wife, a widow and a maid. She died 2nd day of October 1611, having lived 16 years, 4 months and 21 days. The same most Doble baron of Ellesmere, Chancellor of England, a most indulgent aLd sorrowful grand- father, has, in his love for his dearest grand- daughter placed this here. 1] CHILDREN'S CORNER, Conducted by UNCLE CALEB.

_ A CHINESE OPINION OF US. I have often seen boys and girls staring after Chinamen and Japanese as they have passed them in the street, and have no doubt they have been thinking of them as very curious creatures and full of peculiarities. So they are from our point of view ; but does it ever occur to us that they think of us as being curious top. Just read the following lines. They are what an intelligent Chinaman wrote as his opinion upon the English : " Englishmen spend whole months without swallowing the smallest quantity of rice. Instead they consume an astonishing quantiy of beef and mutton. Their baths are frequent. Their apparel is the same, in the case of all the men, that is to say, and to judge from appearances they arc all workmen. They carry no fans, no umbrellas; they seem to be ignorant of the utility of these things and disdainfully leave them to the women. Not a single one of them can boast of nails more than a tenth of an inch long. At their meals they use forks. They never take a holiday to go and sit on the tombs of their ancestors, but they run and give great kicks to leather balls as if they were paid to do it. They have no idea of dignity, else they would not be seen walking with women." NED'S TWENTY-SIX SERVANTS.

- - " I wish I had somebody," sighed doleful Nod, "To spsll my hard lessons for me; I try and I try—but the words are s-) long I never can learn them," said he. " Why, call on your servants," laughed big sister Nan, " They'll do all your spelling for you. Just tell them to take their right places, and then The spelling is done -it is true ! " " My servants !" and /sTcd's two blue eyes opened wide. "I -rye never had even one." " You have twenty-six," said his sister, " in all !" And she just bubbled over with fun. " All you've got to do (as I told you before, And lam mite sure that you heard) Is to tell each wee servant, Run quick to your place,' And presto ! they've spoiled you the word. I "The servants are a, b, c, d, e and f,
_ And all the rest down to z ; They not only help you, tney do all the work In spelling the word—don't you see?" FAIRY AND CHILD.

Oh, liAen, little Dear-My-Soul, To the fairy a °ices calling, For the moon is high in the misty sky And the honey dew is falling; To the midnight feast in the clover bloom The bluebells are a-ringing, And it's "Come away to the land of fay" That the Katydid is singing. Oh, slumber, little Dear-My-Saul, And hand in hand we'll wander— Band in hand to the beautiful land Of Below, away elf yonder; Or we'll sail along in a lily leaf Into the white moon's halo— Over a stream of mist and dream Into the land of Below. Or, you shall have two beautiful wings Two gossamer wings and airy, And all the while shall the old moon smile And think you a little fairy; And you shall dance in the velvet sky, And the silvery stars shall twinkle And dream sweet dreams as over their beams Your footfalls softly tinkle.

div.p: A WOMAN'S CRUEL SUSPENSE.

"There were times when I felt that something terrible was hanging over me," writes a Bradford lady. "Pain, and the fear of pain, had made me unfit for work or pleasure. I knew that for three or four days every movement would be a drag." This is the case of thousands of women. It is not only pain, but the fear of pain that makes them pale and anxious- looking. But note what follows "Thanks to a friend, I have put all that behind me She gave me what was left of a bottle of Lydia E. Pinkham'a Com- pound, at the time whin I was really beside myself with misery. Almost at once I began to feel better. My beck and loins were not so racked : after the next dose I felt able to move about a little, and by the morning I was almost myself." This is the experience of a refined, educated lady in a good station of life. A sister-woman had been her friend. She was eager to pass on the good news to other suffer- ers from the same ailments. POPULATION IN PANAMA CANAL ZONE. NEARLY HALF BRITISH SUBJECTS. Despatches from New York correspondent say the the report of the census recently taken in the Panama Cenal zone shows that the total population of 62,810 resident in the zone, no fewer than 30,859 or nearly half, are British subjects. The number of United States citizens in the zone is 11,850, Panama coming third with 7,636. Of tbe total populstion, 19,413 are white, 41,525 black and 516 yellow; while 10,323 are of mixed blood,

A ST. HELENS ITEM. On Monday morning, Mr. Charles areenvv sad, upon whom that appointment was conferred the other week, entered upon his new duties as engineering assistant in the surveyor's department of the St. Helens Cor- poration. The promising young fellow (he is 23 yea's of age) is a native of Todmorden, and came under my persmal notice when I was stationed in that district about a dozen years ago. He was then attend- ing one of the elementary day schoo's in that borough. In due course he Tamed to the Secondary school, and eventually entered the office of the surveyor to the Corporation. By means of evening classes at Burnley and Manchester which he regularly attended for special inattuctirn along the lines he had chosen, he made steady and solid progress; and, when a project was launched for the complete sewerage of the district, he was often entrusted with the oversight of important sections. A while ago, he accepted a private engagement with an eminent Manchester firm having a remarkable clientele and a big staff, and so added materially to his already varied experience. Thus, yourg Mr. Greenwood comes to St. Helens well equipped for the work he has undertaken, and assuredly ha will do credit therein alike to himself and those who have chosen him for the position in question. "THE FIGHT AGAINST CANCER." The Rev. A. M. Mitchell's characteristic article in his Parish Magazine brought to my mind the sensation created a few years ago by the claim of a Mr. John Clay, of Hebden Bridge (which is four or five miles over the county border beyond Todmorden) to the dis- covery of a cure for cancer. I promptly ran over for an interview with the bold layman, and was somewhat impressed by his confidence in his new remedy. More- over, I kept the movement under observation for some time, and found among the numerous patients from far and near who sought his aid quite a number who to all appeatance distinctly benefited under the treat- ment. However, now that the excitement at first caused has subsided, I cannot learn what promised so well at the outset is being continued. As far as lam able to gatber,the bad old conditions still unfortunately pre. vail. Mr. Mitchell's strong advocacy of vegetarianism as the panacea for this, not to mention many other ills that those who have a weakness for the fl sh pots are supposed to be heirs to, recalls for me a time when an equally earnest professor of the cult of the carrot thrust into my unwilling hands a bundle of terrible vegetarian tracts, one of which, bearing the ominous title " The perils of pork," was calculated to spoil one's keen relish for one's breakfast bacon, and to cause a nervous reader to dream dreams and see vi-ions of a horrible and untimely fate compared with wh:ch that of the miserable suicide were enviable, if not positively blissful. How these well meaning faddists do love to make our flesh creep! Perhaps it serves us right for having flesh. But, then, how about the vegetarians themselves ? I daresay some will be ready to point out that all flesh (all human flesh, of aourse) is grass ; but that were to lay them open to pretty obvious retort. CURIOUS BEQUESTS. The frequent paragraphs respecting local wills in the news columns of this paper set me thinking on the general subject, and brought to my mind several remarkable bequests. There was that of the outraged husband who some 80 years ago left his widow £5OO, with the proviso that she was not to Come into the enjoyment of it until after her death, in order that she might be buried as became his widow. On the 27th of next month will be celebrated at Sherborne, in Dorptshire, what is thereabout known as "The Earl of Bristol's Tolling Day." By the will of Baron Dighy, Earl of Bristol, in 1698, a sum of money was left for the bell of Sberborne Abbey to be tolled all day, and for a special sermon to be preached. Browne Willis, the antiquary of Fenoy Stratford, was equally deter- mined that his death should be kept in remembrance, for he left money for the annual firing of guns, known as "Fenny Poppers," for a church service, and a dinner at the Bull Inn. So was one Randall of St. Miniver, Cornwall, who provided for a minion to be preached on December 27th for one thousand years These latter are mentioned in "Chambers," along with many others, and to which I can add only the following :—On Midsummer Day under the will of Isaac Duckett, who died in 1620, the interest of the sum tol four hundred pounds, which he left "in order to encourage fidelity and long service among domes- tics," is distributed in sums varying from twenty pounds to five pounds among eleven people dwelling in the parish of St Andrew's, Holborn, who have been in one service seven years. 0 ing to various social changes since the fit st distribution was made in 1639 chief among them being the disus tn, of the City of London as a residential centre, and tale fact that faith- ful domestic service has ceased to be an object of pride and self-satisfaction— the scope of this charity has been altered and widened. Of a similar character is the bequest of one Meyrick of Launceston, in Corn- wall, by which, on July 12, the first day of Lauceston Fair, what is known as "pretty maid's money," amounting to two pounds ten shillings, is bestowed on an elected maid of good character and regular attend- ance at church. GOOD FUN. At the Primrose League garden party at his tempor- ary residence in the Middleton Division, Mr. B. S. Townroe, the prospective Unionist candidate for that extensive constituency, told his supporters that his wife and be could honestly and frankly say they had never in all their lives had a happier summer than the present one. Fle attributed this unexampled felicity to " the kind welcome which the electors in the division had extended to them." I quote from a local paper, a copy of the current number of which was sent to me early in the week by a journalistic friend cn the spot. According to the report, Mr. Townroe, after touching upon national insurance and other questions, went on to advocate the need of a strong and reconstructed Second Chamber, and the necessity of a strong defence for the security of our homes, and said that Unionists

CONCERNING WEDDINGS. -

Pre(fy weddings of Eufficient local interest to warrant more cr has extended press notices are of almost weekly cecut rem e. There are some remark- able superstitions associated with such events. The old rhyme that had to do with the days of the week still holds considerable power in the choice of the wedding day in 801113 distticts. Iu Scotland one seldom hears of a Saturday wedding, while in both France and Ireland Sunday is the favourite day. The Romans consideied Wednesday the luckiest of the week, and the old rhyme referred to carried out the same idea. It runs:

" Monday for health, Tuesday for wealth, Wednesday the best day of all; Thursday 1r crosses, Friday for losses, And Saturday no luck at all!" The old superstitions anent the wedding gown have been rhymed to suit almost every country and every class of wearer. The rhyme hath it: " Married in white, you've chosen all right. Married in blue, you will be true. Married in yellow, ashamed of the fellow. Married in green, ashamed to be seen. Married in gray, you'll live far away. Married in brown, you'll live in the town. Married in red, you'll wish yourself dead. Married in black, for luck you'll lack."

OLYMPIA. The circumstances under which Sir Gilbert Greenall has become intimately associated with this great London show place were explained in these columns a week ago. For myself, I never have any sort of rrminder of Olympia but I think of the time when it was the subject of a popular song. Some of those who essayed to sing this in public i culd persist in pronouncing the leading word " Olymphia." I last heard it so rendered at a Liberal gathering which I had attended for the purpose of reporting a presentation. An entertainment litid been arranged, and the offender was a humorist who had been engaged to contribute to the evening's gaiety. We ceitainly laughed a good deal when he came to detail his frivolcus doings at" Olymphia." Each recurrence of the leading word—which was often repeated,cspecially in the chorus—tickled his hearers immensely. Since then, the fortunes of 'Olymphia" have varied consider- ably, and this district will follow future developments with peculiar interest.

They were spoiling for a fight in the Middleton Division, and they would be there when the time came, fighting shoulder to shoulder in a true spirit of comradeship, fighting in a great cause. "We shall (he said in Closing) be fighting for the defence of the Church in Wales, for the union of Ireland with this country, and for the union of our colonies with this country. We shall be fighting for the union and the welfare of all classes under that old flag, the good Union Jack." Good old, never-failing Union Jack! I was on the look-out for it all the way along as 1 read. div.head: OUR UNIQUE TOWN HALL.
div.p: OUR UNIQUE TOWN HALL.
WILL PROPOSED ALTERATIONS SPOIL IT?
INTERESTING COUNCIL DEBATE.

For a considerable time the inadequacy of the Council Chamber at the Town Hall for the purposes of the numerous meetings held within its w ills has ben a source of complaint, and a scheme for the alteration of the building, so as to afford better accommodation, has recently been under consideration. There is, however, fear in the minds of certain mem- bers of the Council that the proposed extension will detract from the appearance of the building and this view found expression at the meeting of the Town Council on Tuesday evening. The question arose an intimaticn that the Borough Surveyor had sub- mitted to the Town Hall, Parks and Baths Committee, his instructions t‘i architects, and conditions for com- petition for a proposed new Commit Chamber or in the alternative f,r the alteration of the existing Council Chamber, which be was authorised to have printed and to advertise for tenders in the local papers. Alderman SMETHURST moved and Councillor HALLIWELL seconded, the passing of the minutes of the Committee.

Alderman BENNkTT moved an amendment that the miuu'e be referred beck. He said he had eeldom approached a municipal question with a graver sense of responsibility. They all admitted that the present Council Chamber was not ideal and they admired the public spirit of the Mayor in raising the question, but they bad stood the Chamber, with all its faults, for forty years and the improvement could not be des- cribed as really urgent. It would be much better to move slowly and to bear the disc mfort a little longer than to make a mistake on such a vital matter. In his opinion it would b 3 wiser to wait until they were able to consider the question as part of a scheme for the centralisation of the municipal offices. They could ntt afford that at present, but it was bound to come, and any proposal which was not part of a definite and well-considerei scheme would neither be economical nor satisfactory. The Town Hill was their principal municipal jewel. Built in 1750, by Gibb, the famous architect, for Thomas Patten, it bad excited the admiration of each succeed- ing generation in its turn and had attracted the atten- tion of all our visitors. It was quite unique in its way and he hal a horrible fear that, if they began to meddle with it, they ivJuld do somethine to derogate from its beauty and uniereeness. Ile would like to see the hall left exactly as it was and, when they wore able to afford new municipal uflices, including a new Coun- cil Chamber, to see it retained RS the official home and headquarters of the Mayor. But if they were to alter it, surely it ought to be with the utmost care, and with the assistance of the most skilful architects they could obtain. The proposed conditions of competition had obviously been tastily thrown together reed would be fatal to any hope of reit success. rho premiums to be offered for the best designs—twenty guineas, ten guineas, and five guineas respective iy—were ridiculously inadequate and it would be useless to expect architects of real eminence to compete, lie was usually in favour of local architects, but this matter was so importset that they ought to endeavour to attract the skill and experience of the hle profession. Under proper conditions any aribitect in England might be proud to chip in and have the credit of designing such a scheme. As it was, the architects were limited to two proposals, both of which were objection- able. To enlarge the present Chamber successfully he r believed would be impossible. It would interfere with the lights in the basement and destroy the steps and the beck elevation. If they adopted the other alternative and built the Chamber at one end of the building, they would have a difficulty as to levels and spoil the balance of the building. Further, there were no restrictions as to the materials to be used. He could not recall a single local building of importance which had been enlarged without its architectural beauty suffering to some extent, lie was not criticising the skill of the architects but somehow they did not seem to try to carry out the alterations in the same style as the original building. He instanced the Drill Hall, the Infirmary, the School of Art, the Museum, Wyoliffe Church, the Grammar School, the Training College, and the Cemetery Lodges. Generally several kinds of stones and bricks were used and in one case he counted no fewer than nine kinds of chimney pots. (Laughter.) The very first essentill to a successful scheme was that any extensions should be carried out in strict accordance with the original style and in the same material. Discussing alternatives, Alderman Bennett said that if the building could be extended on the lines of Harewood House it might be made even more dignified and attractive than it was, but that would probably be expensive. Then the Council Chamber might be provided on the right of the building is part of a large scheme. A further suggestion was that a separate Council Chamber, in the form of the Rotunda, should be built on lawn at the rear of the existing building. It would be symmetrical, comfortable and easy of access, and it would not destroy the steps or any other feature ef the ball. He implored the Council to send the minute back and defer the matter until it could be considered as patt of a large scheme or, if they insisted upon having a new Council Chamber now, to offer an adequate premium, to give the-architects a wider lati- tude, and to make one vital condition that, under no consideration, should the scheme be allowed to inter- fere with the beautiful proportions or destroy the harmony of that building which was their greatest local treasure.... _ _

Councillor PRInfIEnTON seconded the amendment. He did not agree with one-half the Alderman hitcl said, but there was a great deal in the pltm that the question should not be rushed. This was such an important matter that it should have been brought first before the General Purposes Committee. It was possible to extend the building in a satisfactory way. He did not I agree with the suggestion of Alderman Bennett that a separato structure should be erected as a Council Chamber. It would be a great shame to build anything en that lawn. (Hear, bear). If a wing could be added at each end of the building and the municipal offiees arranged in them, it would not spoil the architectural effect. Alderman Bennett had frequently jumped on him (Councillor Pemberton) for venturing to find fault with architects, but hs (Councillor Pemberton) had never before heard such a criticism of the archi- tects of Warrington as Alderman Bennett had uttered ; it was the moat sweeping condemnation he had ever heard. What the Alderman had said was true but in the case of the Infirmary it was probably a question of cost. When an architect was tied down to a certain expenditure he could not exercise much choice with regard to materials. He (the speaker) disagreed with Alderman Bennett with regard to the amount of the premium, !IR many architects would probably be only too willing to compete for the honour of carrying out such a scheme. The premium offered for plans or the new Liverpool Cathedral Was only zno. It would be a pity to spoil the architectural beauty of the Town

Councillor JENKINS: Beauty . Councillor PEMBERTON : Yes, it is a beautiful building-- The Merort : Of its sort. Councillor PEMBERTON said the building was of a pure style of architecture and well-built. They could not expect the ratepayers of Warrington to build such municipal palaces as were to be found in Manchester and Liverpool. The rates were high enough and be should oppose any great expenditure at the present time.

The Mayon said be had taken a great interest in 1 this matter, and he had a special grievance. It had I been said that this matter had been rushed. There had , not been much sign of rushing ; it had been the other way about. He (the Mayor) had waited patiently after the matter was referred to the Town Hall, Parks and Baths Committee, to see what would be done. At intervals of two, three or four months be had attended meetings of the committee and had brought the matter ' forward, but he had been put off from time to tirne,and finally the present resolution was passed when he I was absent on Mayoral business connected with the town. That raised the important question of the relations of the Mayor towards the Council. He said , this more in the interests of his successors in the chair than in his own interests, and he Epoko very plainly. Certain duties were imposed upon the Mayor, and it was hard upon him when it was known that he might be absent, or it ought to be known, that questions should be introduced in which he took great interest and which he bad brought forward. (Hear, hear.) He did not say that the convenience of the Mayor should invariably be studied, but if it could be done without unduly postponing or damaging the business, a little in stance he should be shown. In the present he knew nothing about the conditions of competition and had never heard of them until that evening. If other members of the Council were in the same position it was quite sufficient reason for postponing the matter. The alteration of the Town Hall was a difficult qual. tion. They were all agreed that the Council Chamber wanted improving but they did not want to spoil the beauty of the building. It was therefore expedient that they should get the beet talent by throwing the work ore!' to competition, but whether they would obtain it by offering e larger premium be did not know. He was inclined to think that Councillor Pemberton might be right in his view that the honour of sending In the best design and the fact that the successful architect would probably have the supervision of the alterations, would make a comparatively nominal premium sufficient. That, however, was not a matter that he would lay stress upon. Alderman BENNETT : For Market Gate circus we offered a premium of fifty guineas, and that was limited to local architects. Councillor IltrertEs said he was informed that the proposed conditions of competition were not even read to the committee before they were approved. He did not know whether the committee really knew where they were. The addition of two wings to the building , would make very little difference to it, if built to con- form with the present architectural design, In addition

to a new Council Chamber, they were all agreed they wanted additional offices for the clerk. Twonty-yeare ago they acquired land in Sankey-street upon which to build their municipal offices. Those offices had not been htarted,and would not be for another twenty years. They ought, therefore, to be determined to have the best possible scheme for the enlargement of the existing building. There was hardly any Town till in England that was so beautifully situated. Ho thought the matter was so important that a special committee ought to be appointed to deal with it. (Hear, hear). If that committee had special powers it ought to push the matter forward without the procrastination that had been experienced in the enlargement of the public bat ha.

Alderman SM ETII URST said the matter of the exten- sion had Leon discussed on and off for the last fifteen or sixteen years. They did not want any classical architects on the building, and he did not see where all the fantastical work came in. They wanted the addition simply to correspond with the present building. They did not propose to alter the style one iota. Councillor JAcKsog HoLmits, referring to Alderman Bennett's suggestion that the lawn at the rear of the building might ba used for the erection of a new Council Chamber, said he had always been under the impression that when the hall was purchased for the benefit of the town nod largely subscribed to by private gentlemen, an undertaking was given that the green was not to to built upon. The MAvon : No. At the same time I agree it would be a great calamity to do away with it. It is one of the great charms of the place. (Hear, hear). Councillor JENKINS supported the appointment of a special committee, presided over by the Mayor, in order that the matter might be more fully and carefully discussed. He bad not seen the conditions of competi- tion and knew nothing whatever about them. Councillor PEMBERTON : Shame. Councillor JENKINS : Your mannerisms and your nonsensical observations don't appeal to me. I don't appreciate them at all, and I am not going to have them without dissenting. The MAYOR : I cannot help thinking that on this occasion Councillor Pemberton meant it sincerely. Couucillor JENKINS : I don't care what he meant. I don't intend to have these paltry observations mode to me. My observations are perfectly sensible, that is from my point of view, and I have a perfect right to my own opinion. I don't usually try to make an ass of myself, and am not going to do to-day. Councillor PEMBERTON : I did mean it sincerely, as you say Mr Mayor. I think it is a great shame that the committee have not seen the conditions. If Councillor Jenkins likes to think it nonsensical he can hold that opinion. Councillor JENKINS : Councillor Pemberton is in the constant hat it of making the exclamation "shame" to gentlemen who are speaking in this chamber, and I am quite at liberty to regird his observation as a rude and unnecessary one. The MAYOR: It is the case of the boy and the wolf. Councillor Pemberton does it very frequently, but I cannot help thinking that on this occasion he was right. As far as I can gather very few of the members of the Council have seen any of the conditions named in the minute, and that in itself is quite enough to make me vote for the amendment. This matter has been before the Council previously, and I don't know why they did not form a committee at that time. Councillor STEEL asked if the appointment of a special committee would mean that they would get any more forward with the question. If they referred the minute back, the Town Hall, Parks and Baths Com- mittee would probably wash their hands of it. Councillor PEMBERTON : Hear, hear and a good job too.
.- - Councillor STEEL : We will be bandying it about from on, committee to another.
On a vote being taken only Alderman Smethurst and Councillors Cunnington and Halliwell voted against the amendment, which was, therefore, carried.

div.head: INSURANCE ACT.
div.p: INSURANCE ACT.
Deductions for Sanatorium Benefit.

The National Health Insurance Commissioners have issued an Order stating that for the purpose of defray- ing the expenses of sanatorium benefit during the period between July 15.1, 1912, and January 1261 1913, both inclusive, there shall be deducted from the amounts standing to the credit of deposit contributors and from the amounts standing to the credit of approved societies such sums as may be determined by the Comm;ssioners to be necessary for the purpose of meeting the expenditure incurred in connection with the provision of sanatorium benefit during the period, not exceeding in the case of a deposit contributor ld. for every four contributions paid in respect of him during the period, and not exceeding in the case of an approved society Id. for every con- tribution credited to the society in respect of the period, and all sums so deducted shall be transferred to the proper insurance committees. No deductions are to be made from the amounts standing to the credit of deposit contributors not entitled to sanatorium benefit, and contributions from such deposits are not to be taken into account in calculating the amount to be deducted from the ' amount standing to the credit of an approved society In the application of this Order to aliens three is• to be substituted for four and 1-3rd is to be substituted for id.

div.head: tALL RIGHTS RESERVED.
div.p: tALL RIGHTS RESERVED.
GUY HALLIFORD'S SECRET.
By BEATRICE HERON -MAXWELL, Author of "The Clerk at Pay Corner," "The Doomed Name," "The Adventures of a Lady Pearl Broker," "A Forbidden Love," &e.

"I cannot help wondering, Mrs. Ilallifori," said Sir Richard Weylesmore, contemplatively, "how it is that you never write yourself. Your opinions are marked on most subjects, and you seem to possess originality; you are reflective and .Iritical. Yet your husband,who appears devoid of these qualities, gives to the world interesting and Jeliglstful books, beyond the average, while you are silent."

They were sitting on the balcony,with fragrant boxes of mignonette and scented geraniums all round them; the light from the street-lamps below falling on Selena, and glancing here and there on the folds of her white dress. It was an attractive face, with its soft,ereamy paleness, its intense dark grey eyes, its frame of brown, gold- tinted hair, worn in a fashion peculiarly her own, that seemed uncommon and yet not out of date. Sir Richard, criticising her, as he had often done before in the short time he had known her, could find no fault either in features or figure. Both were harmonious, refined, graceful, and both possessed a distinction that claimed his admiration. Yet he was difficult to please, as his fifty years of unfettered bachelorhood emphasised. She looked across at him smilingly. This man, of all the men whom her husband ifiwited to the house, pleased her best. She liked the strength expressed in the dark, handsome face, in the length and breadth of limb, in the dignified bearing. She had even began to feel a certain confidence in him, as women of strong natures feel instinctively in natures stronger than their own, but sympathetic. "I don't know why it is," she answered after a pause. "I should like to write; it would interest me more than anything—but I can't. It was the same when I was a girl; they used to let me off my essays at school because I invariably went to sleep over theni. There is some strain of indolence in me that asserts itself as soon as I put pen to paper." "But you write letters," lie said; "and, if you will allow me to say so, very charming ones." "They involve no effort," she replied. "If I began to consider what I should say, as one must in the ease of a book or an article, I should succumb at once."

A burst of laughter came at this moment through the open window. Selena glanced into the drawing-room and noted her husband's flushed face as he dealt the cards round for bridge. The laugh was a boisterous and discordant one. It seemed out of place in the cool quietness of this flower-scented balcony. A shade crossed her face. Sir Richard noted it, and remembered that it was not the first time that a laugh or speech from her husband had brought a temporary cloud to h expression. Ilc too glanced at the card players, while he said: "I am interested, as you know, in the study of characters ; it is, in fact, my chief hobby. Your husband puzzles me even more than you do; he seems to have such a keen love for cards or any kindred amusement From my observation of him on this and many evenings, I should have said that his tastes were not intellectual, yet his writings are a direct contra- diction to that idea. You don't care for cards, Mrs. Halliford ?" "Not at all," die said "I almost dislike them.

There was 'evident reticence in her words. She avoided discussing her husband with anyone. As a matter of fact, there was no bond of union between them except his literary work, though in that respect he had no more ardent admirer than his wife. She always felt as if he had said exactly what was in her own mind—what she would say herself if she possessed his powers of expression. She rose, and, stepping inside the room went to the piano and sang and played softly room, the rest of the evening, Sir Richard meanwhile cogitating over this problem that had begun to occupy a place in his thoughts of late. They were BO incongruous, this husband and wife; he could never reconcile them together in his mind. And there was the additional surprise that Guy Halliford's personality had been to him in its marked contrast to the books upon which the world had been pleased to set the seal of its approval. There must be more in the man, he told him- self, than appeared on the surface. But as he caught from time to time his jarring laugh and noticed his face, it seemed almost impossible to believe that any great work could come from him, and when the evening ended and he took his leave, he felt that he had come no nearer to a solution than before. .

"What a wet blanket Weylesmore is," said Ilalliford, as the door closed on tho last of their guests. "He may be useful to me later on, other- wise I should drop him." Selena looked at her husband in surprise. His handsome face wore a more restless ex- pression than usual, and his eyes betrayed that his mood was not a very sober or peaceable one. "He seemed to me clever and interesting," she remarked, quietly. "Oh, yes, you women always succumb to egregious vanity," he sneered. "Weylesmore has a reputation for clever talk and for fastidious taste in his selection of a listener. You are com- plimented because he preferred talking to you to taking a hand at bridge." "I did not think of it in that light," she replied, gently. "It seemed to vie only ordinary politeness, as there were sufficient men to make up the game without him. Besides, he told me he did not care for cards!" _ _
"Of course not. Men who have plenty of money to lose are seldom interested in anything that risks the loss of it." _ -

"Did you lose much, Guy?" "More than I could afford. The luck was all against me." "But," she continued, "we have a balance at Coutts's, have we not? Your last hook--" He interrupted her curtly. "Is paid for, and the money spent. There is nothing for it but to write another. Simpkin asked me for one the other day. Look here, what do you make of this plot ? " _ _

He drew her down on to the sofa beside him, and sketched in rapid phrases a very ordinary drama of modern social life. Selena listened, endorsing, supplementing, correcting, idealising, until when, with the suggestion of a few concluding sentences, the idea seemed complete, she said, enthusiastically: "Oh! that is very good, Guy. I like that immensely. Write it at once, while it is all fresh in your mind. Don't let it simmer and coo/ down.; it won't be so brilliant."

"Ali right," he said, "I'll and write now. You go to bed and to sleep." She stood for a minute in the doorway, looking back at him and telling him not towork too hard, and something in her face and voice appealed to him with unwonted power. He crossed the room to her and kissed her with a tenderness that she recognised as unusual. In spite of her sympathy with him in his literary career, she had found it an effort lately to keep herself from drifting apart from him. The social and domestic sides of his nature were so uncongenial to her own. His love of gambling, in any form, distressed her; his constant money difficulties, coupled with an invariable refusal to curtail any expenses that touched him personally, filled her with a weary disgust at times; and she had grown a little tired of life lately, and felt that there was a void in it which her husband had _never filled and never would till.

She pondered over all this and over his sudden accession of fondness for her, and went to sleep With a great regret in her thoughts that the intellect she loved in him should be so spoilt by all these other failings of mind and heart. Meanwhile Mr. Halliford, seated in an arm- chair in his study, with a cigar and a brandy- and-soda, was burnieg the midnight oil in the pursuit of comfortable leisure instead of that of the fickle goddess Inspiration. Now and then he consulted his betting-book, with an exclamation of annoyance after each little sum in addition. Finally he rose, walked to the writing-table, and unlocked the centro drawer where lay, in packets, sheets of MSS. closely written in an orderly hand. The outside pages of each bore the name of the book, with his own added beneath it, in a different handwriting; He looked at them with a .singular concentration of regard, a gaze that held in it a hint of mistrust and shrinking, a possibility of fear. A curious onlooker, surpris- ing him in this attitude, with this expression. migns nave guessea that some secret inn:dying dishonour held him under a spell. Yet, in common with most .offenders against 'al; written or unwrAten; ho did not at any time

div.head: Examiner, Saturday, August 17, 1912
div.p: The Examiner, Saturday, August 17, 1912

seriously contemplate discovery; it seemed to him impossible. Nevertheless, he himself preserved the only proofs that could render it possible. He put aside some of the packets, in search for one I pecial manuscript, and, finding it, read it through with many exclamations of irresolution and disem.tent.

"I'm afraid it wouldn't do," he said at last, out loud; "it is too disconnected. She must have lost the thread. Yet some parts of it are so good. If I only had the sense and energy to put it together myself! He leant his head on his hand after this strange speech, musing and perplexed; and while he sat lost in a reverie the door of the study opened noiselessly, and Selena, her long hair falling in a cloud over her shoulders, her white dressing-gown draping round her in diaphanous folds, advanced slowly into the room. Her eyes were bright, and fixed with the unseeing gaze of one who sleeps. A look of pleasure flaPhed across Halliford's face as ho caught sight of her. Quickly and silently, as one performing an accustomed task, he placed pencil and paper on the table, while he watched with breathless anxiety Selena's movements.

Without the slightest hesitation she seated herself at the table, in the chair that her husband had vacated, and took the pencil in her hand. There was a momentary pause while her fingers strayed restlessly about as though in search of something. Then she drew the paper towards her, and began to write rapidly. Meanwhile Halllford stood close behind her chair. His attitude was one of extreme nervous tension. He scarcely dared to breathe for fear of breaking the spell and rousing her to con- sciousness. Familiar as he had become with the spectacle of his sleeping wife at work, he had never been able to suppress a feeling of horror at the sight. To-night he was more than usually apprehensive. An intense stillness was over everything. Only the regular sound of the pencil working its way over the paper and the ticking of a clock disturbed the silence.

Nearly halt-an-hour passed, anct the steeper still wrote on. To the guilty watcher behind her it seemed an eternity. And yet, as page after page was completed, his satisfaction grew. Suddenly there broke on the stillness a sound in the room beneath—a sort of stealthy scraping and grating. Halliford listened intently. It came almost as a yeller after tho deathly quiet. With a flash of intuition he understood that it must come from someone entering the house below.

For a moment he paused, irresolute, realising his dilemma. He dared not leave Selena, and ya he dreaded still more the effects of noise or any sudden shock to her. On the whole it seemed best to go down and face the cause of the dis- turbance.• In physical courage he was by no means wanting. All his pluck returned to him as he crept noiselessly downstairs to the basement. Ho stood still in the dark passage and listened. Grasping the stout stick he had brought from the hall he turned the handle quickly. The latch caught with the movement, and before he could enter the room two men sprang upon him. There was a sharp scuffle. The stick was wrenched from his hand and fell with a clatter; he was conscious of a terrific blow on the forehead and a piercing scream from the room above. Then he tottered and fell heavily, and all turned to blackness.

To Selena, as she wrote, there had come a fearful shock. The pencil dropped from her hand, and she sprang up from her chair with fright trembling in her limbs. Her terrified gaze shewed her that she was alone in the dimly- lighted room, with a great clamour going on beneath. Her brain reeled, and for a moment she felt as though her mind were unhinged. Then realisation came to her. She had been walking in her sleep. Her gazo fell on the closely-written pages before her, and almost mechanically she gathered them up and com- menced to read. The words danced beneath her eyes, as gradually it was forced upon her bewildered brain that it was a story in her own handwriting, the very story, too, that she had discussed with her husband that same evening.

• She noticed the open drawer, the key of Zell was always kept by Halliford, and she could feel no surprise when she found it contained the whole of the last novel, published in his name, and written with her own hand.

Everything was so strange to-night—so strange But the groan that reached her ears roused her remembrance. Something awful had happened, and her husband was hurt. Taking a lighted :iandle she found her way downstairs, while a sickening horror crept upon her. She longed to scream, to cry out for help, but fear paralysed her. She stumbled over Halliford's prostrate form as she entered the kitchen. ....... .

Ha'llford was dead The heavy fall had pro- duced concussion of the brain, and he died on the morning of the third day. There had been no hope that he could survive, and his suffering made a speedy termination desirable to those most wishing him to live. Selena nursed him with unwearying patience, refusing to quit his side even when exhaustion rendered it almost necessary. She was waiting for the moment of conscious- ness that she knew would come before Lt.-. end, when remembrance would probably Kiturn to him of what had happened just before he was struck down. Would he recall the fact of having left her at the writing-table ? Would he understand that she now knew everything ? The moment she anticipated came, and as his eyes, wandering and dazed at first, sought and dwelt upon her face, their expression changed to one of dread and appeal. His lips moved, the words hovering on them too breathless and in- distinct to convey any meaning. But Selena, kneeling beside him, understood. "Don't try to speak, Guy," she said, in low, clear aceentg, laying her hand gently on his. "Listen, dear. I know all—and I forgive, freely and entirely. No one else shall ever know." , Tears of regret and weakness shone in his eves; i he pressed her hand n grateful response, and no other word was said. Before the day ended he had drifted peacefully away. In the exaltation of spirit that had been hers during the hours that he lay dying, Selena had never fully thought out nor appreciated this question of right and wrong between herself and him. She had allowed her mind to approach only one side of it; to make allowances for his weakness of nature, to feel that the punishment of knowing she had discovered his secret and of dying in the belief that he was condemned and

untcrgiven for it would be too great for tnis sin of his against honour. She resolved to think of nothing but the necessity of setting his'mind at rest, if an interval of sufficient consciousness should make it possible. But when all this was over, and the whole matter ranged itself clearly before her mental vision she felt an inexpressible loneliness in her bereavement that was beyond the ordinary sense of widowhood. _ _
The knowledge of the deception that had been practised on the world and on herself descended like a wall between her and the man who had been her husband.

It created a deep gulf between them, on one side of which he stood, no longer the man whose shortcomings she felt were atoned for by the higher and intellectual part of his nature, but a stranger to her. A man who, for the sake of a repute, a name, the passing distinction of an hour, had sacrificed his honour and had practi- cally lived a lie. She could imagine how he must have by chance discovered this extraordinary dual power she possessed of retaining in her sleep the memory of what bad interested her mind in waking moments and of using it as the foundation for a capability that was denied to her while her physical life was in the ascendant. She sought to make excuses for him, suggest- ing to herself that he might have feared her losing this power if she were conscious of possessing it, but an answer presented itself at once. If this consideration influenced him why did he not publish the books anonymously? Their own merits would have ensured as ready a sale and as high a price as any that the addition of an author's name could command.
- • Ilis motive, then, could have been only one of self -glorification,. of dishonest trading on another's claim to the esteem or admiration of the world.
Guy Halliford was dead to her, and she felt that there were no memories, no dream, no cherished thoughts or hones to take his 'dace

div.head: FUNERAL OF THE BOY SCOUTS.
div.p: FUNERAL OF THE BOY SCOUTS.

Impressive scenes were witnessed in the All along the route the streets were lined streets of South London on Saturday after- with thousands of people, who waited for noon, when the funeral of the eight boy scouts, hours to pay a last tribute to the dead boys. who "let such a tragic end at Leysdown a Our photograph shows the procession after week ago, took place at Nunhead Cemetery. leaving St. John's Church, Walworth. .

Rim tOnsoie nee tired heart; for to her ne nan never really existed. The Guy of her girlish affection who had wooed an won tier,wouia long since, in revealing the wholly material nature that was his, have alienated her from himself, as she gradually awoke to the comprehension of all her own intellectual faculties demanded. In his place had come someone who satisfied her sentiments at idealism, and so bouna ner to himself by a chain woven of fancies and beliefs, through which the glimpses she caught of his real self were constantly obliterated by fresh links. She felt now that she had been living a dream. life, and that the husband who played a part in it had faded away as dream-figures fade at dawn. But the morning of life Wa9 still hers, and she resolved to rouse herself and live her best in spite of all that had happened. The tragedy of her husband's death, occurring as it did just when his fame" as an author had begun to make his name prominent, attracted universal attention to his widow, and Selena, tired of evading the sympathy and curiosity with which she was besieged, went abroad to find in travel and change of•seene the rest her mind and soul needed.

It was a year and a-half before she returned to London, and one of her first visitors was Sir Richard Weylesmore. "You are well ?" he said, solicitously, taking her hand. "I have been wondering so much how the world has gone with you. What have you been doing with yourself, Mrs. Halliford ? " "I have been writing," she answered, with a faint blush. "I have overcome the indolence I told you of and persuaded my brain to work at my will at last." "Your book is published P" "It has been accepted by a publisher." ' "Is it true," he asked, "that you have with- drawn the books written by your husband, and have forbidden the publication of any new editions ?"
"It is quite true," she replied, quietly; "that part of my life holds memories that are dis- tressing to me. I wish to forget it entirely." "I will never refer to it again," he said. "I understand."

For an inkling had come to him that Guy Halliford's literary success —always a matter of perplexity to him—had been due in some way to his wife's assistance, and the admiration Sir Richard had felt for her from the first deepened now to a stronger feeling, a love that was reverential.
It was on the day when the book was published that he ventured at last to tell her all that was in his heart.

"Your past shall be a sealed book to me, Selena," he said. "I shall not ever try to turn its pages; it is your present and your futuro that I want. I have never asked any woman before to be my wife, for I have never until now found my ideal of womanhood." And Selena felt that with his words the last shadow of her dream-life was dispelled—she had reached the haven where she would be,
[THE END.]

div.head: FLOWER SHOW AT PENKETH.
div.p: FLOWER SHOW AT PENKETH.

To secure" the home beautiful " is the Englishman's one ambition in domestic life and the fact that land- lords have 'seen the resessity for and ate including small plots of land to be used as gardens to almost eveiy modern house, is viewed with an immense degree of satisfaction by all. It is true there is not much evidence of pregrtss in the aft of horticulture in the towrs, wit. re the atmospheiic conditions are anything but encouraging, but a stroll into the ne;ghbouring suburbs and villages reveals the ideal home surrounded by trim gardens, well stocked with sweet smelling flowers and shrubbery. In face of the discouraging conditions in the town and the increased inters st in the villages, it is not to be wondeied at that hotticultural shows are declining in popularity in the towns, whilst from the villages C 011129 the news that similar functions are meetieg with uniaalified success. Penketh, like many similar places, prides itself on its possession of many ardent enthusiests in the exit of horticulture and the annual garden and cage bird show is always a popular event. The 19th of the teries weis held on Saturday aud an encouraging result accrued. The show is held under the auspices of the Penketh, Sankey and District Garden and Cage Bird Society - an otgan'zatica worked by a willing body of intelligeot officials whose one aim it is to provide the best fur their patrons. A large marquee was filled with various kinds of flowers, vegetables and fruit, and the entry was a record ose all round. The weather el the pest few weeks has been just the opposite of " growing weather," and as a ems( qucnce the exhilitions of roses and sweet peas suffered considerably. A special feature of the show was the exhibition of wild fl mess olle.tsd by the children aho had bsen g.estly I mow:lw d in tier work by the new school master (Mr. D.
