"The xhibi ions if brush w rk and essay writ.ng by the children wells very praiAlverilly and the show all thrcugh was a very good me. The vegetables 1 xhibited were pa, ft ct and the judges wet e greatly impressed by this branch. In the cage bird section wt re to be seen many fine specimens if gay- plumaged bitds and this section ef the show is very po ular. Those who lent decoiattons of Ills ors eX: t. were Mr and Mrs C E Parker, Mr J B Aitken, Ms Robert Garnett, and Mr Philip Garnett, and the com- mittee were very gr it. ful to all of them as well as to these vvho had assisted ia any way. There was a go, d attendance chr, u,-hout the day and the Penkets '['anti' ry Pe ize Band played nurneious eelecti us of delightful music as well as accaunpanj it g the gay couples who redulged in dancit g. Three clever sod spect cular perform- ances of an old English dance were given by 16 girls under the dire( tion of Miss F. Watson and these received she whole hear fed approbation of all. A few remarks were given by Dr. Slurray on the poi,ularity of the Council School venture in the encoulagstneut I the children in the art of horticultu e and botany, evidence of which was aff tided by the fact that the gardens had been so well kei t thst three extra prizes bad had to be given. Extra prizes had also to be given in other Kellen:B of the children's classes. (Applause.) Mr. Watson the late schoolmaster had examined the essays and brush work and there is ere no fewe r than ten highly cum nended and seven com- mended. It was plain that the children's interest was increasing as they grew older aid that was a goad sign. (Hear hear, and applause.)

div.head: OPENING CERENION Y.
div.p: OPENING CERENION Y.

The opening ceremony was perfi rmed by Mr. E. A. Murphy who said they were thankful and proud in the possession of so many beautiful and well kept gardens In the villege. (Hear' hear.) They were eve r increasing In beauty and size and that was q die a good sign. It was one of his few firm convictions that the happiness 'of mankind and the human rice could be increased by cultivating that love of the beautiful which was more or less in all of them. A pleasing feature of the show was the encouragement given to the children in garden- ing. (Hear, hear.) He thought the spirit of rivalry was a good thing for them. (Hear, hear.) The %hole show was a good thing, for they must have the spirit of rivalry to stimulate them in their efforts. (Hear, hear.) All the exhibitors must, he felt sure, he proud of the good resells of their extensive labours and he had great pleasure in declaring the show open. (Apple( se.) Mr. J B. Aitken, in proposing a vote of thanks, said competition Wl,B the finest thing in trade and alto in horticulture. (Applause). Mrs:Garnett, in seconding, said that was a depart- ment of their village life which had grown from the time when a few beds of flowers were put in the infants school} ard. (lleer, hear.) The exkibits on this t ciasion were certainly below par because of the weather, which was a thing they could not cot trol and complain of. The exhibits by the children were now large, and they were highly pleased they were making such rapid pro- gress in their work at the Council school. She was glad the CJuncil schools throughout the country were developing in the hearts of the childri n that glorious love of flowers. (Hear, hear.) It augured well for the coming men and women of the village that when they grew up and when they had pa dens of their Own, they would see the results of what had teen going on in the Council schools. (Hear, hear a d pplause.) She was thankful to s.y they lad mai ng much to complain of about the children and the destruction of flowers. They were growing pto be typical ladies and gentlemen, and she saw an improvement everywhere. In the direction of the education of the people in the benefits of temperate habits and the parents' behaviour towards their faruilies, there was a marked improvement. Their lives and indeed everything was better, and they were well on the way to perfection. (Applause).

div.head: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
div.p: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.

CRUELTY AT WIDNES. At Widnes on Monday, Henry and Mary Cosgrove, 13, Grenfell-stteet, WitlDefi. were charged with neglecting thetr four children. Mr. Poole, N.S.P.C.C., said the mother was of drunken habits, and the husband alleged that she sold the furniture and children's clothes and spent the money on drink. The husband said they had had three homes in two years, and whenever he bought anything for his children, his wife sold it the next day for drink. He had not ssen his wife sober for three months. The magistrates said that on the understanding that the man would find a home for the children be would be acquitted. The woman was sent to gaol for six months' hard labour.

div.head: RUNCORN RURAL DISTRICT COUNCIL
div.p: RUNCORN RURAL DISTRICT COUNCIL
The fortnightly meeting of the Runcorn Rural District Council was held at Dutton on Tuesday, Mr. Linaker presiding.

SANATORIUM SCHEME. The Clerk read a letter from the Clerk to the County Council stating that conferences bad recently taken place between representatives of the County Councils and representatives of County Boroughs of Birkenhead, Chester, Stockport and Stoke-on-Trent and the non-County Borough of Wallasey, with a view to the provision and maintenance of IA sanatorium for the treatment of patients suffering from pulmonary tuberculosis, with the result that sub- ject to the approval of all the interested Councils it nad been agieed to constitute a combined area by an order of the Local Government Board in accordance with the scheme the print of which was enclosed out to three paragraphs of which the Birkenhead representa- tives objected. The average population of the com- bined areas on the basis of 30 members to constitute the Joint Committee equalled 39,619 per representative and the accommodation to which each constituent authority would he entitled under the scheme was as follows :—County, 56 compulsorily insured and 14 other than compulsorily insured ; Birkenhead, 16 and 4 ; Chester. 4 and 1 ; Stockport, 12 and 3 ; Wallasey. 8 and 2 ; and Stoke-on-Trent, 24 and 6, a total of 120 com- pulsorily insured and 30 other than compulsorily insured. The Council were asked to appoint two reprEsPntatives to attend a conference. The Chaim an said the matter was a very important one, and in view of the tact that it was impossible to form any ides of what the scheme would cost it was imperative that the matter should be considered very carefully. On the proposition of Mr. Davies, it was decided that the Chairman and Mr. Woodward attend the Conference as delegates from the Council. A letter was read from the Local Government Board enclosing copies of an order which they had made pre- scribing the manner of domiciliary treatment of Insured persons suffering from tuberculosis of which they approve tor the purpose of Section 16 (1) (b) of the National Insurance Act. The Clerk pointed out that the matter would come up for consideration at a meeting of the County Council.
REGULATING HOARDINGS.

A letter was received from the Clerk to the County Council enclosing copy of Bye-Laws passed bv the County Council under the Advertisements Act 1907 with regard to advertisement hoardings, to be operative in a number of Urban and Rural Districts of the County. The Clerk having read the whole bye-laws, The Chairman said they were most useful regulations. (Hear, hear). IMPROVEMENTS AT HALTON AND KELSEY. The Clerk reported to the Housing and Town Planning Committee that the tender of Mr. John Garner of Halton, which was accepted at a previous meeting for alteration at Bates Bridge property, Halton, had been withdrawn and that he (the cleric) had accepted the tender of Mr. John Henry Green amounting to £293 2s. 3d. on behalf of the Council. The action of the Clerk was confirmed. The Committee accepted the tenders of Mr. Hugh Davies for conversion of privies to W.C.'s and other sanitary improvements in Helsby. Toe minutes of the Committee were approved. SUCCESS OF WATER UNDERTAKING.
------ The Chairman referred to the success of water under- takings in their area, and said that the balance from the water works at Frodsham was equal to a rate of 22d in the £.

div.head: DANGEROUS _ROAD AT HILL CLIFF&
div.p: A DANGEROUS _ROAD AT HILL CLIFF&

When the question of the roads of the district were up for consideration, Mr Britch said the approach to Hill Calle Chapel at Appleton was in a very dangerous state. Formerly the road was very narrow, but owing to the erection of property on one side, it had been widened considerably and the chapel now abutted on the road on the north side. The result was that the steps leading up to the chapel jutted out into the toad quite three yards. There was only a single railing fence as protection, and when winter came there would be no warning on a dark night, and anyone coming up the road would be likely to come into con- tact with the fence on the edge of the steps. He sug- gested that a small committee be elected to visit the place and report. Mr Hallows seconded and said the trustees would be willing to meet the Council in regard to the danger of the stops. ' The preposition wns unanimously carried. sitwErtecit AO WATERWORKS. The Council having asked Messrs Wright and Hamlyn for an estimate of work required in preparing plans showing sewage rad water works within the Council's area, the Surveyors replied to the effect that it was almost impossible to give any idea as to the amount of work entailed in preparing such plans and suggested that the arrangements should be on the same lines as they at present hold the surveyorsbip. The clerk said he had felt for years that the Council were in a hopeless condition with regard to sewers and water works. It was decided that the surveyors pre- pare an ordnance map showing where the Warrington Corporation water mains unlit in tho,Councirs district and to treat Stockton Heath first. RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
The fortnightly meeting of the Guardians was held on Tuesday at Dutton, Mr. J. Spruce presiding.

div.head: LATE DR. CARRUTHe,RS,
div.p: THE LATE DR. CARRUTHe,RS,

Prior to the general but-iness of the Board being transacted, the Chairman referred to the death of Dr. Carruthers, who was their medical officer for Halton District. lle moved " that they tender to the widow, their sincere sympathy and condolence on the sudden death of her hosband. They assured Mrs. Carruthers that the Guardians appreciated the uniform kindness the doctor had always shown to the patients who came under his care in charge of the Union." He (the chairman) did not know a medical gentleman in the country who could have been more devoted to his duties or have shown more diligence and attention. His sense of duty and his kindly manner had commanded univers respect. (Hear, hear.) He had expected signs and alevidences of it at the funeral but all his expectations bad been exceeded. The great i companies who joined n the procession and the large people in the Aston Church were evidence out; mthbeer of high respect and esteem in which the deceased gentleman was h&c' by the public at large. He was well skilled in his profession and gave the best of his attention to all the patients, poor and rich, who came under his csre. (Hear, hear). Mr. Wright, in seconding the resolution, referred to his life-long friendship with the late doctor. He did not believe it possible for a man to be more beloved than Dr. Carruthers had been. Be had never heard anyone speak in any but the highest terms of him. He had been their medical oilictir in Ualton for 35 years, and had discharged his duties willingly, and at many times at most inconvenient hours. (Hear, hear.) He had given out-door patients the same attention that he would have given a patient from whom be got is big fee. He had a fine practice, and the poor all round Halton and district had lost not only a beloved doctor but a very great friend. (Hear, hear). Mr Linaker endorsed all that had been said. He had known Dr. Carruthers all his life and besides earning the appreciation of all in his duties, no one could excel him in being a Christian man. He had been a most conscientious officer of the Board, and he had gone to his grave amid the universal regret of all who knew him. The vote of condolence was passed, all the members standing. The question of appointing a successor to Dr. Carruthers was left with the Finance Committeee to report upon.

div.head: MR. STOKES' ILLNESS.
div.p: MR. STOKES' ILLNESS.

Mr. Wright referred to the iline;s—C-Fone of the merc- ben of the Board, Mr. Stokes, and moved that a letter of sympathy and encouragement be sent. Mr. Stokes had been absent for many weeks and he (the speaker)),

div.head: Examiner, Saturday, August 17, 1912.
div.p: The Examiner, Saturday, August 17, 1912.

was sorry to say he was still in very poor health des- pite the tact that he had been away two months at Rhyl. He had had a relapse on his return from his holiday and for the past three weel,s he hld been con- fined to his bed. They all hoped he would soon recover and be with them once again. (Hearo.hear.) The Board agreed to send the letter as suggested by Mr. Wright.

PAUPER LUNATICS. The Clerk reported that the rate of maintenance of Pauper Lunatics in the Chester A.ylum for the quarter ending September 30th had been fixed at Ss 9d per head per week. The Clerk pointed out that the amount was the same as for last quarter. THE MASTER AND MATRON. An application for increase of salaries was received from the Master and Matron at the Workhouse. They stated they had been three 3ears in the service of the Guardians during which period they had endeavoured to Rive of their hest in the interests of the Guardians, the inmates and the institution. The matter was referred to the Finance Committee to be considered at their next meeting and to report thereon.

div.head: VISITING COMMITTEE.
div.p: VISITING COMMITTEE.

• At a meeting of the Visiting Committee it was decided that Mr. Wardell of Aston be thanked for gifts of flowers. It was also decided that an appeal for con- tributions to the annual children's trip, which takes place on the 23rd inst., be made. The minutes of the Committee were approved. WIDNES TOWN COUNCIL. LOSSES ON MUNICIPAL MOTOR-BUSES. "'

At the Widnes Town Council on Tuesday, Councillor Clarke, moving the adoption of the Highway Com- mittee's minutes, referred to the motor-buses, and welcomed the better conditions of service. Councillor Millar asked for information regarding the heavy loss on the motor-bus service duriug the last three months of £560 and the reduction of pasEr

,Eengers carried of 96,000 less than last year. Councillor Clarke, in reply, said it arose from loss of revenue occasioned by breakdowns and a disorganised service. The actual loss on the 'buses was something like £285. Interest on the money borrowed for the purchase made the deficiency larger, because the Government forced them to pay the money back in five years. He was sorry to say the motor-buses ever since their inception bad teen exceedingly unfortunate. Alderman Owens deplored the loss, which almost equalled a penny rate. It was a Eerious matter, and they would have to face it heroically. WATER EXTENSION SCHEME:. _

The gas and water minutes, as proposed by Alderman Smith, contained an application from the Sutton Manor Colliery Company and the Wigan Colliery Company to supply gas and water to property in course.of erecticn at Sutton Manor and Bold. If the suggestion is enter- tained by Widnes, the revenue from this source alone will reach £1,350 a year. The houses already in exist- ence number 113, and these are at present supplied by the St. Helens Corpo•ation. It is estimated that during the next few years 1,113 houses will be erected. To cope with this scheme a new tower will have to be erected on Pex Hill because of the high-lying nature of the Bold district. The tower will have a capacity of half-a-million gallons, at a cost of £8,5t0. The whole cost of the scheme will be .£16,000, exclusive of such sums as may be necessary to purchase the gas and water plant used for distribution in the Clock Face area. Several members deprecated the scheme until the whole of the houses were erected. They did not relish the idea of such a big outlay for the number of houses at present in the district. Councillor Davies said that, as a business Corpora- tion, they could not hope to make profit right away. A scheme of these dimensiors was bound to be a good source of revenue in a few years time. Upon further details of the scheme being promised to the members, they agreed that the minutes should pass.

div.head: ST. HELENS.
div.p: ST. HELENS.

GAS EXPLOSION AT RUNCORN. An alarming gas explosion occurred at the house of Mr William H Harrison, 37, Windmill-street, Runcorn, late on Tuesday night. Mrs. Harrison went to put a copper in the slot meter, which is fixed in the parlour of the house, and immediately she did this an explosion occurred, shattering the windows and damaging the door. Some of the furniture caught fire, but this was soon extinguished by the crowd that was attracted to the scene. Fortunately, Mrs liar-ison was not injured, and is none the worse for her experience. The front room of the house was wrecked. The cause of the explosion is a mystery. Mrs. Harrison did not take a light into the room, but says that the gas was lighted some time before. DEATH OF A VETERAN BANE MANAGER. News was received at St. lielens on Tuesday evening that Mr Andrew J Speeden, J.P., of Huyton, who retired recently from the management of Parr's Bank, St. Helens, had died somewhat suddenly while on holiday with his family at Bundoran, in the north of Ireland.—Mr :I)oe:ten, who was about seventy years of age, began his career with the Western Bank of Scotland at Linlithgow over fifty years ago, and for ten years was connected with Parr's Dank, Warrington. In 1871 he was appointed manager of the St. Helens Bank, and retired last June after completing forty years. He was treasurer of the St. Helens Hospital from its establishment in 1873 up to his death. The deceased gentleman was very widely respected, and on his iretirement last year Alderman C J Bishop, on behalf of the prominent residents of the town and district, presented to him a handsome Georgian tea service and tray and a purse of gold, with a handsome diamond pendant for Mrs. Speeden. Mr Speeden was appointed a county magistrate about three years ago. During the existence of the St. Helens Liberal-Unionist Association be took a prominent part in its meetings and deliberations. •

div.head: BULLY AT A _DANCE,
div.p: BULLY AT A _DANCE,

At St. Helens on Tuesday, Edward Taylor, son of a Rainford farmer, was charged before the county magis- trates with assaulting Ruth Ashcroft, a young woman living in Pemberton. Mr. W. Webster defended. Mr. T. Garner said that the circumstances that would be disclosed in the case were most extraordinary. On ruesday, the 6th inst., a dance was held in the village ball at tcainford. It was an annual event and attncted all the people of the countryside. The assault complained of took place about a quarter to twelve at night. Complainant and her girl friend were sitting by the aide of the room, when her friend consented to dance with a young man. Taylor went to Miss Ashcroft and asked her to dates with him. She declined, and he sat down beside her and asked if he could take her home. She declined his company, but he took hold of her and assiulted her. She struggled to get away, but it was not until a young man who was dancing in a set of Lancers left his place and interfered tnat she could get free. Miss Ashcroft gave evidence, and said that defendant up to the time of the assault was a complete stranger to her. . . .

harry Green, insurance agent, 65, Church-road, Rain- ford, said that while he was dancing in the Lancers he saw Miss Ashcroft struggling to get away from Taylor. He did not interfere until he saw that she was crying. Defendant had had some drink, but was not drunk. The dance was generally well conducted. Other witnesses gave corroborative evidence. The defendant denied the charge, hut the magistrates convicted him, and ordered him to pay a flue of 50s and costs, in all £4 13s 6d.

div.head: EARLESTOWN AND NEWTON.
div.p: EARLESTOWN AND NEWTON.

"NO INDICATION OF A POLITICAL CHANGE." MR. J. A. SEDDON ON THE NORTH-WEST MANCHESTER ELECTION. Speaking at the quarterly meeting of the Newton Division Labour party at Rainbill on Saturday, Mr. J. A. Seddon said the Conservative press had gone wildly enthusiastic over North-west Manchester. The various placards were most amnsing—" Deathblow to the Goverment," "A knock-out blow," and all sorts of statements that would lead them to believe that the Government was tottering to its doom and that one I election, as if one svcallow made the summer, had put the Tory party into power. Those who had followed events in Manchester were not so easily gulled. They knew that North-west Manchester had a capacity for wobbling, BO that they could take it that the elec- tion was no indication of a political change in the country. There were, however, some things which demonstrated that there was a mighty change taking place among The great mass of the electors of the country. The chief problem for SU per cent. of the people was the condition of employment, the rate of remuneration, and the safety of their lives in earning their daily bread. (Hear, hear.) The chief problem that concerned them was tbe changed economic relationship between the owners of capital and the pro- ducers of wealth so far as manual labour was concerned, and it was this change which had brought about the great labour upheaval which had taken place during the past twelve months. Whatever their politics, capitalists were united against labour, and it was the duty of the working class to see to it that they, too, were thoroughly united. (Applause).

THE TITANIC ENQUIRY will undoubtedly have far- reaching results on British shipping, which in the wider sense comprises more than 50 per cent. of the total tonnage of the wcrld. A high official of the Canadian Nlarine Department who was visiting this country during the Titanic enquiry, in connection with the question of steamboat inspection. has stated on his return to Canada that it is the intention of the Canadian Marine Department to apply to shipping vritt ever additional aafegnarda ere ultimately adopted by the British Board of Trade.

div.head: HAY CROP.
div.p: THE HAY CROP.

In view of the unsettled character of the weather and of the consequent difficulty in securing the hay crop in some districts in which the crop is late, the Loard of Agriculture and Fisheries invite the attention of farmers to Leaflet Ivo. 9 which describes the process of making Ensilage. Copies of the Leaflet may be obtained free of charge and post free on application to theiSecretary, Board of Agriculture and Fisheries, 4, Whitehall Place, London, S.W. Letters of application to addressed need not he stamped.

div.head: EX-DIRECTOR'S ACTION.
div.p: EX-DIRECTOR'S ACTION.
MR. LOUIS HENSHALL'S SUCCESSFUL
CLAIM.

His Honour Judge Stanger, K.C., delivered judg- ment at the Warrington County Court on Thursday, in the action. in which James Henshall, of Bouverie- street, Chester, administrator of the estate of Louis Henshall, of Warrington, sued Messrs. H. A. Naylor Limited, Howley Mills, Warrington, for alleged to be due as dividend declared in April, 1007, on 2,000 shares owned by him in the company. His Honour pointed out that the defence first set up wasthat although the dividend had not been paid to Louis Ilenshall in case, it was accounted for in a settlement I arrived at between the defendants, the executors of the late Mr. R. A. Naylor, and Louis Henshall, on July 20th, 1009. As an alternative it was alleged that there wasan estoppel. It was clear, therefore, that the burden of proving the defence lay on the defendants. Reviewing the facts, his Honour said the dividend was declared on April 11th, 1907. At that time Louis Henshall, as the holder of shares, was undoubtedly entitled to that dividend. Afterwards be was prosecuted and, out of a good many charges against him, he pleaded guilty to three and was sentenced to a term of penal servitude. The plaintiff was appointed administrator of his brother's estate, and it was in that capacity he brought the present action. Before the conviction, which took place in March, 1909, two actions were begun against Louis lienshall —one by the company and one by the representa- tives of the-late Mr Naylor. Louis lienshall had been suspended in Novemoer, 1903, and the actions were brought, against him not very long afterwards. The particular action which was discussed when the case was argued a fortnight ago, was one in which the defendant company claimed an account. They first of all claimed certaiu specitio sums which they alleged to be payable by Louis Hensisall as monies received by him to the use of the plaintiffe. What became of con- siderable importance in the discussion, however, was a claim for an account to be taken of all monies received by Louis Heneliall to the use of the plaintiffs and not accounted for, and for an order that he should pay such sums as should be found due to the plaintiffs on the taking of such account. One of the facts upon which Mr Acton (for the defendants in the present action) relied was that an order was acoordingly made that the defend ant should make an account, but that order was not complied with. In the course of some months, Louis Henshall in the meantime having been convicted and sent to penal servitude, a further peremptory order was made that he should make an account within seven days. That order vvas not again complied with. Mr Acton contended that if that account had been made, it was almost certain that if a dividend had been due, Louis Henshall would have brought it into the account as a set off pro tanto to any amount that was payable by him to the company and it was his fault that the account was not prepared. Meanwhile the action did not, proceed beyond that stage. There was no statement of claim or Of defence. Ttie present plaintiff, the brother of Louis Henshall, having been appointed administrator of the estate,enteied into negotiations with a view to a settle- ment of both actions. The settlement was in these terms : "We acknowledge to have received from the representatives of Mr Louis Henshall the sum of £1,500 and the certificates of 2,0e0 shares in It A Naylor, Ltd., on transfer ttereot, in settlement of all claims against him by It A Naylor' Ltd., or the executors of R A Naylor, deceased." It went on to give an undertaking to consent to the dismissal of the two actions, the dis- solution of injunctions, and to procure the discharge of the guarantee given by Louis Henshall to Parr's Bank, Ltd. It was obvious that in terms this did not affect to be a settlement of anything which was due or alleged to be due from Messrs Naylor to Louis lienshall. Therefore the argument of Mr Greaves Lora for the plaintiff was that if they took the words of the settlement, there was nothing in it to show that the claim of £lO had been discharged. Mr Acton, how- ever, said he must look at all the negotiations and invited him (His Houour),to come to the conclusion that, although according to the literal interpretation of the settlement, the claim had not been expressly discharged, the intention of the parties was that it should be a complete settlement of everything that was outstanding between Louis Henshall and the company. His Honour then referred to the correspon- dence wnich had passed and quoted a letter in which Messrs Tatham, Worthington end Company, the solicitors to the company, stated "Our clients will be prepared to accept £l,lOO in cash and the whole of Mr Ileusball's 2;1100 shares in It A Naylor, Ltd., in settle. meat of all claims." In order to appreciate that, one must consider what the position of the two parties was. On the one hand the administrator knew that in con- sequence of his brothers acts and defaults there was a considerable liability to the company, and it was in order to clear up that liability and put an end to it once and for all, that the negotiations were entered upon. The question was on whit terms the actions should be diemissed. Throughout the correspondence there was no definite offer which was definitely accepted so that one could lay one's hands on two letters and say is contract was contained in them. Each side made a counter proposal. Messrs Walker, Smith and Way, on behalf of Mr Henshall, wrote stating they felt some evidence of the indebtedness of their client should be given, for as the matter then stood they were entirely in the dark as to the real position. Louis Henshall, commented his Honour, was then serving his term of penal servitude, but there were means of com- munication, and no difficulty would be put by the authorities in the way of his communicating with his solicitors as the administrator of his estate. It was,of course, obvious that there could not be quite the same ease in obtaining information as if Louis Henshall had been at liberty. The letter of Messrs. Walker, Smith and Way went on to accept the proposal to pay £1,5e0 and transfer the whole of Louis Henshallei shares in settlement of all claims which Messrs Naylor or the executors had against him. It, however, added a proviso that "any salary and dividends due to the defendant and any commission due, to be credited on account of the £1,500 cash." To that Messrs Tatham, Worthington and Co. replied : "There are no salary, dividends or commission due to the defendant. All, accounts between them were settled to October 31st last." On that passage Mr. Greaves Lord laid very great stress. He said that here was a statement made ray a firm of repute, no doubt perfectly bona yide, but a statement which in point of tact was exactly contrary to the truth. How it came to be made had not been explained. Some blunder was made. Either the solicitors misunderstood the instructions which they received from the company or by some curious mistake the person who was charged by the company to give information to the solicitors had failed to give them correct information. The letter did not demur to the suggestion that the dividend should be credited towards the £1,510 ; it did not say it was unfair. It said there was no dividend due. No one would suggest that the statement was made with the knowledge that it was false. It was, however, an entirely untrue statement and he had to consider, in the light of that statement which appeared to have been accepted by the administrator, whether the settlement subsequently arrived at could betaken to be a discharge of the dividend which was in fact owing but which was said by one of the parties to the negotiations not to be owing at all Was there a contract by which the claim that undoubtedly existed at the time of the settlement was put an end to ? He had come to the conclusion that he could not find there was any such coutract.According to the literal interpretation of the language of the settlement the dividend was not included. It was merely a settlement of claims which the company were seeking to enforce and, looking at the negotiations which preceded it and having regard to the statement made on behalf of the company that there was no dividend owing, he did not think he would be justified in coming to the conclusion that there had been any contract by which the claim to the dividend was dis- charged and put an end to.M r Acton further argued that

if there was an action for an account, it meant that everything which was a matter of account between the parties was to be dealt with and that therefore any cross- claim which Louis Henshall had should have been brought into it. On looking at the writ, however, he found it was not a claim for an account of that general character It was only a claim for an account of monies due from Loeis Henshall to the bank. Mr. Acton said that fact made no difference, for if Louis Henshall bad complied with the order he would have been certain to bring the dividend in. He was not, however, bound to do it and was not ordered to do it. As to the alleged estoppel, it was stated that Louis Henshall was a director who had been guilty of dishonesty, that his fellow-directors were not aware of it at the time the dividend I was proposed and passed, and that if they bad known, they pr ibabiy would not have resolved that the dividend should be declared, or they would have taken steps to have got rid of any liability they might have towards Louis Henshall in respect of it. Mr Acton also argued that Louie Henshall was unfaithful to the company in his office of director at the time the dividond was being earned. The only matter in that respect that he (his Honour) could deal with was that to which Louis Henshall had pleaded guilty.lt was not to be said that merely because a great many charges were made, he most presume that Henshall was guilty of them all. He did not think he was at liberty to make any such presumption. Louis Henshall had pleaded guilty to three and he (his Honour) could only consider the legal liability that followed from that plea. With regard to the others, it was an open question as to whether he was guilty or not. Mr Greaves Lord effectually answered Mr. Acton's argument on that point. He showed that the first offence, in order of titne,to which Louis Henshall pleaded guilty was some time after the end of the year in respect of which the dividend was paid. Mr. Acton's contention was that Louis Henshall was presenting a false balance sheet and was responsible for it. Mr. Greaves Lord sufficiently answered that by saying there was no evidence ou the point. One could not bay that because a man in the year 1909 pleaded guilty to offences some considerable tlne after the year in respect of which the balance sheet was presented, therefore they must assume he had been dishonest its the preceding years. It would not be justice to assume that and to take away rights that would have belonged to him if he had not been guilty of dishonesty. There was nothing to show that it was a false balance sheet or that there was any dishonesty on

In the election of Officers Mr Joseph Pomfrey was unanimously elected president and Mr William Clegg, vice-president, for the year. Mr Frederick S Massey was duly elected anditor for the ensuing two years. A very lengthy and interesting agenda was gone through during the evening, affecting the general interest of the members.

The following members took part in the discussion ; —Messrs John Haley, Joseph Adams, William Ratcliffe, terederick Massey, William Eckerslev, John Jones, Thomas Baskerville, William Massey, )), illiam Taylor, Peter S Edgar and others. div.head: WARRINGTON SUMMER CAMP.
div.p: WARRINGTON SUMMER CAMP.

Friday last was sports day in the camp, when some capital sprint races took place, almost all the boys taking part. The chief event however, was a minia- ture Marathon race which aroused considerable interest. About 50 competitors entered. The course was from the top of a railway bridge, along the roads, finishing in the camp in front of the bungalow. The boys were handicapped. After the start a rare struggle was witnessed for supremacy about, 20 of the boys being close up at the finish. Marsh, Wycliffe School, was eventually the winner. On Friday night the first contingent (12'J boys) was despatched to War- rington, all arriving safe and sound, and were met by Mr. W. H. J.Jenkins the indefatigable hon. secretary. On Saturday morning a further batch of 130 boys arrival in the camp and were soon allocated to their various huts. On Sunday the boys had a long walk along a mountain side amid pretty scenery. Afterwards a short service was conducted, Mr. Firth giving a practical address. On Monday the weather being bright and cheery most of the boys indulged in bathing. Later in the day they were taken to see the Pierrots who perform on Prestatyn beach. On Tuesday morn- ing the officers took the boys to Dysrrth waterfall and the afternoon was spent on the beach. Wednesday was an exceptionally wet day, so the boys were brought in the Pavilion and a miscel- laneous concert arranged which consisted chiefly of ilsongs and recitations. The first prize for best per- formance was won by John Clare of Heatheide School who really recited well the classical piece "Cardinal Wolsey " in which appear the words " Cromwell ! Cr,,rnwell ! Had I but served my God with half the zeal I serv'd my King, He would not in mine age have left me naked to my enemies." We may say that in an open competition at the Pierrots' the two chief prizes were won by boys from the camp. We have had during the past week several visitors from Warrington and district notably Mr and Mrs Ransome, Mrs Locker, Mr Coventry, Mr and Mrs Ireland, of Penketh and others. Owing to the mixed weather that has been experi- enced the officers in charge have had a:rather trying and arduous time in attending to the wants and enter- tainments of the boys and keeping an " eye " upon the wilder and more mischievous spirits. Thanks to regulations and discipline good order has been the " motto " and the boys have had a really good time. This year we might add that 257 girls and 259 boys have been accomodated at the Camp most of whom, if it had not been for the kindness and gener- osity of subscribers, would not have had a " real " holiday.

div.head: WARRINGTON BURIAL SOCIETY.
div.p: THE WARRINGTON BURIAL SOCIETY.

The members in connection with the above society assembled at the British Workman Public-house, Horse- market-street on Monday, the occasion being the 41st anniversary of the establishment of the society. The , attendance was exceedingly good, the meeting being ' presided over by the President, Mr. William Taylor, who was supported by the vice-president, Mr Joseph Pomfrey ; treasurer, Mr James Parr ; trustees, Messrs William Eckel%ley, James Gresty, Joseph Adams ; auditor, Mr Frederick S Massey; the general secretary, Mr Lawrence Weir and others. The CHAIRIIAN in his opening address assured the members how gratified he felt to have the honour of presiding over such a large gathering of parents and representatives of members connecters with the society. The condition of the society was such that every member shouldifeel proud of the success they had achieved during , the past year. Although the amounts they had paid for death had been heavy they had been able to place to the credit of the society a very satisfactory and substantial gain which you will gather from the Secretary's report. He desired to state that the work of the Committee had been carried on during the year in a most praiseworthy manner and it had been a pleasure to work with all concerned. He hoped the society would continue upon the progressive lines it had done since its establishment. (Applause.) The general secretary, SI r Lawrence Weir, presented his annual balance sheet which showed that the society's funds new amounted to £4,744 10s 2id as against .£4,458 lls 611 the previous year, a gain of £255 18s Sd. The numerical condition of the society was unaltered. The report further showed that the society had paid away in death claims £65 les compared with £47 103 the previous year. The secretary in conclusion briefly dealt with the investment of the funds which he pointed out had now almost reached £5,000 yielding a yearly interest that entirely covers the whole of the working expenditure of the society. (Applause.) The auditors, Messrs. div.head: ANGLING.
div.p: ANGLING.
WARRINGTON WORKINGMEN'S ANGLING ASSOCIATION.

(N.A. CENTRE). The unfavourable conditions, together with the rumour that the canal at Norton was polluted, caused not a few Northern anglers to lose their week end nrigling. The notes in the " Examiner " are written for the Northern Anglers in Warrington and district and we have never yet reported on any waters that is not rented by them or free waters where most locals go, so members may take it for granted that if any of our waters get polluted, they will bear through this paper at the earliest opportunity. We admit and have done so for this last week or so, that the Norton length has not fished up to its reputation, but then have other canals (with the exception of the Chester length) been up to expectations ? The weather, we presume, is all against them. As was reported fast week, fish were taken from Norton with red patches on them similar to the fish at Hartford last year, but this does not prove that the water is polluted, although after the heavy downpours we have had lately, there can be little wonder that we have had more water from the Trent and Mersey Canal than was wanted, and this seems to be in a very bad state at present. If there is much more of it Norton will certainly feel the effects. A list of members who visited Norton last week end, and their catches will be found below, and members may judge for themselves the form the canal is in up to the time of writing. NORTON. The canal here was visited by very few, from 10 to 12 only fishing on Sunday last instead of the usual 30 or 40. Those who visited here had plenty of sport with the small ones only one specimen being taken by a novice. This is the second weighed in this month and they stand 2nd and 3rd for home waters. The members who did best were : Messrs Stout, Potter, Hargreaves, jun., Wilson, Singleton and Cox ; Stout, 9 roach; Potter, 14 roach; Oakes,3 roach, 1 eel ; Eaves, 4 roach, 1 eel ; Wilson, 2 roach; Hargreaves, 3 roach, 2. eels. Monday, Singleton, 20 rcach ; Cox, 17 roach, 1 eel. These numbers do not include the small ones thrown back.

M. BORDEN'S MESSAGE TO ENGLAND.—The follow- ing expressions of opinion taken from Mr Borden's speeches while in this country are typical of the Canadian Premier's utterances on repented occasions in connection with the great object which has brought him and his ministers to these shores :—" I would like you to understand that Canada does not propose to be an 'adjunct,' even of the British Empire, but to he a great part in a greater whole. It there is one thing upon which the people of Canada are united and deter- mined. it is this—that Canada shall work ont that destiny as one of the great nations within the British Empire. We realise, as you do, that the supremacy of Britain upon the seas is the very brvath of life of the Empire. Our ideal has been one King. one Flag, one Empire, one Navy—one navy powerful enough to vindicate the flag and maint,ip the integrity of the Empire. In the constitution of the navy, none of the Dominions should lose their entonomy or their control. There should be one navy under one control and one 'direction.

i-denying Class." Sir,—A manifesto signed by Sir Herbert Raphael to his constituents, condemning the manner in which the Government is investigating the Land Question. and upholding lamlowners as one of the most self- denying classes of the community, was published in the Press yesterday. In this document he gives it as his opinion that no new scheme of increased taxation of Vaud is going ti benefit the working classes. Surely Sir Herbert has faiiel to grasp the elementary _principles of the policy which be ao emphatically con- denaflg. In the first place it is useful to note that the proposed tax on land values, as embodied in the Land and, Tpxati TW97111 I:‘fcm,arol tc thtg Quernment signed by 175 members ot Parliamat, is not a tar In. addition to. but in substitution of, existing rates and taxes. The proposal is to abolish the breakfast table duties and to exempt improvements from taxation by providing the necessary revenue by means of a tax on the value of all land irrespective of the use to which it is put. Although Sir Herbert regards landowners as a self-denying class, it is certainly apparent to the meanest intelligence that by withholding land from use or by demanding a prohibitive price for it, they directly affect the interests of the workers. Evidently Sir Herbert does not realise how the rural districts of this country are being depopulated by the" dog-in-the- manger " policy of landowners ; nor does he seem to understand how this constant flow of men from the countryside permanently depresses vvages in the industrial centres. As long as landowners are rated and taxed only on the use they make of their land, they will continue to lay waste the countryside and to told up for exorbitant prices building "land in and around cities and towns. But if rates and taxes were imposed on the true economic value of all laud, whether well used or ill used, they would be forced to put every acre to its best possible use themselves or else allow others to do so. This would mean that countless opportunities for productive labour would be thrown open to the workers in agriculture, in mining, and in all the various industries connected with the building trade ; the flow of labour from the rural uistricts would be cut off, and with the increased demand for labour the wages of all workers would immediately rise. To-day we tax men on their industry and their enterprise ; if they build houses or enlarge their business premises they are heavily penalised by the local rates. Moreover, we impose taxation on such necessary commodities as tea and sugar, taxes which fall with the greatest force on the poorest classes. Instead of these unfair impositions, surely it would be juster and wiser to raise at least a portion of our revenue from a tax on the value of all land, a value justly described by Mr. Asquith as a communally earned one. Sir Herbert fears that such a policy may cause a rift in the Liberal Party. It may be that it will alienate the support of those who are Liberals in name only. but it will cement together more firmly than ever the party of progress, and will unite in a common bond and common ideal all those who are waging the battle of the democracy against established privilege and monopoly.--Yours HARRY DE PASS. National Liberal Club, Whitehall, S.W. 9th August, 1012.

Paltry Progress. Sir,—With a supreme effort to throw away a morbid apathy one tries to wonder where, as a nation, we are getting to. Taking a survey of our politi.ml partite certainly does not assist us. In fact it does little twore than accelerate our return to that serene state of immobility known as apathy. Our newspapers delight us daily with things of 'little consequence, unless Cowes yachting, who shall ride the Derby losers, Mr Churchill's remonstrance to Boner Law, are things that matter. The paltryness of our thoughts and actions.and considering what ought to be our thoughts and actions, are enough to make us wonder what all the great men and women who have striven to push us a little further along the path of progress would think of how little value their efforts had been. For in spite of all the so-called progress we have made there is more ugliness, more poverty, more disease, more immorality, more ignorance than ever known, What astounds one is the apparent impossibity of the nation, it leaders and followers, to take a compre- hensive understanding of the situation. I take it as a common understanding that a people possessed of intelligence would abolish these evils as quick as possible. I think, however, that we will agree that the death of an aviator, however sad such an occurrence may be, or the English cricket team beat- ing South Africa, are immeasurably insignificant occurences to ponder over in comparison with the question of poverty, &c. The parties supposed to be considering how to treat these questions do not seem to raise the faintest glimmer of hope. The Liberal party consider the first essential to our welfare is that we must have as free an exchange of com- modities between us and other lands as possible. I think it will take the superhuman perception of a Churchill or an Asquith to make us believe that the free exchange of pig-iron, cotton goods, motor-cars, &c., will in anyways subtract from the sum total of poverty, misery and degradation. Then again, we have another section of our people who assert that to minimise poverty and social deterioration we must have more work. Tax the foreigner and all will be well. And we have the spectacle of the mass of the people divided into two sections arguing which is right. Meanwhile, poverty, disease, and ignorance are still with us. Worst of all, however, is that men who had given us some hope seem to have led us astray. We now have the Socialists, with their unanswerable case, divided into two sections ; one part plumping for labour representation in Parliament, and falling into the traditional political game of talking about things that don't matter, or else doing nothing. And then we have the other section of Souialists who assert that the only way to secure a better standard of life is to force the owners of capital to give us better wages through the medium of the strike. However earnest we know these advocates to be, one cannot believe that strikes and better wages will abolish poverty, etc. This is the spectacle that one surveys to-day after centuries of time and innumerable millions of money have gone before. With all the past experience of great nations and great men to refer to, the dominant objectives that fill cur minds are Free Trade, Tariff Reform and strikes, sprinkled with Home Rule and what is going to win the Grand Natioinal. I believe that the first duty of a great nation is to see that we have a healthy animal exist- ence, that we attain the physical development neces- sary to class ourselves as men and women. Before we can appreciate our higher emotions this must be done. The second duty of a nation is to develops all the faculties we possess. Can anyone show me where Free Trade, Strikes, Tariff Reform or Home Rule are tending to lead us from our present black morass to a human, happy life? The panorama of England and its people at present makes one wonder whether men and women are essentially bad. Some of us try to believe that the people of all time have always been struggling for something better, that whatever may be the elommant aspect nevertheless the mass of the people are essen- tially good. But when we look back upon the great nations of the past and read of how they rose, jiourished and died away, it makes one wonder Whethe r the present nations are doomed to die away or develops ioto a state of existence wherein the con- tinuity of the race is assured. In my view the signs are discouraging.—Yours truly, LABOR OMNIA "VINCIT.

MOTOR-CAR ACCIDENT. TWO BOYS INJURED IN KNUTSFORD-ROAD Knutsford-road was the scene of a serious motor-car accident on Thursday, two youths, William Higgin- son, 32, Wellington-street, and James Eckersley, 33, Ellesmere-street, receiving injuries which necessitated their detention in the Infirmary. It appears that Mr. Ernest Adey Workman, a commercial traveller, of Foxton, (Houcester- road, Cheltenham, was driving a motor-car at the rate of about twelve to fifteen miles an hour. When about twelve yards from the end of St. Mary's- street he noticed a cart, and just as he got level with it the youths ran from behind the cart riglat in front of his car. They were knocked down, and Higginson received a nasty wound on the forehead, while Eckersley escaped with less serious injuries. They were immediately placed in the car and taken to the Infirmary by Mr. Workman.—They are progressing as well as can be expected.

KERSLAKE, lI.M Inspector of Schools, at the opening of the Evelyn- street Council school on Thursday afternoon. The occasion was] a notable one in the educational history of the borough, for the new school provides accommodation for districts where it is urgently needed—the Whitecross and St. Austin's wards. Councillor 11. Roberts (chairman of the Education Committee) performed the opening ceremony, in the presence of a large and representative gathering, and delivered an interesting speech in which he emphasised the tzttch7doateci qtvotiou ef tbc ?..r.re at which children sllsttld be allowed to leave school.

The Evelyn-street school is the third elententaiy school which the local Education authority have erected, and ,it is built and equipped on the most efficient and up-to-date lines. It provides accom- modation for 1,2C0 schnlars and includes mixed and infants' departments. Thera is also a special subfects block where domestic science and woodwork will be taught. A novel feature is the introduction of shower baths and it is claimed that the Evelyn-street school is the first in England to he fitted with them. It is intended later to provide a svvimming bath. A caretaker's house of six rooms has been built in such a position as to afford full, control over the school buildings and playgrounds. A portion of the land round the buildings has been reserved for gardens for horticultural 'instruction and the rest of the playground is fined in concrete. The schools are built of kcal brickt and roofed with Welsh slates. Messrs. J. -Dolan and Son, Napier- street, Wrrrington, have carried. out the work to the designs and under the superintendence of Mr. T. A. Buttery. F.R 1.8. div.head: LUNCHEON AT THE TOWN HALL.
div.p: LUNCHEON AT THE TOWN HALL.

Prior to the ceremony, Councillor Roberts enter- tained a large company at luncheon in the Council Chamber at the Town Hall. The function was in every respect a very pleasant and successful one. Councillor Roberts presided and the following ladies and gentle- men had accepted his invitation :—Mrs Roberts, Mrs C Jackson Holmes and Mrs Brereton leaf rclough. Alder- men A Bennett, J Smethurst, D Tinnion and James Evani, Councillors T Birtles, AV H Bellian, J Dicken- son, C Jackson Holmes, W H J Jenkins, Dr McKee, T S Steel, and 0 Toole, the Revs G C Briggs and Neville Wilson, Messrs A J Joliey, C S Burgess, H Kingdom .1 Chrimes, R T Fairclough, E Plinston, F H Roberts,C H Unsworth and G Walker (members of the Education Committe) ; AT Kersdale (H.M. inspector of echocls) ; J E Richardson, C E Bromley, G Dale, A Tilling, 3 Rose and W Miles (managers of the new school),F J Norman,H G Roberts, John Dolan (Messrs J Dolan and Son, builders of the school), L C Hirst (representing Mr Buttery, the archi- tect), J Moore Murray (director of education), It B Roberts (assistant director), A T Hallavvay (deputy town clerk), T H Spinks (ass:stant town clerk, A M Ker (assistant borough surveyor), and M Nicholls (chief constable). There was no set programme of speeches, but several toasts were honoured.

The CHAIRMAN, before submitting the health of" The King and Queen and members of the Royal Family" expressed his pleasure at seeing so many of his friends and colleagues around the festive board. He gathered from their attendance that they all took a serious interest in the important cause of education. Speaking to the toast, Councillor Roberts alluded in felicitous terms to his Majesty's deep and practical interest in the material and moral welfare of his people and to the able and sympathetic support which he received from his excellent wife. In the coming generation they had promise of great things, for the greatest qualifications which had characterised the monarchs of this country for a long period seemed likely to be reproduced in an eminent degree in the children of our King and Queen. (Applause). Mr. KERSLAKE proposed the health of the Chairman and expressed his indebtedness to Councillor Roberts in his official capacity, for the steps he had taken to push forward the work of education in Warrington. He (the speaker) was less fitted than any of those present to say anything as to Mr. Roberts's ability as an organizer and business man, but he could say that those traits came out in his work for the Education Com- mittee. The ceremony at which they would assist that afternoon was only one step in the educational progress,of the town. While the new building was a very excellent one and would relieve schools which had needed relief for some time, it would still leave other schools in various parts of the town in a very crowded condition. He was, however' glad to know that other schemes were going forward and that Warrington, which had seemed to hang back a little bit, was on a fair way to making good progress with its school provision. (Applause). The toast was accorded musical honours. Councilloi ROBERTS, in responding, said that of all the public offices which he had ever held, there was none which he appreciated so highly as that of chairman of the Education Committee. The whole cause of education was very dear to him, and because he knew of its material value to the young people of this town, and because he himself had benefitted so largely by the sacrifices of a father who did great things for him in years gone by, he felt that on every possible occasion it was not simply a duty, but a very sincere pleasure t 3 do all he could to make the way a little easier for those whose circumstances were not quite so well placed as they would like them to be. (Applause). Alderman SMETHURST proposed the health of Mrs Roberts and family and referred to the grace and tact with which Mrs Roberts discharged the 'duties of Mayoress some years ago. Expressing his piesaire at the attendance of the ladies at the luncheon the Alder- man said the members of the Council woad probably be better men in every way if ladies attended their meetings. div.head: PALACE AND HIPPODROME.
div.p: PALACE AND HIPPODROME.

Probably the moat remarkable thing about Tom Jack, the ice-king, is his hair. Whether being born in Iceland has anything to do with it we are not told, but for a young man he presents a remarkable and weird appearance with a snow-white frizzy " mop nearly a yard across. The whites of his eyes are said to be red, but across the footlights the phenomenon was not obvious. The Ice-lander's special line is being tied up with chains and ropes, and getting out of them in full view of the audience. It is quite a strenuous business to perform twice in the evening. The trussed fowl of the kitchen is not in it with Tom Jack when he has been laced into a straight jacket and bound to a chair with ropes and chains of considerable length and strength. It looks quite impossible for him to get free, but he performs the feat eventually after many contortions on the floor. It struck us that Mr. Jack's peculiar abilities would have been an acquisi- tion to the pioneer in the good old Fenimore Cooper days when the Indians bound their prisoner to a tree preparatory to filling him up with arrows fired at the regulation distance. Tom Jack would have given them a better turn and a surprise at the same time. Quite a novel dancing speciality act is presented by the Great Northern Troupe, three ladies and two men who were heartily applauded for their smartness. Frank Melvin is a comedian with a genuine sense of humour and an eye for originality. His two songs and patter brought down the house and nearly sent one lady in the pit into convulsions. She made Melvin himself laugh. A gips,' scene with acrobats as the centre is the speciality of the Creo Brothers, who not only do some clever tumbling but leave the audience in doubt as to the sex of the bizarre performer in tights. Constance Mori, comedienne and dancer, is a bright little lady who allies her [art to some choke scenic effects. Yettmah and lady are mystery-makers in a Japanese setting. Their illpsions are exceedingly clever, and the whole turn is quite in the front rank of its kind. Yeticsall is a bit prone to over-do the patter which is not essential to good trickery. The Milsted

ll3ad a stranger who wcs c,ming amongst them with the highest educational credentials and they believed that very shortly he would leave his impress upon the youth of that neighbourhood. They hoped his connection with that school and with the Education Committee would , be a long and happy one. (Applause). Mr Richardson also taid a tribute to the work of Miss Bee and Miss Pugh in connection with Holy Trinity infants and Sankey Bridges (infants) Council schools. Continuing, he urged the pressing necessity of the child problem as regarded not only this country but all the nations of the earth. The child was the keystone of the arch of our imperial greatness, the pin in the wheel of the car of imperial progress, and he was convinced that unless they took care of the child, not only in infancy but in those formative years which in-raedia'ely followed, before they lauached it on the sea of life, the future of the race would be black indeed. Our neighbours across the sea—and be hoped we would alwars be able to call them our friends —the German nation, had undoubtedly solved or were in the process of solving many of the problems that confronted us as educationalists. In many respects they were far in advan-:e of our educational system. Let us not be too proud and arrogant to sit at their feet and learn something from them as a nation. With the future of the child was the future of the nation and with the future of the nation was the future of the world. (Applmee,) Mr. Richardson concluded by bcar!na- te;titnony to the dev3ted puhlic Aerk of Councillor R Councillor nonnti>, in the course of an able address, 7aid those buildings marked a distinct advance, in their sin-not re, npon anything ths Warrington Education Authority already possessed. (Hear, hear.) That part of the town bad not been specially favoared by muni- cipal cogoisance up to the present time. (Hear, hear.) Perhaps he might be forgiven if he referred to the fact that they had something in the wore of an apology for recreationkround oil the right—(l.ughter)—while more favoured parrs of the her mg!) had something which might definitely be called a recreation ground for the

people. He hoped that now they had got those schools which were an object lesson of what municipalities could and ought to do, they would insist upon their fair share of recognition in other direc- tions. (Applause.) Councillor Roberts next paid a compliment to the architect and builders, and said the conditions under which education would be carried on at that school would make it a source of pleasure to the teacher and of profit and enjoyment to the child. He emphasised the fact that the school was the property of the ratepayers and that, in seeking to carry out their responsibilities, they shonld see that they got value for their money in every respect. He pleided for a spirit of cordial co-operation between the parents and the teachers and said any suggestions which were advanced in a friendly spirit woula be appreciated by the staff. Passing on to the larger question of education. Councillor Roberts drew attention to the early age at which many of the children left school. exemptions being obtainable at the age of 13. Of the 2,000 children who annually left the schools, only 20 per cent had reached their fourteenth • year and passed the seventh standard. There were strongly diversified views on the question but he telt it would be very greatly to the interests of the children if the percentage could be reversed and 80 per cent, of the children kept at school until they were fourteen years of age and bad passed the seventh standard. (Hear, hear). The children who were exempted at the age of thirteen were very often the

CHILDREN OF THE VERY POOR and the reason given for taking them from school was that their earnings would be a big factor in the family income. Perhaps for immediate materiel purposes, there was a strong argument in favour of exemption in those cases. He would be the last man to deny assistance, especially of that kind, to any family that was a bit below par in its material conditions but, on the other hand, the Education Authority was concerned primarily and finally with the interests of the child and not so much with the interests of the pareats. Prior to the year 1900 a boy or girl could not leave school under 14 years of age without passing an examination which would qualify the child for a labour certificate. He could not tell for what reason, and therefore he did not want to sit in judgment upon those who altered those duaditions in the year 1900 and instead of rFquiring an educational qualification to enable the child to leave school before attaining the age of fourteen insisted only upon an attendance qualification. Apart from the fact that it was much easier to make attendances than to acquire knowledge, the proportion of attendances insisted upon was in Itself so much below the possible maximum as to be a source of very great weakness and

danger. Assuming the ordinary school life of a child was from five to thirteen years of age, it would be possible for him to make 3,360 attend- ances. In order to secure exemption, however, the committee insisted upon only 350 attendances per annum for five years, or 1,750 gross attendances. They were therefore to some extent offering a

PREMIUM FOR INCOMPLETE ATTENDANCES and children were allowed to leave school at an age when they would be for better employed in fitting them- selves educationally for life's battle. Of the children who had been exempted at the age of thirteen, twenty- three had]gone to work on reaching the second standard, 1f:0 the third standard. 511 the fourth standard, 1,332 the fifth standard, 2,277 the sixth standard, and 2,447 the seventh standard. There had for some considerable time been a strong outcry against the expendi- ture on our elementary educational system. If did not require a very great amount of ability, in view of the disclosures he had made, to realize that they might build excellent schools, equip them with the best material, and staff them with men and women of the highest Efficiency, but if the children were taken away to the extent of 80 per cent, before they reached the age of fourteen or had acquired Seveuth etandard knowledge, was there not at once a large explanation of the fact that a great deal of their money was being wasted, when it ought to be applied in the interests of the children ? (Hear, hear.) What earthly chance had those children in competition with the better advan- taged and better educated children who were allowed to remain at school for the full time ? The children who left school so early usually went to fill situations which were absolutely casual. They went te be errand boys, messengers, and domestic drudges, and had no chance of apprenticeships or of introduction to large concerns where there were prospects of advancement. He thought he was justified in suggesting that the Education Committee should reconsider the whole question of exemption, and make the conditions more strict. (Hear, hear.) Finally Councillor Roberts pleaded for a revival of the spirit of selt,acrifice on the part of parents, which had been the glory of our nation, and which had brought out from; amongst us so many men and women who had been a crsdit to all those with whom they had been associated. (Applause). Alderman BENNETT moved a vote of thanks to Coun- cillor Roberts who, he said, was an ideal chairman of an Education Committee. He recalled the fact that years ago when Councillor Roberts was enjoying a holiday in Germany he sent him (the speaker) a must I intere,ting letter in which he pointed out how, in many respects, the ImuLicipalities of Germany were miles ahead of the municipalities of this country. He (the speaker) read that letter with a certain amount of scepticism, because John Bull was apt to think he knew everything and that no other country was comparable with his own in any sense, and he wondered whether Councillor Roberts had not perhaps over-painted the picture. Two years ago he Alderman Bennett) went to Germany and found " the half had not been told him," and that even Councillor Roberts's glowing account had not over-stated the case in any degree. He came back, like Councillor Roberts, inspired with a new desire to apply German knowledge, skill and science to the problems with which they had to deal in Warrington. It was folly not to take advantage of the lessons we might learn from other nations, and in regard to education in particular we might learn a great deal from Germany. If we did not learn the I lessons Germany had to teach us, he was inclined to:think that in the near future she would teach us in a way that would not be at all pleasant. Having expressed special pride in the fact that Warrington was the pioneer in the introduction of shower baths in schools, the Alderman said that apart from the fact that the school was somewhat smothered in smoke on one side and in smells on the other, and that Sankey brook flowed past its eastern boundary, it was a very admir- able school. If the children were not able to take advantage of the opportunities afforded them, he was sorry for the children. (Applause). Councillor BELLIAN seconded and expressed the opinion that Councillor Robert's speech was worthy of publication throughout the country. In years to come Councillor Roberts would be able to look back with pride upon having opened schools which had made educational history in Warrington. (Applause). The vote was heartily passed. Mr A J JOLLEY moved a vote of thanks to the Chair- man and commended the high tone of his address. In the work of education it was highly importent not only to have fine ideals but, as far as possible, to make their actions square with their ideals. Since the Education Committee came into existence nearly ten years ago It had to undertake the evolution of a new system out of the existing one. Transition processes were often painful, and in Warrington that process was by no means complete. He believed, however, that in comparison with some other places, the process, so far as it had gone, had been effected with as little friction as possible. Throughout there had been cordial co-operation between the local anthority and the school managers in furthering educational progress, and they could congratulate themselves upon the spirit of moderation and goodwill which had prevailed. Mr. BROMLEY seconded andthe votewas heartily passed. At the invitation of Mr. Richardson, the visitors then Partook of afternoon tea. PRESENTATION TO MISS BEE.

In the evening a presentation was made by the parents of past and present scholars to Miss Bee, the late head mistress of the Trinity Infant school, and present head mistress of the girls' department of the Evelyn-street Council school. Mrs J m MURRAY said the parents of the past and present scholars of the Trinity Infants' school were desirous of showing their appreciation and esteem of all that Miss Bee had done during her long career at the Trinity school for their children and she (Mrs. Murray) was very pleased, at their request, to make the presentation and to assure Miss Bee that her vv,,rk in the school was thoroughly appreciated by the parents and the little present was only a slight indication of the regard they felt for her. She asked Miss Bee to accept from them a beautiful electro-plated plant pot stand. .

Miss BE said she coul4 not find words to thank the parents. She bad tried to do her best and would con- tinue in her new sphere to do her best for their children. ( A pplause.) Mr J M Murray addressed a few words to the parents inviting them to take a practical interest in the schools and not to hesitate to see the teachers and seek their advice as to the welfare of their children.

div.head: WATER POLO.
div.p: WATER POLO.
WARRINGTON v, WIDNES.

There was a good attendance in the Corporation Baths on Thursday evening when, in connection with the third division of the Liverpool and District Water ' Polo League, Warrington met Widnes. Prior to the match taking place the 50 yards club handicap was , decided, the winners being: i, L Graham; 2, H Sisson; 3, R Pepper. The squadron race was a very keen one and the last two men, Roberts (Warrington) and J Pearce entered the water practically on level terms. The local soon got a lead and on the second length swam in fine style to win by two yards. In the polo match the teams were evenly matched and in the first half each goal was tested in turn, the shots from both sides being successive and rapid. Both custodians played well and kept their goals intact, and the interval arrived with a blank score. Shortly after the resumption of play the locals soon assumed the aggressive, and the forwards worked to the opposite goal in fine style. Inca received and delivered quickly, and sent the leather right through. The Warrington players kept up their brilliant play, and on many occasions the ball was sent only inches wide. The Widnes defence were having a warm time, but one of the visitors secured the ball and sent to Pearce, who with only the goal keeper to beat, equalised the scores. This proved to be the last score, and after a few minutes more of good tackling and shooting, the game finished with the result :—War- rington, 1 ; Widnes, 1,

After lunch the guests proceeded by special tram car to the new school. The interest which the opening ceremony had aroused in the neighbourhood was evident from the large and representative gathering. The members of the Committee and officials having taken up their position at the main entrance Mr Dolan, on behalf of the architect and contractors, presented Councillor Roberts with a gold key. Councillor ROBERTS, in accepting the gift, said he would keep it as a memento ot the event, and he believed his wife and children after him would prize it as he would. (Applause). Councillor ROBERTS then unlocked the door and formally declared the school open. The company then assembled in the boys' central hall where some interesting speeches were delivered. Mr J E RICHARDSON (chairman of managers), who presided, submitted some particulars of the accommoda- tion, equipment and cost of the new building which, he said, was replete with all that educational experts con- sidered necesssary for the successful conduct of a new Council school,without elaborate lavishness or anything bordering upon that excessive expenditure which tney sometimes heard about. Alluding to the intention to teach domestic science, Mr Richardson said it was particularly appropriate that attention should be given to that subject in the centre of a large artisan population. If there was one thing he was impressed with as he grew older, it was the great want. In certain classes of society, of know- ledge of the necessities of home lire. (Hear, hear.) In undertaking such an interesting departure, the Educe- Coo Committee was doing a work for which the town might indeed be grateful. Another knovation was the provision of douche baths, the plans for which were, he understood, the first to be passed by the Local Govern- ment Board for any school in the United Kingdom. (Applause.) In view of the increasing regard for cleanliness and the public health, the baths should prove one of the most valuable accessories of the school. He believed it was only a matter of time before a swimming bath would also be provided. With regard to the staff- ing of the school, in Mr Appleton, the headmaster, they

div.head: LOCAL WEDDING. _ Cliffe—Johnson.
div.p: LOCAL WEDDING. _ Cliffe—Johnson.

----• A pretty and interesting wedding took place at St John's Presbyterian Church on Thursday afternoon when Mr. Ernest Foster CHI-Fe (of the Borough Treasurer's department), only son of Mr. and Mrs. Peter Cliffs, of 15, Cawdor-street, Stockton Heath, was married to Miss Amy Maud Johnson, youngest daughter of Mr and Mrs J W Johnson, of Bella Vista, Grappenhall-road, Stockton Heath. The Rev Wm. Reid was the officiating minister. The hymn " The voice that breathed o'er Eden " was sung by the cors.segation and appropriate selections were ably rendered by the organist (Mr. Albert Trovr) prior to the service. The bridal party left the church to the strains of%Mendelssohn's Wedding March. The bride, who was given away by , her father, was charmingly attired in ivory satin ' mousseline with bodice and underdress of silk lace. She also wore a tulle veil surmounted with orange blossom and carried a shocser bouquet of whiie heather, roses and lilies. The bridesmaids were Miss Frances Johnson (sister of the bride) and Miss Cissie Pearson who wore ;pretty Wedgewood blue silk dresses trimmed with Irish lace, and large tegal hats trimmed with pink roses and forget-me-nots. Their shower bouquets consisted of sweet peas and carnations, the gifts of the bridegroom. Mr. Douglas Travis discharged the duties of best man. The reception was held in a marquee at Bella Vista, and between thirty and forty guests sat down to breakfast. Later the happy couple left for London and Bournemouth, the bride travelling in a tailor-made costume of grey whin cord, with black tegal hat trimmed with French rosos. The presents were numerous and handsome, including one fi orn the Corporation officials.

Plans may be seen and Bills of Quantities obtained from the Architect (Mr. Thomas Chadwick, 16, Princess Street, Manchester).
